The diameter is 7 parts, which is 140 m.
Be careful here, because 140 m is the diameter and the question asks for the radius. Halve it. The radius is 70 m.

notes.A: The halving has been done once too often. The diameter is 140 m, and half of that is the radius.
notes.B: 140 m is the diameter, so most of the work is done. The radius is half of the diameter.
notes.C: Yes! The diameter is 140 m, so the radius is 70 m.
notes.D: This is just half of the circumference. To get across the circle, divide 440 by 22 and multiply by 7, and then halve that for the radius.

hints: This question works backwards. You know the distance round the park and must find the distance straight across it.
The circumference is 22/7 times the diameter. So for every 22 m round the circle there are 7 m across it. Start by dividing 176 by 22.
A similar example: the circumference of a circular pond is 132 m. Dividing, 132 ÷ 22 = 6. The diameter is 6 × 7 = 42 m.

steps.text: The circumference is 22/7 times the diameter. So the circumference is 22 equal parts when the diameter is 7 of the same parts.
Find one part by dividing the circumference by 22.
The diameter is 7 of these parts.
The diameter of the park is 56 m.

notes.A: This is half of the circumference. To get the diameter, divide 176 by 22 and then multiply by 7.
notes.B: 28 m is the radius of the park. The question asks for the diameter, which is twice as long.
notes.C: This is a quarter of the circumference. To get the diameter, divide 176 by 22 and then multiply by 7.

hints: This question is about the area of a circle, the space inside it. The area is found from the radius and π.
The area of a circle is π times the radius times the radius. Start by working out 7 × 7.
A similar example: a circle has radius 14 cm. First 14 × 14 = 196. The area is 22/7 × 196. Since 196 ÷ 7 = 28, this is 22 × 28 = 616 cm².

steps.text: The area of a circle is π times the radius times the radius. First multiply the radius by itself.
Now multiply 49 by 22/7. Divide 49 by 7 first, which gives 7.
Then multiply 22 by 7. The area is 154 cm².

notes.B: 44 is the circumference, the distance round the circle. For the area, multiply π by the radius and then by the radius again.
notes.C: This is double the area. The area is π times the radius times the radius, with no extra 2.
notes.D: This multiplies π by the radius only once. For the area the radius is used twice, so it is 22/7 × 7 × 7.

hints: This question is about the area of a circle. The area is found from the radius, so look carefully at which length you have been given.
You are given the diameter, 14 cm. Halve it to find the radius first. Then the area is π times the radius times the radius.
A similar example: a circle has diameter 42 cm. The radius is 42 ÷ 2 = 21 cm. Then 21 × 21 = 441. The area is 22/7 × 441. Since 441 ÷ 7 = 63, this is 22 × 63 = 1386 cm².

steps.text: The area uses the radius, and we are given the diameter. Halve the diameter to find the radius.
Multiply the radius by itself.
Now multiply 49 by 22/7. Since 49 ÷ 7 = 7, this is 22 × 7.
The area is 154 cm².

notes.A: This is double the area. Halve the diameter to get a radius of 7 cm, and then work out 22/7 × 7 × 7.
notes.B: 44 is the circumference, the distance round the circle. For the area, multiply π by the radius and then by the radius again.
notes.C: Yes! The radius is 7 cm, and 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154.
notes.D: This uses 14 cm as the radius. 14 cm is the diameter, so halve it first to get the radius.

hints: This is a two-part question. One lap of a circular track is the circumference of the circle, and the runner goes round more than once.
Find one lap first. The circumference is π times the diameter, and the diameter is 2 × 35 = 70 m. After that, remember there are 3 laps.
A similar example: a circular track has radius 14 m and a runner does 2 laps. The diameter is 28 m, so one lap is 22/7 × 28 = 88 m. Two laps are 2 × 88 = 176 m.

steps.text: One lap is the circumference. First double the radius to get the diameter.
The circumference is 22/7 times the diameter. Since 70 ÷ 7 = 10, one lap is 22 × 10 = 220 m.
The runner does 3 laps, so multiply by 3. The runner goes 660 m.

notes.A: Yes! One lap is 220 m, and 3 laps are 3 × 220 = 660 m.
notes.B: This multiplies π by the radius, which is only half a lap. One lap is 22/7 × 70, and there are 3 laps.
notes.C: 220 m is one lap, so the first part is done well. The runner goes round 3 times.
notes.D: 440 m is two laps. The runner goes round 3 times, so multiply one lap of 220 m by 3.

hints: This question is about the names of the parts of a circle. Think about what fraction of the circle each part is.
A diameter passes through the centre and cuts the circle into two equal parts, so each part is half of the circle. Think of the word that means half a circle.

A similar example: two diameters that cross at right angles cut a circle into four equal parts. Each part is a quarter of the circle, so it is called a quarter circle. One diameter makes only two parts, so here each part is a half.

steps.text: A diameter passes through the centre of the circle, so the two parts it makes are equal.
Each part is exactly half of the circle. The word semi means half.
So each of the two equal parts is called a semicircle.

notes.A: A quarter circle is one of four equal parts. One diameter makes only two equal parts, so each is a half.
notes.B: A sector is a slice shaped like a piece of pizza, between two radii. Half of a circle has its own special name.
notes.C: Yes! Semi means half, and each part is half of the circle.
notes.D: An arc is only a piece of the curved edge. Here each part is the whole half of the circle.

hints: This question is about a special name for a set of circles. Look closely at what the circles share and what is different about them.
Picture the rings on a target board, or the ripples when a stone drops into a pond. The rings all have the same middle point but different sizes. Think of the word that means sharing a centre.

A similar example: circles that have the same radius are exactly the same size, so they are called equal or congruent circles. Here it is the other way round, because the sizes are different and the centre is the same.

steps.text: These circles have different radii, so they are different sizes. They cannot be equal or congruent.
They all share one centre, like the rings on a target board.
Circles with the same centre but different radii are called concentric circles.

notes.A: Yes! Concentric means sharing the same centre, like the rings on a target board.
notes.B: Tangent circles touch each other at just one point, and their centres are in different places. These circles share one centre.
notes.C: Equal circles have the same radius. These circles have different radii, so look for the name that is about the shared centre.
notes.D: Congruent circles are exactly the same size. These circles have different radii, so look for the name that is about the shared centre.

hints: This question works backwards. You know the area of the circle and must find the radius. Think about how the area is made from the radius.
The area is 22/7 times the radius times the radius. Undo the 22/7 first by dividing 616 by 22 and then multiplying by 7. That gives the radius times itself.
A similar example: the area of a circle is 1386 cm². Dividing, 1386 ÷ 22 = 63, and 63 × 7 = 441. So the radius times itself is 441. Since 21 × 21 = 441, the radius is 21 cm.

steps.text: The area is 22/7 times the radius times the radius. Undo the 22/7 by dividing by 22 and then multiplying by 7.
Divide the area by 22.
Multiply by 7. This is the radius times itself.
Do not stop at 196. We need the number that gives 196 when it is multiplied by itself. It is between 10 and 20, because 10 × 10 = 100 and 20 × 20 = 400.
Trying 14 gives 14 × 14 = 196. The radius is 14 cm.

notes.B: 28 is what you get from 616 ÷ 22. You still need to multiply by 7, and then find the number that multiplies by itself to give that result.
notes.C: A radius of 7 cm gives an area of 154 cm², which is too small. Find the number that multiplies by itself to give 196.
notes.D: 196 is the radius times itself, so you are nearly there. Find the number that gives 196 when it is multiplied by itself.

hints: This question asks you to find two measurements of the same circle and compare the numbers. One is the distance round it and the other is the space inside it.
Work out both. The circumference is π times the diameter, and the diameter is 14 cm. The area is π times the radius times the radius. Then see which number is bigger.
A similar example: for a circle with radius 14 cm, the circumference is 22/7 × 28 = 88 and the area is 22/7 × 14 × 14 = 616. As numbers, 616 is larger than 88, so the area is the larger number.

steps.text: The diameter is 2 × 7 = 14 cm. The circumference is 22/7 times the diameter, which is 44.
The area is 22/7 times the radius times the radius, which is 154.
Looking only at the numbers, 154 is greater than 44. So the area is larger, since 154 > 44.

notes.A: The two numbers here are right, but look at them again. 154 is the bigger number, and 154 is the area.
notes.B: Work out both numbers. The circumference is 22/7 × 14 and the area is 22/7 × 7 × 7, and they do not come out the same.
notes.C: Yes! The area is 154 and the circumference is 44, and 154 is the greater number.
notes.D: It is true that one is measured in cm and the other in cm². The question asks only about the numbers, and those can be compared.

hints: This question is about counting the lines you could draw in a circle. A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle, and a diameter goes right across through the centre.
Think about how many points there are on the circle that a radius could reach. Then think about how many directions a line through the centre could take.

A similar example: how many points are there on a circle? Between any two points on the curve you can always mark another one, so the count never ends. We say a circle has infinite points. Use the same idea for the lines drawn from the centre and through the centre.

steps.text: A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle. There is no end to the points on a circle, so there is no end to the radii.
A diameter is a straight line through the centre. It can point in any direction, and there is no end to the directions, so there is no end to the diameters.
So a circle can have infinite radii, infinite diameters.

notes.A: We often draw just one of each, but many more can be drawn. Every point on the circle can be joined to the centre.
notes.B: The part about the radii is right. Diameters can also be drawn in every direction through the centre, not just up-and-down and side-to-side.
notes.C: One diameter does contain two radii, but it is not the only diameter. Lines through the centre can be drawn in every direction.
notes.D: Yes! There is no end to the radii or to the diameters you could draw in a circle.

hints: This question is about the perimeter of a semicircle, the distance all the way round its edge. Look at the shape carefully, because the edge has more than one part.
A semicircle has a curved edge and a straight edge. Start with the curved edge, which is half of the circumference of the whole circle. Then think about the straight edge.

A similar example: a semicircle has diameter 42 cm. The whole circumference would be 22/7 × 42 = 132 cm, so the curved edge is 132 ÷ 2 = 66 cm. The straight edge is the diameter, 42 cm. The perimeter is 66 + 42 = 108 cm.

steps.text: The circumference of the whole circle is 22/7 times the diameter.
The curved edge of the semicircle is half of this.
The perimeter goes all the way round, so it also includes the straight edge. The straight edge is the diameter, 14 cm.
Add the curved edge and the straight edge. The perimeter is 36 cm.

notes.A: Yes! The curved edge is 22 cm and the straight edge is 14 cm, which makes 36 cm.
notes.B: 22 cm is the curved edge only. The perimeter goes all the way round, so the straight edge of 14 cm must be added.
notes.C: 44 cm is the circumference of the whole circle. A semicircle has half of that as its curved edge, and the straight edge as well.
notes.D: This adds the diameter to the whole circumference. Only half of the circumference is on a semicircle, so use 22 cm for the curved edge.

hints: This is a counting question. A game of chess needs two players, so think about how many different pairs of players can be made.
List every pair of players in order, starting with A and B, then A and C, and so on, taking care not to list any pair twice. Then remember how many games each pair plays.

Here is a similar one: P, Q and R play, and each player plays three games with every other player. The pairs are P and Q, P and R, and Q and R, which is 3 pairs. Each pair plays 3 games, so 3 × 3 = 9 games are played.

steps.text: Each game is played by a pair of players, so first count the different pairs. Pairs with A: A and B, A and C, A and D. That is 3 pairs.
New pairs with B: B and C, B and D. That is 2 more. B and A is not new, because it is the same pair as A and B.
The last new pair is C and D. Altogether there are 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 pairs.
Each pair played two games, and 6 × 2 = 12. So 12 games were played altogether.

notes.A: Yes! There are 6 different pairs of players, and each pair played 2 games, so 6 × 2 = 12.
notes.B: 8 is 4 × 2, which gives each player only two games in all. Each player plays two games with every one of the other three, so count the pairs of players first.
notes.C: 16 is 4 × 4, as if each player had four others to play. Each player has only three others, and a game between two players should be counted once.
notes.D: 14 is close. List the pairs slowly, A and B, A and C, A and D, then the new ones with B and with C, and give each pair two games.

hints: This is a counting question about joining points in pairs. Every line segment joins two of the points, so think about how the number of segments grows as points are added.
Build up slowly. With 2 points there is 1 segment. A 3rd point can be joined to both of the earlier points, so it adds 2 more. Keep adding points until the total reaches 15.

A similar example: suppose the most segments that can be drawn is 28. The 2nd point adds 1 segment, the 3rd adds 2, and so on. Adding 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 gives 28, and the point that adds 7 segments is the 8th. So there are 8 points.

steps.text: With 2 points there is 1 line segment. Each new point can be joined to every point already there.
The 3rd point adds 2 segments, making 3. The 4th point adds 3 segments, making 6.
The 5th point adds 4 segments, making 10. The 6th point adds 5 segments, making 15.
The total reaches 15 with the 6th point. So there were 6 points on the circle.

notes.A: With 4 points you can draw only 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 segments. More points are needed to reach 15.
notes.B: Yes! With 6 points you can draw 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15 segments.
notes.C: With 5 points you can draw 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 segments. One more point is needed to reach 15.
notes.D: With 7 points you could draw 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21 segments, which is more than 15.

hints: This is a counting question about joining points in pairs. Every chord joins two of the points, so you need to count the pairs without counting any chord twice.
Name the points A, B, C, D and E. Start at A and count the chords it makes with the other points. Then move to B and count only the chords that are new.

A similar example: 4 points P, Q, R and S are marked on a circle. P joins to Q, R and S, which is 3 chords. Q joins to R and S, which is 2 new chords. R joins to S, which is 1 new chord. That makes 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 chords.

steps.text: Name the points A, B, C, D and E. From A we can draw chords to B, C, D and E. That is 4 chords.
From B the chord to A is already drawn, so only the chords to C, D and E are new. That is 3 more.
From C there are 2 new chords, to D and E. From D there is 1 new chord, to E. From E every chord is already drawn.
Add them up. So 10 chords can be drawn.

notes.A: Try naming the points A to E and counting from each one in turn: 4 chords from A, then 3 new ones from B, then 2, then 1.
notes.B: 5 chords only join each point to the one next to it. Points that are not next to each other can be joined as well.
notes.C: This counts 4 chords from each of the 5 points, so every chord is counted twice. The chord from A to B is the same as the chord from B to A.
notes.D: Yes! Counting each chord once gives 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10.

hints: This question multiplies and divides by 10 and 1000. Multiplying moves the digits to the left, and dividing moves them to the right.
Work from left to right. First multiply 0.045 by 1000, which moves every digit three places to the left. Then divide that result by 10.
A similar example: 0.008 × 1000 ÷ 10. Multiplying by 1000 moves the digits three places to the left, giving 8. Dividing by 10 moves them one place to the right, giving 0.8.

steps.text: Multiply by 1000 first. Every digit moves three places to the left.
Now divide by 10. Every digit moves one place to the right.
The answer is 4.5.

notes.A: 45 is 0.045 × 1000, so the first part is done well. That result still has to be divided by 10.
notes.C: 0.45 has its digits one place too far to the right. Multiplying by 1000 moves the digits three places left before the one move to the right.
notes.D: 450 comes from multiplying by 10 at the end. The last sign is a division, so the number gets smaller after 0.045 × 1000.

hints: The word difference tells you to subtract. With decimals, the key is to line up the decimal points first.
The two numbers do not have the same number of decimal places. Write 7.9 as 7.90, and then take it away from 9.07.
A similar example: find the difference between 8.03 and 5.6. Write 5.6 as 5.60. Then 8.03 − 5.60 = 2.43.

steps.text: To find the difference, subtract the smaller number from the bigger one. Write 7.9 as 7.90 so both numbers have two decimal places.
Subtract with the decimal points lined up. The 0 tenths cannot give 9 tenths, so borrow from the ones.
Check by adding back: 7.90 + 1.17 = 9.07. The difference is 1.17.

notes.A: Check by adding back. 7.9 + 2.02 = 9.92, which is more than 9.07. Line up the decimal points and write 7.9 as 7.90.
notes.C: Check by adding back. 7.9 + 1.02 = 8.92, which is less than 9.07. Write 7.9 as 7.90 and subtract again.
notes.D: Check by adding back. 7.9 + 1.07 = 8.97, which is a little less than 9.07. Write 7.9 as 7.90 and watch the borrowing.

hints: This question has two parts. First compare the decimals to find the smallest and the greatest, and then add those two together.
The numbers all use the digits 2 and 3, but in different places. Write each one with four decimal places so that they are easy to compare.
A similar example: for 0.5, 0.05, 5.5 and 0.005, the smallest is 0.005 and the greatest is 5.5. Their sum is 5.500 + 0.005 = 5.505.

steps.text: Write every number with four decimal places: 0.0230, 0.2300, 0.0023 and 2.3000.
The greatest is 2.3, the only one with a whole number part. The smallest is 0.0023, where the first digit that is not zero comes latest.
Add the smallest and the greatest with the decimal points lined up.
The sum is 2.3023.

notes.A: This adds 0.23 and 0.0023. The greatest number is 2.3, because it is the only one with a whole number part.
notes.B: The right two numbers may have been chosen, but the digits have slipped out of place. Write 2.3 as 2.3000 and add 0.0023 underneath it.
notes.C: Yes! The smallest is 0.0023 and the greatest is 2.3, and together they make 2.3023.
notes.D: This adds the smallest number to itself. The question asks for the smallest and the greatest added together.

hints: This is a question about change. The cashier returns the difference between the money given and the cost of the groceries.
You need Rs. 50 take away Rs. 39.46. One easy way is to count up from 39.46. Start by finding how much takes you to Rs. 40.
A similar example: a bill is Rs. 27.35 and it is paid with Rs. 40. From 27.35 to 28 is 0.65. From 28 to 40 is 12. So the change is 12 + 0.65 = Rs. 12.65.

steps.text: The change is Rs. 50 take away Rs. 39.46. Count up from 39.46 to 50.
From 39.46 up to 40 is 0.54.
From 40 up to 50 is 10.
Add the two jumps. The cashier needs to return Rs. 10.54.

notes.A: Check by adding back. 39.46 + 11.44 = 50.90, which is more than Rs. 50. Remember that 39.46 is already nearly 40.
notes.B: Check the paise. From 39.46 to 40 is 0.54, not 0.44, and then there is Rs. 10 more to reach 50.
notes.C: Yes! 39.46 + 10.54 = 50, so the change is Rs. 10.54.
notes.D: Check by adding back. 39.46 + 11.56 = 51.02, which is more than Rs. 50. Count up from 39.46 to 40 and then to 50.

hints: This question asks how far apart two decimals are. To find how far apart two numbers are, subtract the smaller from the bigger.
The student should have written 9.7 but wrote 0.97. Write 9.7 as 9.70 so both numbers have two decimal places, and line up the decimal points.
A similar example: instead of writing 6.4, a student wrote 0.64. Write 6.4 as 6.40. Then 6.40 − 0.64 = 5.76, so the student's number was 5.76 too small.

steps.text: We need the difference between the number he should have written, 9.7, and the number he wrote, 0.97.
Write 9.7 as 9.70 so that the decimal points line up, and subtract.
Check by adding back: 0.97 + 8.73 = 9.70. His number was off by 8.73.

notes.B: The digits are right, but the decimal point has moved. 9.7 is more than 9 and 0.97 is less than 1, so the difference must be more than 8.
notes.C: The digits are right, but the decimal point has moved. Both numbers are less than 10, so their difference cannot be as big as 87.3.
notes.D: This is far too small. 9.7 is more than 9 and 0.97 is less than 1, so they are more than 8 apart. Subtract 0.97 from 9.70.

hints: This question is about comparing decimals. Decimals are compared one place at a time, starting from the left, so both numbers should have the same number of places.
Write 2.005 as 2.0050 so that it has four decimal places, like 2.00d5. The two numbers match until the thousandths place, where one has d and the other has 5. Test the digits there.

A similar example: for how many digits d is 3.0d2 > 3.07? Write 3.07 as 3.070. If d is 8 or 9 the number is bigger. If d is 7 we get 3.072, which is also bigger than 3.070. Any smaller digit makes it smaller. So there are 3 values: 7, 8 and 9.

steps.text: Write 2.005 as 2.0050 so that both numbers have four decimal places.
Compare 2.00d5 with 2.0050 from the left. The ones, tenths and hundredths match. In the thousandths place we compare d with 5.
If d is 6, 7, 8 or 9, then d is more than 5, so 2.00d5 is greater. That is 4 values.
Do not forget d = 5. Then the number is 2.0055, and 2.0055 is greater than 2.0050 because of its last digit. If d is 4 or less, the number is smaller.
So d can be 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9. That is 5 values.

notes.A: You found 6, 7, 8 and 9. There is one more: when d is 5 the number is 2.0055, which is greater than 2.0050.
notes.B: Yes! The values 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 all work, and that makes 5 values.
notes.C: Check d = 4. It gives 2.0045, which is less than 2.0050, so 4 does not count. Only 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 work.
notes.D: Test the small digits. With d = 4 or less, the number is at most 2.0045, which is less than 2.0050. Only the digits from 5 upwards work.

hints: This question is about comparing decimals. A decimal is not smaller just because it has fewer digits, so look at the place where each 7 sits.
Write every number with three decimal places so that they are easy to compare. Then look at the whole number part first, then the tenths, then the hundredths.
A similar example: for 0.5, 0.05, 5.05 and 0.005, write them as 0.500, 0.050, 5.050 and 0.005. These are 500, 50, 5050 and 5 thousandths. The smallest is 5 thousandths, which is 0.005.

steps.text: Write each number with three decimal places: 0.007, 0.070, 7.070 and 0.700.
7.07 has 7 ones, so it is the biggest. The others are 7 thousandths, 70 thousandths and 700 thousandths.
7 thousandths is the least. The smallest decimal fraction is 0.007.

notes.A: Yes! In 0.007 the 7 is in the thousandths place, the smallest place of all four numbers.
notes.B: 0.07 is small, but its 7 is in the hundredths place. Look for a number where the 7 is even further to the right.
notes.C: 7.07 has 7 whole ones, so it is the biggest of the four. The smallest will have zeros in the ones, tenths and hundredths places.
notes.D: 0.70 has 7 tenths. Look for a number where the 7 sits in a smaller place than the tenths.

hints: This question is about place value in a decimal. After the decimal point, the places are tenths, hundredths and thousandths, in that order.
Find the digit 5 in 7.256 and count how many places it is after the decimal point. The name of that place tells you its value.
A similar example: in 8.371, the digit 3 is the first digit after the decimal point. That is the tenths place, so the place value of 3 is 3 tenths, written 3/10.

steps.text: In 7.256, the 7 is in the ones place. The digits after the decimal point are 2, 5 and 6.
The first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths and the third is thousandths. So 2 is in the tenths place and 5 is in the hundredths place.
The digit 5 stands for 5 hundredths. Its place value is 5/100.

notes.A: 50 would mean the 5 is in the tens place, to the left of the decimal point. Here the 5 comes after the decimal point.
notes.B: The tenths place is the first one after the decimal point, and that holds the 2. The 5 is one place further to the right.
notes.C: Yes! The 5 is the second digit after the decimal point, so it is 5 hundredths.
notes.D: The thousandths place is the third one after the decimal point, and that holds the 6. The 5 is one place before it.

hints: This question changes a mixed number into a decimal. The whole number part stays as it is, and only the fraction part needs changing.
Keep the 9 as the whole number part. To change 1/8 into a decimal, turn it into a fraction out of 1000. Think about what 8 must be multiplied by to make 1000.
A similar example: change 6 3/8 into a decimal. Since 8 × 125 = 1000, multiply top and bottom by 125 to get 3/8 = 375/1000 = 0.375. So 6 3/8 = 6.375.

steps.text: The whole number part, 9, stays the same. We only need to change 1/8 into a decimal.
Since 8 × 125 = 1000, multiply the top and the bottom of 1/8 by 125.
125 thousandths is written 0.125.
Put the whole number and the decimal part together. 9 1/8 as a decimal is 9.125.

notes.A: This just writes the digits 1 and 8 after the decimal point. The fraction 1/8 means 1 divided by 8, which is 0.125.
notes.B: The digits are right, but the decimal point has moved. The whole number part is 9, so the decimal must begin with 9 and then the point.
notes.D: The whole number part is right, but check the fraction part. 1/8 is 125 thousandths, which is 0.125.

hints: This question divides a decimal by 1 followed by zeros. Dividing like this makes the number smaller, and the digits move to the right.
Count the zeros in 10000. That tells you how many places each digit moves to the right. Fill any empty places with zeros.
A similar example: 36.4 ÷ 1000. There are 3 zeros in 1000, so the digits move 3 places to the right: 36.4 becomes 3.64, then 0.364, then 0.0364. So 36.4 ÷ 1000 = 0.0364.

steps.text: 10000 has 4 zeros, so dividing by 10000 is the same as dividing by 10 four times. Each time, the digits move one place to the right.
Dividing by 10 once gives 1.25, and dividing by 10 again gives 0.125.
Dividing by 10 a third time gives 0.0125, and a fourth time gives 0.00125.

notes.A: The digits have moved only 3 places here, which is dividing by 1000. There are 4 zeros in 10000, so move one place more.
notes.B: The digits have moved 5 places here, which is one too many. There are 4 zeros in 10000, so the digits move 4 places.
notes.C: Yes! The digits move 4 places to the right, giving 0.00125.
notes.D: The digits have moved only 2 places here, which is dividing by 100. There are 4 zeros in 10000, so the digits move 4 places.

hints: This is a division that does not come out as a whole number. After the whole number part, the remainder can be shared out too, as tenths.
Find how many whole times 5 goes into 28 and what is left over. Then think of the remainder as tenths and share those by 5 as well.
A similar example: 34 ÷ 5. 5 goes into 34 six times, since 5 × 6 = 30, with 4 left over. The 4 left over is 40 tenths, and 40 tenths ÷ 5 = 8 tenths. So 34 ÷ 5 = 6.8.

steps.text: 5 goes into 28 five whole times, because 5 × 5 = 25. There are 3 left over.
Change the 3 left over into tenths. 3 ones are 30 tenths.
Share the 30 tenths by 5. That gives 6 tenths.
Put the 5 ones and 6 tenths together. So 28 ÷ 5 = 5.6.

notes.A: Check by multiplying. 5.4 × 5 = 27, which is 1 short of 28. Share the remainder of 3 as 30 tenths.
notes.B: Check by multiplying. 5.8 × 5 = 29, which is 1 more than 28. Share the remainder of 3 as 30 tenths.
notes.D: 5 × 6 = 30, which is already more than 28, so the answer must be less than 6. Start with 5 × 5 = 25 and share the remainder.

hints: This is dividing a decimal by a whole number. Divide just as you would with whole numbers, and keep the decimal point in the answer above the one in the question.
Start with the whole number part. Find how many times 4 goes into 11 and what is left over. The left over ones join the 2 tenths.
A similar example: 13.5 ÷ 3. 3 goes into 13 four times, since 3 × 4 = 12, with 1 left over. The 1 one and the 5 tenths make 15 tenths, and 15 tenths ÷ 3 = 5 tenths. So 13.5 ÷ 3 = 4.5.

steps.text: 4 goes into 11 two whole times, because 4 × 2 = 8. There are 3 ones left over.
The 3 ones left over are 30 tenths. With the 2 tenths already there, that makes 32 tenths.
Share the 32 tenths by 4. That gives 8 tenths.
Put the 2 ones and 8 tenths together. So 11.2 ÷ 4 = 2.8.

notes.A: Check by multiplying. 2.6 × 4 = 10.4, which is less than 11.2. After the 2 ones, there are 32 tenths to share by 4.
notes.B: Check by multiplying. 2.4 × 4 = 9.6, which is less than 11.2. After the 2 ones, there are 32 tenths to share by 4.
notes.C: Check by multiplying. 3.2 × 4 = 12.8, which is more than 11.2. 4 goes into 11 only two whole times.

hints: This is dividing by a decimal. It is much easier to divide by a whole number, and you can change the question without changing the answer.
Multiply both numbers by 100 so that 0.04 becomes the whole number 4. The other number must be multiplied by 100 too. Then divide.
A similar example: 1.356 ÷ 0.06. Multiply both numbers by 100 to get 135.6 ÷ 6. Then 120 ÷ 6 = 20 and 15.6 ÷ 6 = 2.6. So the answer is 20 + 2.6 = 22.6.

steps.text: Multiply both numbers by 100 so that we divide by a whole number. The answer does not change. The question becomes 126.4 ÷ 4.
Split 126.4 into 120 and 6.4. First, 120 ÷ 4 = 30.
Add the two parts. So 1.264 ÷ 0.04 = 31.6.

notes.B: The digits are right, but the decimal point has slipped. Check by multiplying: 0.04 × 316 = 12.64, which is ten times too big.
notes.C: The digits are right, but the decimal point has slipped. Dividing by a number as small as 0.04 gives an answer much bigger than 1.264.
notes.D: The digits are right, but the decimal point has slipped. Check by multiplying: 0.04 × 3.16 = 0.1264, which is ten times too small.

hints: This is dividing by a decimal. It is much easier to divide by a whole number, and you can change the question without changing the answer.
Multiply both numbers by 100 so that 0.07 becomes the whole number 7. The other number must be multiplied by 100 too. Then divide.
A similar example: 2.56 ÷ 0.08. Multiply both numbers by 100 to get 256 ÷ 8. Since 8 × 32 = 256, the answer is 32.

steps.text: Multiply both numbers by 100 so that we divide by a whole number. The answer does not change. The question becomes 343 ÷ 7.
7 × 40 = 280. Taking 280 from 343 leaves 63.
63 ÷ 7 = 9. So 7 goes into 343 exactly 40 + 9 times.

notes.B: The digits are right, but the decimal point has slipped. Check by multiplying: 0.07 × 4.9 = 0.343, which is ten times too small.
notes.C: The digits are right, but the decimal point has slipped. Dividing by a number as small as 0.07 gives an answer much bigger than 3.43.
notes.D: The digits are right, but the decimal point has slipped. Check by multiplying: 0.07 × 490 = 34.3, which is ten times too big.

hints: This question divides a decimal by 10. Dividing by 10 makes a number ten times smaller, so think about which way the digits move.
When you divide by 10, every digit moves one place to the right. The 7 ones become 7 tenths. Move the other digits in the same way.
A similar example: 5.08 ÷ 10. Every digit moves one place to the right, so the 5 ones become 5 tenths. That gives 0.508.

steps.text: Dividing by 10 makes the number ten times smaller. Every digit moves one place to the right.
The 7 ones become 7 tenths, the 0 tenths become 0 hundredths, and the 6 hundredths become 6 thousandths.

notes.A: The digits have moved two places here, which is dividing by 100. Dividing by 10 moves them just one place to the right.
notes.B: This is 100 times bigger than 7.06. Dividing makes the number smaller, so the digits move to the right.
notes.C: Yes! Every digit moves one place to the right, giving 0.706.
notes.D: This is 7.06 × 10. Dividing by 10 makes the number smaller, so the digits move to the right, not to the left.

hints: This is a decimal divided by 100. Dividing by 10, 100 or 1000 keeps the same digits and only moves the decimal point.
Count the zeros in 100. Then move the decimal point in 652.7 that many places to the left.
Here is a similar one: 483.9 ÷ 100. There are two zeros in 100, so the point moves two places to the left, and the result is 4.839.

steps.text: 100 has two zeros, so dividing by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the left.
Move the point one place and 652.7 becomes 65.27. Move it one more place and it becomes 6.527.

notes.A: 65.27 is what you get when the point moves only one place, which is dividing by 10. For 100, move it one more place.
notes.B: 0.6527 comes from moving the point three places, which is dividing by 1000. There are only two zeros in 100, so move it two places.
notes.C: 6527 comes from moving the point to the right, which makes the number bigger. Dividing makes it smaller, so move the point to the left.
notes.D: Well done! The point moves two places to the left for the two zeros in 100, which gives 6.527.

hints: This is a decimal divided by 100. The digits stay the same and the decimal point moves to the left.
There are two zeros in 100, so move the point in 3.8 two places to the left. If you run out of digits, fill the empty place with a zero.
Here is a similar one: 5.2 ÷ 100. Moving the point one place gives 0.52, and one more place needs an extra zero, giving 0.052.

steps.text: Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the left, because 100 has two zeros.
Move the point one place and 3.8 becomes 0.38.
Move it one more place. There is no digit left in front of the 3, so a zero fills the gap and 0.38 becomes 0.038.

notes.A: 0.0038 comes from moving the point three places, which is dividing by 1000. For 100, move it only two places.
notes.B: 0.38 is 3.8 divided by 10, with the point moved one place. Dividing by 100 needs one more move to the left.
notes.C: Great work! Two moves to the left, with a zero filling the empty place, give 0.038.
notes.D: 38 comes from moving the point to the right, which multiplies. Dividing makes the number smaller, so move the point to the left.

hints: A fraction is a division waiting to be done. The top number is divided by the bottom number.
Divide 3 by 4. Since 4 does not go into 3, write 3 as 3.00 and begin by dividing 30 tenths by 4.
Here is a similar one: to change 2/5 into a decimal, divide 2 by 5. Write 2 as 2.0. Then 5 goes into 20 tenths exactly 4 times, so 2/5 = 0.4.

steps.text: To change 3/4 into a decimal, divide 3 by 4. Write 3 as 3.00 so there are digits to divide.
4 goes into 30 tenths 7 times, because 4 × 7 = 28. That leaves 2 tenths, which is the same as 20 hundredths.
4 goes into 20 hundredths exactly 5 times, so the digits after the point are 7 and 5.

notes.A: 1.33 comes from dividing 4 by 3, the bottom by the top. Divide the top number, 3, by the bottom number, 4, and the result will be less than 1.
notes.B: 0.34 just places the digits 3 and 4 after a decimal point. A fraction means division, so divide 3 by 4.
notes.C: You got it! 3 divided by 4 is 0.75, which is three quarters.
notes.D: 0.25 is one quarter, 1/4. Three quarters is three times as much, so divide 3 by 4.

hints: A decimal can be written as a fraction over 10, 100 or 1000, depending on how many digits come after the point. Then the fraction is made as simple as it can be.
0.125 has three digits after the point, so write it as 125 over 1000. Then look for a number that divides both 125 and 1000.
Here is a similar one: 0.075 has three digits after the point, so it is 75/1000. Dividing the top and the bottom by 25 gives 3/40, which cannot be made simpler.

steps.text: 0.125 has three digits after the decimal point, so it is 125 thousandths.
Divide the top and the bottom by 25. 125 ÷ 25 = 5 and 1000 ÷ 25 = 40, so the fraction becomes 5/40.
Divide the top and the bottom by 5. The fraction becomes 1/8, and it cannot be made any simpler.
So 0.125 in simplest form is 1/8.

notes.A: Excellent! 125/1000 simplifies all the way down to 1/8.
notes.B: 1/5 is 0.2, which is bigger than 0.125. Write 0.125 as 125/1000 and simplify one step at a time.
notes.C: 5/4 is more than 1, but 0.125 is much less than 1. Write 0.125 as 125 over 1000 and then simplify.
notes.D: 1/4 is 0.25, which is double 0.125. Write 0.125 as 125/1000 and keep dividing the top and the bottom until they share no factor.

hints: This is an addition of decimals with different numbers of decimal places. The digits must be lined up by place value before adding.
Write the three numbers one below the other with the decimal points in a straight line. Fill the empty places with zeros so each number has three digits after the point.
Here is a similar one: 12.45 + 3.7 + 0.006. Write them as 12.450, 3.700 and 0.006. Adding the columns gives 16.156.

steps.text: Line up the decimal points and fill the empty places with zeros. The numbers become 34.560, 7.800 and 0.004.
Add 34.560 and 7.800 first. The tenths give 5 + 8 = 13, so write 3 and carry 1 to the ones.
Now add 0.004, which puts a 4 in the thousandths place.

notes.A: 42.36 is the sum of only 34.56 and 7.8. The 0.004 still has to be added, and it lands in the thousandths place.
notes.B: Great job! With the decimal points lined up, the total is 42.364.
notes.C: 113.4 is far too big, because 34 and 7 make only about 42. A total this large usually means the decimal points were not lined up, so line them up and add again.
notes.D: 42.3604 puts the 4 one place too far to the right. In 0.004 the 4 is in the thousandths place, the third place after the point.

hints: This is a subtraction of a decimal from a whole number. A whole number can be written with zeros after a decimal point so the places match.
Write 50 as 50.00 and put 23.75 below it with the decimal points lined up. Then subtract, starting from the right, or take away the whole part first and the decimal part after.
Here is a similar one: 40 − 16.35. Write 40 as 40.00. Taking away 16 leaves 24.00, and taking away 0.35 more leaves 23.65.

steps.text: Write 50 as 50.00 so that both numbers have two decimal places.
Take away the whole part of 23.75 first.
Now take away the 0.75 that is still left. One whole less 0.75 is 0.25, so 27.00 drops to 26.25.

notes.A: Well done! Taking 23 and then 0.75 away from 50 leaves 26.25.
notes.B: 36.25 is too big, because 50 − 23 is already only 27. Check the tens column again after borrowing.
notes.C: 26.75 keeps the .75 from 23.75 instead of subtracting it. Taking 0.75 from one whole leaves 0.25.
notes.D: 27.25 is more than 50 − 23, which is 27. Taking away the extra 0.75 must bring the result below 27.

hints: This multiplies two decimals. Multiply as if they were whole numbers, then put the decimal point back by counting decimal places.
Leave out the decimal points and multiply 25 by 4. Then count the digits after the point in 2.5 and in 0.4 together.
Here is a similar one: 1.5 × 0.6. First 15 × 6 = 90. The two numbers have two decimal places altogether, so 90 becomes 0.90, which is 0.9.

steps.text: Leave out the decimal points and multiply 25 by 4.
2.5 has one digit after the point and 0.4 has one digit after the point, so the product needs two digits after the point.
Put the point two places from the right in 100. That gives 1.00, which is the same as 1.0.

notes.A: 0.1 comes from moving the point three places. The two numbers have only two decimal places altogether, so 100 becomes 1.00.
notes.B: You got it! 25 × 4 = 100, and two decimal places make it 1.00, which is 1.0.
notes.C: 10 comes from giving the product only one decimal place. Count the places in both numbers: one in 2.5 and one in 0.4 make two.
notes.D: 100 is 25 × 4 with the decimal points left out. Put the point back two places from the right.

hints: This multiplies two decimals. Multiply the digits as whole numbers, then count decimal places to put the point back.
Leave out the decimal points and the zeros in front, and multiply 3 by 6. Then count the digits after the point in 0.03 and in 0.6 together.
Here is a similar one: 0.04 × 0.7. First 4 × 7 = 28. The numbers have two and one decimal places, three altogether, so 28 becomes 0.028.

steps.text: Multiply the digits without the decimal points.
0.03 has two digits after the point and 0.6 has one, so the product needs three digits after the point.
18 has only two digits, so a zero goes in front to make three decimal places. So 0.03 × 0.6 = 0.018.

notes.A: Excellent thinking! 18 with three decimal places is 0.018.
notes.B: 0.18 has only two decimal places. Count the places in both numbers: two in 0.03 and one in 0.6 make three.
notes.C: 1.8 has only one decimal place. The two numbers have three decimal places altogether, so the product must have three as well.
notes.D: 0.0018 has four decimal places, one too many. Two places in 0.03 and one place in 0.6 make three.

hints: The value of a digit depends on the place it sits in. After the decimal point the places are tenths, hundredths, thousandths, and so on.
Name the place of each digit after the point in 2.0639, starting with the tenths, until you reach the 6.
Here is a similar one: in 5.0274 the digit 7 is the third digit after the point, so it is in the thousandths place. Its value is 7 thousandths, which is 0.007.

steps.text: In 2.0639 the digits after the point are 0 in the tenths place, 6 in the hundredths place, 3 in the thousandths place and 9 in the ten-thousandths place.
The 6 is in the hundredths place, so its value is 6 hundredths.
The value of 6 in 2.0639 is 0.06.

notes.A: 6 is the digit itself, called its face value. Its value in the number depends on the place it sits in, so name that place.
notes.B: 0.006 would be right if the 6 were in the thousandths place, but that place holds the 3. Count the places again from the decimal point.
notes.C: 0.6 would be right if the 6 were in the tenths place, but the tenths place holds the 0. The 6 comes one place later.
notes.D: Great job! The 6 is in the hundredths place, so its value is 0.06.

hints: This is a two-part cost problem. Each fruit has its own weight and its own price per kg, so find each cost and then combine them.
Start with the apples. Multiply 2.5 by 120, which you can do as 2 kg plus half a kg. Then do the same kind of sum for the oranges.
Here is a similar one: 1.5 kg of rice at ₹60 per kg costs 1.5 × 60 = ₹90, and 2.5 kg of sugar at ₹40 per kg costs 2.5 × 40 = ₹100. The total is 90 + 100 = ₹190.

steps.text: Apples: 2 kg cost ₹240 and half a kg costs ₹60, so 2.5 kg cost ₹300.
Oranges: 1 kg costs ₹80 and a quarter of a kg costs ₹20, so 1.25 kg cost ₹100.
Add the two costs. Riya spent ₹400 in total.

notes.A: Well done! The apples cost ₹300 and the oranges cost ₹100, which makes ₹400.
notes.B: ₹300 is the cost of the apples alone. The oranges still have to be added.
notes.C: ₹380 adds only ₹80 for the oranges, which is the price of 1 kg. Riya bought 1.25 kg, so the oranges cost a little more.
notes.D: ₹350 is close, so check each cost once more: 2.5 × 120 for the apples and 1.25 × 80 for the oranges, then add.

hints: This is a whole number divided by 10. The digits stay the same and the decimal point moves.
A whole number has its decimal point at the end, so 809 is the same as 809.0. Move the point one place to the left because 10 has one zero.
Here is a similar one: 406 ÷ 10. Write 406 as 406.0 and move the point one place to the left, which gives 40.6.

steps.text: Write 809 as 809.0, with the decimal point at the end of the whole number.
10 has one zero, so dividing by 10 moves the point one place to the left. Every digit stays, including the 0 in the middle.

notes.A: 8.9 has lost the 0 from the middle of 809. Every digit must stay in its order, and only the point moves.
notes.B: You got it! The point moves one place to the left, giving 80.9.
notes.C: 8090 is 809 multiplied by 10. Dividing makes the number smaller, so the point moves to the left.
notes.D: 8.09 comes from moving the point two places, which is dividing by 100. For 10, move it only one place.

hints: This is a product of three decimals. Multiply two of them first, then multiply the result by the third, counting decimal places each time.
Begin with 0.25 × 0.4. Multiply 25 by 4, then count the digits after the point in 0.25 and 0.4 together to place the point.
Here is a similar one: 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.6. First 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.10, which is 0.1. Then 0.1 × 0.6 = 0.06.

steps.text: Multiply the first two numbers. 25 × 4 = 100, and 0.25 and 0.4 have three decimal places together, so the product is 0.100, which is 0.1.
Now multiply 0.1 by 0.8. 1 × 8 = 8, and there are two decimal places together, so the product is 0.08.

notes.B: 8.0 is much too big, because all three numbers are less than 1 and so is their product. Count the decimal places at each step.
notes.C: 0.8 would be right if 0.25 × 0.4 were 1, but it is 0.1. Multiply 0.1 by 0.8 to finish.
notes.D: 0.008 has one decimal place too many. 0.25 × 0.4 is 0.1, and 0.1 × 0.8 has two decimal places.

hints: This is about changing money. Each dollar is worth a fixed number of rupees, so you need to find how many groups of that size fit into the rupees you have.
Each dollar needs 40 rupees. Work out how many 40s there are in 100 by dividing 100 by 40.
Here is a similar one: if 1 dollar = 20 rupees, then for 70 rupees you get 70 ÷ 20 dollars. Three dollars use 60 rupees and the 10 rupees left are half a dollar, so you get 3.5 dollars.

steps.text: Each dollar costs 40 rupees, so split 100 rupees into groups of 40.
Two dollars use 80 rupees, and that leaves 20 rupees.
20 rupees is half of 40 rupees, so it buys half a dollar, which is 0.5 of a dollar.
So 100 rupees give 2.5 dollars.

notes.A: 4000 comes from multiplying 100 by 40. Rupees are being changed into dollars, and each dollar uses up 40 rupees, so divide.
notes.B: 0.04 is far less than one dollar, but 100 rupees is more than the 40 rupees that one dollar costs. Divide 100 by 40.
notes.C: Great job! 100 ÷ 40 is 2 dollars and a half, which is 2.5.
notes.D: Two dollars use 80 rupees and 20 rupees are left. 20 out of 40 is a half, which is 0.5 and not 0.25.

hints: This changes a small unit of money into a bigger one. Remember how many paise make one rupee.
100 paise make 1 rupee, so divide 240 by 100. Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the left.
Here is a similar one: 375 paise. 300 paise are 3 rupees and 75 paise are left over, so 375 paise = Rs. 3.75.

steps.text: 100 paise make 1 rupee, so paise are changed into rupees by dividing by 100.
200 paise make 2 rupees, and 40 paise are left over. The paise are written after the decimal point.
So 240 paise = Rs. 2.40.

notes.A: 24.0 comes from dividing by 10. There are 100 paise in a rupee, so divide by 100.
notes.B: 240 is still the number of paise. Rupees are 100 times bigger, so the number of rupees must be much smaller.
notes.C: Well done! 240 paise is 2 rupees and 40 paise, written Rs. 2.40.
notes.D: 0.240 comes from dividing by 1000. There are 100 paise in a rupee, so the point moves only two places.

hints: This changes rupees into paise, a bigger unit into a smaller one. Remember how many paise make one rupee.
1 rupee is 100 paise, so multiply 4.06 by 100. Multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point two places to the right.
Here is a similar one: Rs. 7.05 is 7 rupees and 5 paise. 7 rupees are 700 paise, so Rs. 7.05 = 705 paise.

steps.text: 1 rupee is 100 paise, so 4 rupees are 400 paise.
The two digits after the point show the paise. Here they are 06, which means 6 paise.
So Rs. 4.06 = 406 paise.

notes.A: 46 has lost the zero. Rs. 4.06 is 4 rupees and 6 paise, and 4 rupees alone are already 400 paise.
notes.B: You got it! 400 paise and 6 paise make 406 paise.
notes.C: 4060 comes from multiplying by 1000. There are 100 paise in a rupee, so the point moves only two places.
notes.D: 4.06 is still the number of rupees. Each rupee is 100 paise, so multiply by 100.

hints: The letters stand for numbers, and one of them is not given. Find the missing number first, then do the division the question asks for.
Put the known values into m = n × p. It becomes 21 = 3 × p, so ask yourself what number times 3 makes 21.
Here is a similar one: if m = 18, n = 2 and m = n × p, then 18 = 2 × p, so p = 9. Then m ÷ p = 18 ÷ 9 = 2.

steps.text: Put the numbers in: 21 = 3 × p. Since 3 × 7 = 21, the value of p is 7.
Now divide m by p, which means dividing 21 by 7.
The value of m ÷ p is 3.

notes.A: Great job! p is 7, and 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
notes.B: 7 is the value of p. The question asks for m ÷ p, so one more step is needed: divide 21 by 7.
notes.C: 5 does not fit here. First find p from 21 = 3 × p, then divide 21 by that value.
notes.D: 4 does not fit here. First find p from 21 = 3 × p, then divide 21 by that value.

hints: This story has two parts: the fruits she bought and the fruits she dropped. In each part the oranges and bananas come in a fixed pattern, so think in equal groups.
Start with the 24 fruits she bought. For every 1 banana there are 3 oranges, so the fruits come in groups of 4. Find how many such groups make 24.

Here is a similar one: Meena buys 30 fruits, with four times as many apples as pears. Groups of 5 give 6 pears and 24 apples. She drops 9 fruits, twice as many apples as pears, so 6 apples and 3 pears fall. She reaches home with 24 − 6 = 18 apples.

steps.text: Three times as many oranges as bananas means groups of 4 fruits: 3 oranges and 1 banana. There are 6 such groups in 24, so she bought 18 oranges and 6 bananas.
She took home 15 fruits, so she dropped 9 fruits.
She dropped twice as many oranges as bananas, so the dropped fruits come in groups of 3: 2 oranges and 1 banana. There are 3 such groups in 9, so 6 oranges and 3 bananas fell.
Take the dropped oranges away from the oranges she bought.
There were 12 oranges when she reached home. Notice that the 15 fruits at home are 12 oranges and 3 bananas, which is no longer three oranges for every banana.

notes.A: 9 is the number of fruits she dropped altogether. The question asks for the oranges she still had at home.
notes.B: 10 does not fit the story. Find the oranges bought, then the oranges dropped, and take one from the other.
notes.C: 6 is the number of oranges she dropped. Take those away from the 18 oranges she bought.
notes.D: Excellent thinking! She bought 18 oranges, dropped 6, and reached home with 12.

hints: Two purchases are described, and only one thing changes between them. Comparing the two totals shows what that change costs.
Change Rs. 1 and 5 paise into paise first. Then find how much more the second purchase costs than the first; that extra money paid for the extra 10 paise stamps.

Here is a similar one: some 5 paise and 10 paise stamps cost 70 paise. With the same 5 paise stamps and twice the 10 paise stamps the cost is 110 paise. The extra 40 paise buys 4 more 10 paise stamps, so there were 4 at first, costing 40 paise. That leaves 70 − 40 = 30 paise, which buys 6 stamps of 5 paise.

steps.text: Rs. 1 and 5 paise is 105 paise. The second purchase costs 50 paise more than the first.
The only change is that the 10 paise stamps were doubled, so the extra 50 paise is the cost of the 10 paise stamps he bought at first. That is 5 stamps.
In the first purchase the 10 paise stamps cost 50 paise, so only 5 paise was spent on 5 paise stamps.
5 paise buys just one 5 paise stamp. Karan bought 1 stamp of 5 paise; the 5 found earlier was the number of 10 paise stamps.

notes.A: Well done! Five 10 paise stamps cost 50 paise, and the 5 paise left buys 1 stamp.
notes.B: With 3 stamps of 5 paise, the 10 paise stamps would cost 40 paise, and doubling them would give 15 + 80 = 95 paise instead of 105 paise. Compare the two totals to find the 10 paise stamps first.
notes.C: With 4 stamps of 5 paise, 35 paise would be left for the 10 paise stamps, and 35 paise cannot be made from 10 paise stamps. Compare the two totals to find the 10 paise stamps first.
notes.D: 5 is the number of 10 paise stamps. The question asks for the 5 paise stamps, so see how much of the 55 paise is left for them.

hints: This is an equation with the letter x on both sides. Collect the x terms together so that x appears only once.
12x − 40 is the same as 2x. So when 40 is taken from 12x, only 2x is left, which means 40 must be the difference between 12x and 2x.
Here is a similar one: 8x − 42 = 2x. The 42 taken away is the difference between 8x and 2x, which is 6x. So 6x = 42 and x = 7.

steps.text: Taking 40 away from 12x leaves 2x, so 40 is the difference between 12x and 2x.
Divide 40 by 10 to find x.
Check: 12 × 4 − 40 = 8 and 2 × 4 = 8, so both sides match. The value of x is 4.

notes.A: With x = 3 the left side would be 36 − 40, and 40 cannot be taken from 36, while the right side is 6. Collect the x terms to get 10x = 40.
notes.B: With x = 1 the left side would be 12 − 40, and 40 cannot be taken from 12. Collect the x terms to get 10x = 40.
notes.C: You got it! 10x = 40, so x = 4, and both sides come to 8.
notes.D: With x = 5 the left side is 60 − 40 = 20 but the right side is 10, so the sides do not match. Collect the x terms to get 10x = 40.

hints: This is a sum and difference problem. You know the total of two groups and how much bigger one group is than the other.
Set aside the 21 extra women by taking 21 away from 105. What is left is two equal groups: the men, and the same number of women.
Here is a similar one: a class has 60 children, with 10 more girls than boys. Taking away the 10 extra girls leaves 50, and half of 50 is 25 boys. So there are 25 + 10 = 35 girls.

steps.text: Set aside the 21 extra women. The people left are men and women in equal numbers.
Half of 84 is the number of men.
The women are 21 more than the men.
There were 63 women at the meeting. As a check, 63 women and 42 men make 105 people.

notes.A: Great job! There were 42 men and 21 more women than that, which is 63.
notes.B: 42 is the number of men. The women are 21 more than the men, so add 21.
notes.C: 21 is how many more women there were than men. It is the difference, so use it to find the two groups.
notes.D: 84 is what is left after setting aside the 21 extra women. Halve it to find the men, then add the 21 back for the women.

hints: This equation has x on both sides and plain numbers on both sides. The aim is to gather the x terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Add 17x to both sides so that all the x terms are together on the right. The equation becomes 97 = 22x + 31.
Here is a similar one: 50 − 4x = 6x + 10. Adding 4x to both sides gives 50 = 10x + 10. Taking 10 from both sides gives 40 = 10x, so x = 4.

steps.text: Add 17x to both sides. The left side becomes 97, and the right side becomes 22x + 31 because 5x and 17x make 22x.
Take 31 from both sides, which leaves 22x = 66.
Divide 66 by 22 to find x.
Check: 97 − 17 × 3 = 46 and 5 × 3 + 31 = 46, so both sides match. The value of x is 3.

notes.A: With x = 11, 17x would be 187, which is more than 97, so it cannot be taken away. Gather the x terms to get 22x = 66.
notes.B: With x = 5 the left side is 97 − 85 = 12 but the right side is 25 + 31 = 56, so the sides do not match. Gather the x terms to get 22x = 66.
notes.C: Well done! 22x = 66, so x = 3, and both sides come to 46.
notes.D: With x = 9, 17x would be 153, which is more than 97, so it cannot be taken away. Gather the x terms to get 22x = 66.

hints: The boxes hold numbers that go up by the same amount each time. Find what is in each box first, and read carefully which boxes the question asks about.
Compare every box with the first one. The second has 2 more, the third has 4 more and the fourth has 6 more. Take all these extra marbles away from 100 to see what four equal boxes would hold.

Here is a similar one: 60 marbles go into three boxes, each with 3 more than the one before. The extras are 3 + 6 = 9, so 60 − 9 = 51 and 51 ÷ 3 = 17 in the first box. The boxes hold 17, 20 and 23, and the first two boxes hold 37 together.

steps.text: Compared with the first box, the other boxes have 2, 4 and 6 extra marbles. That is 12 extra marbles.
Without the extras, 88 marbles are shared equally among 4 boxes, so the first box has 22 marbles.
The boxes hold 22, 24, 26 and 28 marbles.
The question asks about the first three boxes only, so leave out the 28.
The first 3 boxes hold 72 marbles altogether.

notes.A: 60 does not match the boxes. Find the four boxes first, which are 22, 24, 26 and 28, and add the first three.
notes.B: 80 does not match the boxes. Find the four boxes first, which are 22, 24, 26 and 28, and add the first three.
notes.C: Excellent! The boxes hold 22, 24, 26 and 28, and the first three add up to 72.
notes.D: 88 is what is left after taking away the 12 extra marbles. Share it among the 4 boxes to find the first box, then add the first three boxes.

hints: This equation has x on both sides, and on each side something is being subtracted. Keep the two sides balanced while you gather the x terms together.
Add 3x to both sides so that x is only on the right. The equation becomes 15 = 4x − 9.
Here is a similar one: 20 − 2x = x − 4. Adding 2x to both sides gives 20 = 3x − 4. Adding 4 to both sides gives 24 = 3x, so x = 8.

steps.text: Add 3x to both sides. On the left the 3x that was taken away is put back, leaving 15. On the right, x and 3x make 4x, so 15 = 4x − 9.
Add 9 to both sides to undo the subtraction of 9. This gives 24 = 4x.
Divide 24 by 4 to find x.
The value of x is 6. The key idea is that things being subtracted are cleared by adding: adding 3x clears the 3x taken away, and adding 9 clears the 9 taken away.

notes.A: 3 comes from subtracting where adding is needed: 15 − 9 = 6 and 3x − x = 2x. To clear the 3x and the 9 that are taken away, add them to both sides.
notes.B: With x = 5 the left side is 15 − 15 = 0, but the right side is 5 − 9, which is not 0. Add 3x and then 9 to both sides to get 24 = 4x.
notes.C: You got it! Adding 3x and 9 to both sides gives 24 = 4x, so x = 6.
notes.D: 12 comes from dividing 24 by 2. Adding 3x to x gives 4x, so divide 24 by 4.

hints: This equation has the letter T on both sides. Gather the T terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Add T to both sides so that T is only on the right. The equation becomes 31 = 3T + 7.
Here is a similar one: 40 − T = 3T + 4. Adding T to both sides gives 40 = 4T + 4. Taking 4 from both sides gives 36 = 4T, so T = 9.

steps.text: Add T to both sides. The left side becomes 31, and the right side becomes 3T + 7 because 2T and T make 3T.
Take 7 from both sides, which leaves 3T = 24.
Divide 24 by 3 to find T.
Check: 31 − 8 = 23 and 2 × 8 + 7 = 23, so both sides match. The value of T is 8.

notes.A: Great job! 3T = 24, so T = 8, and both sides come to 23.
notes.B: 24 is the value of 3T. One more step is needed: divide by 3 to find T.
notes.C: 12 comes from dividing 24 by 2. Adding T to 2T gives 3T, so divide 24 by 3.
notes.D: 6 comes from dividing 24 by 4. Adding T to 2T gives 3T, so divide 24 by 3.

hints: An equation is like a balance with the same value on both sides. To find the letter, undo what has been done to it.
5 has been added to a to make 12. Undo the adding by taking 5 away from 12.
Here is a similar one: n + 4 = 13. Taking 4 away from 13 gives n = 9, and 9 + 4 = 13 confirms it.

steps.text: 5 was added to a to get 12, so take 5 away from 12 to find a.
Check: 7 + 5 = 12, so a = 7.

notes.A: Well done! 7 + 5 = 12, so a is 7.
notes.B: 17 comes from adding 5 to 12. The 5 is already added to a, so undo it by subtracting.
notes.C: 5 is the number being added to a. Ask what number plus 5 makes 12.
notes.D: 60 comes from multiplying 12 by 5. The equation uses adding, so undo it by subtracting 5 from 12.

hints: An equation is like a balance. To find the letter, undo what has been done to it with the opposite operation.
5 has been taken away from b to leave 12. Undo the subtraction by adding 5 to 12.
Here is a similar one: n − 6 = 9. Adding 6 to 9 gives n = 15, and 15 − 6 = 9 confirms it.

steps.text: 5 was taken away from b to leave 12, so add 5 to 12 to find b.

notes.A: −7 is below zero, but b must be big enough to leave 12 after 5 is taken away. Add 5 to 12.
notes.B: 60 comes from multiplying 12 by 5. The equation uses subtracting, so undo it by adding 5 to 12.
notes.C: You got it! 17 − 5 = 12, so b is 17.
notes.D: 7 comes from subtracting 5 from 12. The 5 was already taken away from b, so put it back by adding.

hints: A number written next to a letter means they are multiplied. To find the letter, undo the multiplying.
3c means 3 times c. Ask yourself what number multiplied by 3 makes 12, or divide 12 by 3.
Here is a similar one: 5n = 35 means 5 times n is 35. Dividing 35 by 5 gives n = 7.

steps.text: 3c means 3 × c, so 3 times c is 12. Divide 12 by 3 to find c.
Check: 3 × 4 = 12, so c = 4.

notes.A: 9 comes from subtracting 3 from 12. 3c means 3 times c, so undo it by dividing.
notes.B: 15 comes from adding 3 to 12. 3c means 3 times c, so undo it by dividing 12 by 3.
notes.C: 36 comes from multiplying 12 by 3. The 3 already multiplies c, so undo it by dividing.
notes.D: Great job! 3 × 4 = 12, so c is 4.

hints: A letter over a number means the letter is divided by that number. To find the letter, undo the dividing.
d divided by 3 gives 12. Undo the division by multiplying 12 by 3.
Here is a similar one: n/4 = 7 means n divided by 4 is 7. Multiplying 7 by 4 gives n = 28.

steps.text: d/3 means d divided by 3, and that gives 12. Multiply 12 by 3 to find d.

notes.A: 4 comes from dividing 12 by 3. Here d is already divided by 3, so undo it by multiplying.
notes.B: Excellent! 36 ÷ 3 = 12, so d is 36.
notes.C: 15 comes from adding 3 to 12. d/3 means d divided by 3, so undo it by multiplying 12 by 3.
notes.D: 9 comes from subtracting 3 from 12. d/3 means d divided by 3, so undo it by multiplying 12 by 3.

hints: This equation says that two numbers add up to a total, and one of them is hidden behind a letter. Find the hidden part.
5 and e together make 12. Take the part you know, 5, away from the total, 12.
Here is a similar one: 6 + n = 15. Taking 6 away from 15 gives n = 9, and 6 + 9 = 15 confirms it.

steps.text: 5 and e add up to 12, so take 5 away from 12 to find e.
Check: 5 + 7 = 12, so e = 7.

notes.A: With e = 2 the left side would be 5 + 2, which is only 7. Take 5 away from 12 to find e.
notes.B: Well done! 5 + 7 = 12, so e is 7.
notes.C: 17 comes from adding 5 to 12. The total is already 12, so take the 5 away.
notes.D: 60 comes from multiplying 5 by 12. The equation uses adding, so take 5 away from 12.

hints: Here the letter is the number being taken away. Think about how much must be removed to get from the starting number down to the result.
15 take away f leaves 6. Find the gap between 15 and 6 by subtracting 6 from 15.
Here is a similar one: 20 − n = 12. The gap between 20 and 12 is 8, so n = 8, and 20 − 8 = 12 confirms it.

steps.text: Taking f away from 15 leaves 6, so f is the gap between 15 and 6.
Check: 15 − 9 = 6, so f = 9.

notes.A: −9 has the right size but it is below zero. Taking away 9 from 15 leaves 6, so f is 9.
notes.B: 21 comes from adding 15 and 6. Here f is taken away from 15, so it must be smaller than 15.
notes.C: You got it! 15 − 9 = 6, so f is 9.
notes.D: 6 is what is left after the subtraction. Taking 6 from 15 would leave 9, so find the gap between 15 and 6.

hints: Here the letter is the number you divide by. Division and multiplication facts belong together, so a times table can help.
32 divided by g gives 4. Ask yourself what number multiplied by 4 makes 32.
Here is a similar one: 45/n = 5 means 45 divided by n is 5. Since 5 × 9 = 45, n = 9.

steps.text: 32/g means 32 divided by g, and that gives 4. So g groups of 4 make 32.
Divide 32 by 4 to find g.
Check: 32 ÷ 8 = 4, so g = 8.

notes.A: Great job! 32 ÷ 8 = 4, so g is 8.
notes.B: 36 comes from adding 32 and 4. 32/g means 32 divided by g, so think of the 4 times table.
notes.C: 128 comes from multiplying 32 by 4. Dividing 32 by 128 would not give 4, so ask what times 4 makes 32.
notes.D: 28 comes from subtracting 4 from 32. 32/g means 32 divided by g, so ask what times 4 makes 32.

hints: This equation has two plain numbers and one letter adding up to a total. Put the plain numbers together first.
Add the numbers you know on the left side, 7 and 2. Then see how much more is needed to reach 15.
Here is a similar one: 4 + n + 3 = 16. The plain numbers make 4 + 3 = 7, so 7 + n = 16 and n = 9.

steps.text: Add the plain numbers on the left side. The equation becomes 9 + h = 15.
Take 9 away from 15 to find h.

notes.A: Excellent! 7 + 6 + 2 = 15, so h is 6.
notes.B: 10 comes from taking 7 away from 15 but then adding the 2. Both 7 and 2 must be taken away from 15.
notes.C: 8 comes from taking only the 7 away from 15. The 2 must be taken away as well.
notes.D: 24 comes from adding 7, 2 and 15. The total is already 15, so take 7 and 2 away from it.

hints: This is a two-step equation: x has been multiplied and then something has been added. Undo the steps in the reverse order.
Undo the adding first. Take 3 away from 11 to find what 2x is worth.
Here is a similar one: 3n + 4 = 19. Taking 4 away gives 3n = 15, and dividing by 3 gives n = 5.

steps.text: 3 was added last, so undo it first. Taking 3 from 11 shows that 2x is worth 8.
2x means 2 times x, so divide 8 by 2.

notes.A: 7 comes from adding 3 to 11 and then halving. The 3 is added to 2x, so undo it by subtracting.
notes.B: 14 comes from adding 3 to 11. The 3 is added to 2x, so take it away, and then divide by 2.
notes.C: 5.5 comes from halving 11 straight away. Take the 3 away first, and then divide by 2.
notes.D: Well done! 2 × 4 + 3 = 11, so x is 4.

hints: This is a two-step equation: m has been multiplied and then something has been taken away. Undo the steps in the reverse order.
Undo the subtraction first. Add 7 to 18 to find what 5m is worth.
Here is a similar one: 4n − 3 = 21. Adding 3 gives 4n = 24, and dividing by 4 gives n = 6.

steps.text: 7 was taken away last, so undo it first by adding. This shows that 5m is worth 25.
5m means 5 times m, so divide 25 by 5.

notes.A: 11 comes from taking 7 away from 18. The 7 was already subtracted from 5m, so undo it by adding.
notes.B: 25 is the value of 5m. One more step is needed: divide by 5 to find m.
notes.C: You got it! 5 × 5 − 7 = 18, so m is 5.
notes.D: 2.2 comes from taking 7 away from 18 and then dividing by 5. The 7 must be added back before dividing.

hints: This is a two-step equation: x has been divided and then something has been added. Undo the steps in the reverse order.
Undo the adding first. Take 5 away from 10 to find what x/3 is worth.
Here is a similar one: n/2 + 4 = 11. Taking 4 away gives n/2 = 7, and multiplying by 2 gives n = 14.

steps.text: 5 was added last, so undo it first. Taking 5 from 10 shows that x/3 is worth 5.
x/3 means x divided by 3, so undo the division by multiplying 5 by 3.

notes.A: Great job! 15 ÷ 3 is 5, and 5 + 5 = 10, so x is 15.
notes.B: 30 comes from multiplying 10 by 3 straight away. Take the 5 away first, and then multiply by 3.
notes.C: 1.67 comes from dividing 5 by 3. Here x is already divided by 3, so undo that by multiplying.
notes.D: 5 is the value of x/3. One more step is needed: multiply by 3 to find x.

hints: This is a two-step equation: y has been divided and then something has been taken away, leaving nothing. Undo the steps in the reverse order.
If taking 8 away leaves 0, then y/4 must be exactly 8. Now think about what number divided by 4 gives 8.
Here is a similar one: n/5 − 3 = 0. Since taking 3 away leaves nothing, n/5 = 3. Multiplying by 5 gives n = 15.

steps.text: Taking 8 away from y/4 leaves 0, so y/4 is worth 8.
y/4 means y divided by 4, so undo the division by multiplying 8 by 4.

notes.A: 12 comes from adding 8 and 4. y/4 means y divided by 4, so multiply 8 by 4.
notes.B: 8 is the value of y/4. One more step is needed: multiply by 4 to find y.
notes.C: Excellent! 32 ÷ 4 is 8, and 8 − 8 = 0, so y is 32.
notes.D: 2 comes from dividing 8 by 4. Here y is already divided by 4, so undo that by multiplying.

hints: This equation has the letter z on both sides. Bring all the z terms to one side so that z appears only once.
On the right, 2z is being taken away. Add 2z to both sides: the right side becomes 12 and the left side becomes z + 2z.
Here is a similar one: n = 20 − 3n. Adding 3n to both sides gives 4n = 20, and dividing by 4 gives n = 5.

steps.text: Add 2z to both sides. The right side becomes 12, and the left side becomes z + 2z, which is 3z.
3z means 3 times z, so divide 12 by 3.
Check: the left side is 4 and the right side is 12 − 2 × 4, which is also 4. So z = 4.

notes.A: 3 comes from dividing 12 by 4. One z and two more z make 3z, so divide 12 by 3.
notes.B: Well done! 12 − 2 × 4 = 4, so both sides are 4 when z is 4.
notes.C: 12 leaves out the 2z that is taken away. With z = 12 the right side would be 12 − 24, which does not match.
notes.D: 6 comes from dividing 12 by 2. The z on the left counts too, so there are 3z altogether and 12 is divided by 3.

hints: This equation has the letter a on both sides. Collect the a terms together so that a appears only once.
Taking 32 away from 6a leaves 2a. So 32 must be the difference between 6a and 2a. Work out how many a that is.
Here is a similar one: 9n − 35 = 2n. The 35 taken away is the difference between 9n and 2n, which is 7n. So 7n = 35 and n = 5.

steps.text: Taking 32 away from 6a leaves 2a, so 32 is the difference between 6a and 2a.
6a − 2a is 4a, so 4a = 32.
Divide 32 by 4 to find a.
Check: 6 × 8 − 32 = 16 and 2 × 8 = 16, so both sides match. The value of a is 8.

notes.A: 16 is the value of each side when a is 8. The question asks for a itself, which comes from 4a = 32.
notes.B: You got it! 4a = 32, so a = 8, and both sides come to 16.
notes.C: 4 comes from dividing 32 by 8, which adds 6a and 2a. The difference between 6a and 2a is 4a, so divide 32 by 4.
notes.D: With a = 6 the left side is 36 − 32 = 4 but the right side is 12, so the sides do not match. Collect the a terms to get 4a = 32.

hints: This equation has the letter b and plain numbers on both sides. Gather the b terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Take 2b away from both sides so that b is only on the left. The equation becomes 2b + 5 = 19.
Here is a similar one: 5n + 2 = 3n + 12. Taking 3n from both sides gives 2n + 2 = 12. Taking 2 from both sides gives 2n = 10, so n = 5.

steps.text: Take 2b away from both sides. The left side becomes 2b + 5 and the right side becomes 19.
Take 5 away from both sides, which leaves 2b = 14.
Divide 14 by 2 to find b.
Check: 4 × 7 + 5 = 33 and 2 × 7 + 19 = 33, so both sides match. The value of b is 7.

notes.A: 12 comes from adding 19 and 5 and then halving. The 5 is added on the left, so it is taken away from 19.
notes.B: With b = 3 the left side is 17 but the right side is 25, so the sides do not match. Gather the b terms to get 2b = 14.
notes.C: 4 comes from adding where subtracting is needed: 19 + 5 = 24 and 4b + 2b = 6b. Take 2b and 5 away from both sides.
notes.D: Great job! 2b = 14, so b = 7, and both sides come to 33.

hints: This equation has the letter c and plain numbers on both sides. Gather the c terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other.
Take 3c away from both sides so that c is only on the left. The equation becomes 7 + 2c = 25.
Here is a similar one: 4 + 6n = 2n + 24. Taking 2n from both sides gives 4 + 4n = 24. Taking 4 from both sides gives 4n = 20, so n = 5.

steps.text: Take 3c away from both sides. The left side becomes 7 + 2c and the right side becomes 25.
Take 7 away from both sides, which leaves 2c = 18.
Divide 18 by 2 to find c.
Check: 7 + 5 × 9 = 52 and 3 × 9 + 25 = 52, so both sides match. The value of c is 9.

notes.A: With c = 6 the left side is 37 but the right side is 43, so the sides do not match. Gather the c terms to get 2c = 18.
notes.B: 4 comes from adding where subtracting is needed: 25 + 7 = 32 and 5c + 3c = 8c. Take 3c and 7 away from both sides.
notes.C: Excellent! 2c = 18, so c = 9, and both sides come to 52.
notes.D: 16 comes from adding 25 and 7 and then halving. The 7 is added on the left, so it is taken away from 25.

hints: An equation is true when both of its sides have the same value. Here you know what x is, so each equation can be tested.
Put 5 in place of x in each equation and work out the left side. Remember that a number written next to x multiplies it.
Here is a similar one: if x = 4, is 3x − 2 = 10 true? 3 × 4 = 12 and 12 − 2 = 10, so the left side equals the right side and the equation is true.

steps.text: Test x + 10 = 16. The left side is 15, which is not 16.
Test 3x + 2 = 18. The left side is 17, which is not 18.
Test 4x + 1 = 20. The left side is 21, which is not 20.
Test 2x − 3 = 7. The left side is 7, which matches the right side.
The true equation is 2x − 3 = 7.

notes.A: Well done! 2 × 5 is 10, and 10 − 3 = 7, so both sides are 7.
notes.B: With x = 5, x + 10 is 15, which is one less than 16. Test each equation by putting 5 in place of x.
notes.C: With x = 5, 3x + 2 is 15 + 2 = 17, which is one less than 18. Test each equation by putting 5 in place of x.
notes.D: With x = 5, 4x + 1 is 20 + 1 = 21, which is one more than 20. Test each equation by putting 5 in place of x.

hints: This is a missing-number problem told in words. Two numbers add up to a total, and one of them is unknown.
The unknown number and 8 together make 23. Take the part you know, 8, away from the total, 23.
Here is a similar one: a number added to 6 gives 20. Taking 6 away from 20 gives 14, and 14 + 6 = 20 confirms it.

steps.text: The unknown number and 8 add up to 23, so the number is 23 with the 8 taken away.
Take 8 away from 23.
Check: 15 + 8 = 23, so the number is 15.

notes.A: With 3 the total would be 3 + 8, which is only 11. Take 8 away from 23 to find the number.
notes.B: 31 comes from adding 8 to 23. The total is already 23, so take the 8 away.
notes.C: You got it! 15 + 8 = 23, so the number is 15.
notes.D: 184 comes from multiplying 23 by 8. The story is about adding, so take 8 away from 23.

hints: This is a number puzzle in words with two steps: the number is multiplied, then something is taken away. Work backwards from the result.
The last thing done was taking away 5 to leave 16. Undo that first by adding 5 to 16; this gives three times the number.
Here is a similar one: twice a number decreased by 4 is 14. Adding 4 gives 18, which is twice the number, so the number is 18 ÷ 2 = 9.

steps.text: Taking 5 away left 16, so before that there was 21. This is three times the number.
Divide 21 by 3 to find the number.
Check: 3 × 7 − 5 = 16, so the number is 7.

notes.A: 21 is three times the number. One more step is needed: divide by 3.
notes.B: 11 comes from taking 5 away from 16. The 5 was already taken away, so add it back and then divide by 3.
notes.C: Great job! 3 × 7 is 21, and 21 − 5 = 16, so the number is 7.
notes.D: 3.67 comes from taking 5 away from 16 and then dividing by 3. The 5 must be added back before dividing.

hints: This is an age puzzle with two steps: the brother's age is doubled, then 3 is added to get Riya's age. Work backwards from Riya's age.
The last thing done was adding 3 to reach 17. Undo that first by taking 3 away from 17; this gives twice the brother's age.

Here is a similar one: Anu's age is 4 years more than three times her sister's age, and Anu is 28. Taking 4 away gives 24, which is three times the sister's age, so the sister is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 years old.

steps.text: Riya's 17 years are twice her brother's age and 3 more. Take the 3 away to get twice his age.
Halve 14 to find the brother's age.
Check: 2 × 7 + 3 = 17, so her brother is 7 years old.

notes.A: 14 is twice the brother's age. One more step is needed: halve it.
notes.B: Excellent! Twice 7 is 14, and 3 more makes 17, so her brother is 7.
notes.C: 10 comes from adding 3 to 17 and then halving. Riya is 3 years more than twice his age, so take the 3 away first.
notes.D: With a brother of 5, twice his age and 3 more would be 13, which is less than 17. Take 3 from 17 and then halve.

hints: This is a working-backwards story. Money was spent, and you know what is left, so the starting amount must be bigger than both.
The money he started with was split into two parts: the ₹45 he spent and the ₹78 he has left. Put the two parts back together.
Here is a similar one: Sita spends ₹30 and has ₹52 left. She started with 52 + 30 = ₹82.

steps.text: The money Aman had at first is made of two parts: the ₹45 he spent and the ₹78 he has left.
Add the two parts.
Check: 123 − 45 = 78, so he had ₹123 initially.

notes.A: ₹33 comes from taking 45 away from 78. He had more money before spending, so add the two amounts.
notes.B: Well done! ₹123 less the ₹45 he spent leaves ₹78.
notes.C: ₹3510 comes from multiplying 78 by 45. The spent part and the part left are added to get the starting amount.
notes.D: ₹45 is only the amount he spent. Add the ₹78 he has left to find what he started with.

hints: Consecutive numbers follow one after another, like 4, 5 and 6. When three of them are added, the total is three times the middle number.
Divide the sum, 36, by 3 to find the middle number. Then think about which number comes just before it.
Here is a similar one: three consecutive numbers add up to 45. The middle number is 45 ÷ 3 = 15, so the numbers are 14, 15 and 16, and the smallest is 14.

steps.text: In three consecutive numbers, the smallest is 1 less than the middle one and the largest is 1 more. So the sum is 3 times the middle number.
Divide 36 by 3 to find the middle number.
The three numbers are 11, 12 and 13.
The smallest number is 11.

notes.A: If the smallest were 10, the numbers would be 10, 11 and 12, which add up to only 33. Find the middle number by dividing 36 by 3.
notes.B: 12 is the middle number. The question asks for the smallest, which is the number just before it.
notes.C: You got it! 11, 12 and 13 add up to 36, and the smallest is 11.
notes.D: 13 is the largest of the three numbers. The question asks for the smallest one.

hints: HCF means the highest common factor. It is the biggest number that divides both numbers exactly.
