List all the factors of 35 first; there are only four of them. Then see which of those also divide 28.
Here is a similar one: for the HCF of 15 and 24, the factors of 15 are 1, 3, 5 and 15. Of these, only 1 and 3 divide 24 exactly, so the HCF is 3.

steps.text: The factors of 35 are 1, 5, 7 and 35.
The factors of 28 are 1, 2, 4, 7, 14 and 28.
The numbers in both lists are 1 and 7. The bigger one is 7, so the HCF of 35 and 28 is 7.

notes.A: 140 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 35 and 28 divide. The HCF is a factor of both, so it cannot be bigger than either number.
notes.B: Great job! 7 divides both 35 and 28, and no bigger number does.
notes.C: 14 divides 28 but it does not divide 35 exactly. The HCF must divide both numbers.
notes.D: 28 does not divide 35 exactly. The HCF must divide both numbers, so compare their factor lists.

hints: The HCF is the biggest number that divides both numbers with nothing left over. Look for factors the two numbers share.
List the factors of the smaller number, 14. Then test them, biggest first, to see which one also divides 35.
Here is a similar one: for the HCF of 10 and 25, the factors of 10 are 1, 2, 5 and 10. 10 does not divide 25, but 5 does, so the HCF is 5.

steps.text: The factors of 14 are 1, 2, 7 and 14.
Test them against 35, biggest first. 14 does not divide 35 exactly, because 14 × 2 = 28 and 14 × 3 = 42.
7 does divide 35 exactly.
So the HCF of 35 and 14 is 7.

notes.A: 70 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 35 and 14 divide. The HCF is a factor of both, so it cannot be bigger than either number.
notes.B: 14 does not divide 35 exactly, since 14 × 2 = 28 and 14 × 3 = 42. The HCF must divide both numbers.
notes.C: 8 does not divide 35 or 14 exactly. List the factors of 14 and see which ones divide 35.
notes.D: Well done! 7 divides both 35 and 14, and no bigger number does.

hints: The HCF is the biggest number that divides both numbers exactly. For larger numbers, breaking each one into prime factors shows what they share.
Break 105 into prime factors first. It ends in 5, so begin by dividing it by 5. Then do the same for 120.
Here is a similar one: for the HCF of 42 and 70, write 42 = 2 × 3 × 7 and 70 = 2 × 5 × 7. Both share 2 and 7, so the HCF is 2 × 7 = 14.

steps.text: Break 105 into prime factors.
Break 120 into prime factors.
The prime factors that both numbers share are 3 and 5. Multiply them together.
The HCF of 105 and 120 is 15.

notes.A: 30 divides 120, but 105 is an odd number and 30 cannot divide it exactly. The HCF must divide both numbers.
notes.B: 105 does not divide 120 exactly. The HCF must divide both numbers, so find the prime factors they share.
notes.C: 840 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 105 and 120 divide. The HCF is a factor of both, so it cannot be bigger than either number.
notes.D: Excellent! Both numbers share the prime factors 3 and 5, and 3 × 5 = 15.

hints: Writing a number as a product of two numbers means finding its factor pairs. Each pair counts once, whichever way round it is written.
Start with 1 × 98. Then test 2, 3, 4 and so on to see which of them divide 98 exactly, and write each one with its partner.
Here is a similar one: 30 can be written as 1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10 and 5 × 6. There are no other pairs, so 30 can be written as a product of two numbers in 4 ways.

steps.text: Every number has the pair made with 1, so the first way is 1 × 98.
98 is even, so 2 divides it.
3, 4, 5 and 6 do not divide 98 exactly, but 7 does.
The next factors of 98 are 14 and 49, and they have been used already, so there are no new pairs.
98 can be expressed as a product of two numbers in 3 ways: 1 × 98, 2 × 49 and 7 × 14.

notes.A: 1 way counts only 1 × 98. Test 2 and 7 as well, because both divide 98 exactly.
notes.B: 2 ways is one pair short. Besides 1 × 98 and 2 × 49, there is also 7 × 14.
notes.C: Great job! The pairs are 1 × 98, 2 × 49 and 7 × 14.
notes.D: 6 is the number of factors of 98. Each product uses two factors, so the six factors make three pairs.

hints: Two ideas are mixed here: which numbers are prime, and which digits they are written with. Only the prime numbers get typed.
A 2 can appear in the ones place or in the tens place. Think about which prime numbers can end in 2, and then look for primes among the numbers from 20 to 29.
Here is a similar one for the 6 key. No prime ends in 6, because a number ending in 6 is even. From 60 to 69 the only primes are 61 and 67. So the 6 key is pressed 2 times.

steps.text: A number ending in 2 is even, so the only prime ending in 2 is 2 itself. That is one press.
Now look at 20 to 29, where 2 is in the tens place. The even numbers there are not prime, and neither are 21, 25 and 27, because 21 = 3 × 7, 25 = 5 × 5 and 27 = 3 × 9.
That leaves 23 and 29, which are both prime. Each one needs one press of the 2 key.
The primes with a 2 in them are 2, 23 and 29, so she pressed the 2 key 3 times. The trap is counting numbers such as 12, 22 or 32, which have a 2 but are not prime.

notes.A: 1 counts only the prime number 2. Look also at the numbers from 20 to 29, where 2 is the tens digit, and find the primes there.
notes.B: Excellent thinking! Only 2, 23 and 29 are primes with a 2 in them.
notes.C: 7 is too many. This can happen when numbers such as 21, 25 or 27 are counted, but each of them can be divided by a smaller number.
notes.D: 19 is how many numbers from 1 to 100 have a 2 in them. Only the prime numbers are typed, so check which of those are prime.

hints: This uses the test for dividing by 11. Each symbol hides one digit, and the test lets you find it.
For a three-digit number, add the first and last digits and subtract the middle digit. If the result is 0 or 11, the number can be divided by 11. Try this on 5 ★ 7 first.

Here is a similar one: the number 6 □ 9 can be divided by 11. The first and last digits add up to 15, and 15 less the middle digit must be 0 or 11. So the middle digit is 4 and the number is 649, which is 11 × 59.

steps.text: The test for 11: in a three-digit number, the first digit plus the last digit, less the middle digit, must come to 0 or 11.
In 5 ★ 7 the first and last digits add up to 12, so ★ must be 1 to leave 11. The number is 517.
In 5 7 ♥ the middle digit is 7, so 5 plus ♥ must equal 7 to leave 0. That makes ♥ equal to 2, and the number is 572.
In Ψ 5 9, Ψ plus 9 less 5 must come to 11. That makes Ψ equal to 7, and the number is 759.
The hidden digits are 1, 2 and 7. Putting the biggest digit first gives the greatest number, 721.

notes.A: 723 uses a 3, but the hidden digits are 1, 2 and 7. Check ★ again: 5 + 7 less ★ must leave 11.
notes.B: Well done! The hidden digits are 1, 2 and 7, and the greatest number they make is 721.
notes.C: 972 uses a 9, but 9 is a digit printed in the question and not one of the hidden digits. Find ★, ♥ and Ψ with the test for 11.
notes.D: 729 uses a 9, but 9 is a digit printed in the question and not one of the hidden digits. Find ★, ♥ and Ψ with the test for 11.

hints: H.C.F. means the highest common factor, the biggest number that divides both numbers exactly. Neither number here is in the easy times tables, so break them into prime factors.
Break 65 into prime factors. It ends in 5, so divide by 5 first. Then test whether the other prime factor also divides 91.
Here is a similar one: for the HCF of 38 and 57, write 38 = 2 × 19 and 57 = 3 × 19. Both share 19, so the HCF is 19.

steps.text: 65 ends in 5, so divide it by 5. Its prime factors are 5 and 13.
91 does not end in 0 or 5, so 5 does not divide it. Try 13, and it divides 91 exactly.
Both numbers share the factor 13 and nothing bigger, so the H.C.F. of 65 and 91 is 13.

notes.A: 17 does not divide 65, because 17 × 3 = 51 and 17 × 4 = 68. Break 65 into 5 × 13 and test those factors on 91.
notes.B: 1 divides every number, but there is a bigger common factor here. 91 looks prime, yet it is 7 × 13.
notes.C: You got it! 65 = 5 × 13 and 91 = 7 × 13, so the H.C.F. is 13.
notes.D: 15 does not divide 65, because 15 × 4 = 60 and 15 × 5 = 75. Break 65 into 5 × 13 and test those factors on 91.

hints: The L.C.M. is the smallest number that both numbers divide exactly. Every pair here has 15 in it, so find each L.C.M. and compare them; the pair with the biggest numbers does not always win.
For each pair, go through the multiples of 15, which are 15, 30, 45, 60, 75 and 90. Stop at the first one that the other number also divides.

Here is a similar one: which is greater, the LCM of 10 and 25 or the LCM of 10 and 12? The multiples of 10 are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60. 25 first divides 50, and 12 first divides 60. So 10 and 12 have the greater LCM, even though 12 is smaller than 25.

steps.text: For 15 and 25, the first multiple of 15 that 25 divides is 75.
For 15 and 20, the first multiple of 15 that 20 divides is 60.
For 15 and 18, none of 30, 45, 60 and 75 can be divided by 18, but 90 can.
For 15 and 12, the first multiple of 15 that 12 divides is 60.
The greatest L.C.M. is 90, which belongs to 15 & 18. The trap is that 25 is the biggest partner, but it shares the factor 5 with 15, and that keeps its L.C.M. down to 75.

notes.A: 25 is the biggest partner, but the L.C.M. of 15 and 25 is only 75 because they share the factor 5. Work out the L.C.M. of every pair before choosing.
notes.B: The L.C.M. of 15 and 20 is 60, and another pair reaches higher. Work out the L.C.M. of every pair before choosing.
notes.C: Great job! The L.C.M. of 15 and 18 is 90, the greatest of the four.
notes.D: The L.C.M. of 15 and 12 is 60, and another pair reaches higher. Work out the L.C.M. of every pair before choosing.

hints: Factors are the numbers that divide a number exactly. They come in pairs that multiply to give the number, so listing the pairs in order helps you miss none.
Start with 1 × 84 and 2 × 42. Carry on testing 3, 4, 5, 6 and so on, writing each factor with its partner.
Here is a similar one: the factor pairs of 100 are 1 × 100, 2 × 50, 4 × 25, 5 × 20 and 10 × 10. The last pair uses 10 twice, so it adds only one factor, and 100 has 9 factors.

steps.text: List the factor pairs in order. The first four are 1 × 84, 2 × 42, 3 × 28 and 4 × 21.
5 does not divide 84 exactly. The next pairs are 6 × 14 and 7 × 12.
8 and 9 do not divide 84 exactly, and the next factor is 12, which is already in the list. So every pair has been found.
There are 6 pairs, and each pair gives 2 factors.

notes.A: Well done! 84 has six factor pairs, which makes 12 factors.
notes.B: 8 factors is too few, so some pairs are missing. Go through 1 to 9 in order and check 3 × 28, 4 × 21, 6 × 14 and 7 × 12.
notes.C: 10 factors is one pair short. Go through 1 to 9 in order and make sure 4 × 21 and 6 × 14 are both on your list.
notes.D: 14 factors is too many. Check each number you listed by dividing; 5, 8 and 9 do not divide 84 exactly.

hints: Prime numbers have exactly two factors; the first few are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11. Test each number to see whether two primes can add up to it.

Remember that 2 is a prime, and it is the only even prime. Two odd numbers always add up to an even number, so an odd total needs the prime 2 as one part. For each odd number, take 2 away and see whether what is left is prime.
Here is a similar one. Is 9 the sum of two primes? 9 − 2 = 7, and 7 is prime, so 9 = 2 + 7. Is 17? 17 − 2 = 15, and 15 = 3 × 5 is not prime, so 17 is not the sum of two primes.

steps.text: 5 is the sum of the primes 2 and 3.
7 is the sum of the primes 2 and 5.
12 is the sum of the primes 5 and 7.
11 is odd, so one of its two primes would have to be 2, the only even prime. That leaves 9, and 9 is 3 × 3, so it is not prime.
So 11 is not the sum of two prime numbers. The trap is that 11 is a prime itself, but that does not make it a sum of two primes.

notes.A: 5 is 2 + 3, and both 2 and 3 are prime. Remember that 2 counts as a prime number.
notes.B: 7 is 2 + 5, and both 2 and 5 are prime. Remember that 2 counts as a prime number.
notes.C: Excellent thinking! An odd total needs the prime 2, and 11 − 2 leaves 9, which is not prime.
notes.D: 12 is 5 + 7, and both 5 and 7 are prime. Look for the number that cannot be split into two primes at all.

hints: Each die shows a number from 1 to 6. You need three such numbers that multiply to the given product, and breaking the product into prime factors shows which numbers are possible.
Break 90 into prime factors. Then look for a prime factor that cannot be joined with any other and still fit on a die.
Here is a similar one: three dice have a product of 75, and 75 = 3 × 5 × 5. No die shows 15 or 25, so the dice must show 3, 5 and 5. Their sum is 3 + 5 + 5 = 13.

steps.text: Break 90 into prime factors.
A die has no 10 or 15, so the 5 must be on a die by itself. The other two dice then multiply to 18.
Using numbers from 1 to 6, 18 can only be made as 3 × 6, because 2 × 9 would need a 9.
So the dice show 3, 5 and 6. There is only one possible set, so the sum can be found.
The sum of the three numbers is 14.

notes.A: You got it! The dice must show 3, 5 and 6, and 3 + 5 + 6 = 14.
notes.B: 18 is the product of the other two dice once the 5 is set aside. Find those two numbers, then add all three dice.
notes.C: 10 is 2 + 3 + 5, the different prime factors of 90, but 2 × 3 × 5 is only 30. The three dice must multiply to 90.
notes.D: It may seem that several sets of numbers could give 90, but with only 1 to 6 on a die, just 3, 5 and 6 fit. So the sum can be found.

hints: A number can be divided by 5 exactly only when its last digit is 0 or 5. So you only need the last digit of the product, not the whole product.
Find the last digit of 267 × 348 by multiplying just the ones digits, 7 and 8. Then ask how far that last digit is from the next 0 or 5.

Example: what smallest number should be added to 24 × 32 to make it divisible by 5? The ones digits give 4 × 2 = 8, so the product ends in 8. The next ending that works is 0, so add 2. Check: 24 × 32 = 768, and 768 + 2 = 770.

steps.text: A number is divisible by 5 only when it ends in 0 or 5. So we only need the last digit of 267 × 348.
The last digit of a product comes from the ones digits. 7 × 8 = 56, so the product ends in 6.
After a number ending in 6, the next number that ends in 0 or 5 ends in 0. That is 4 more, because 6 + 4 = 10.
Check: 267 × 348 = 92,916, and 92,916 + 4 = 92,920, which ends in 0. The smallest number to add is 4.

notes.A: Yes! The product ends in 6, and adding 4 makes it end in 0, so it can be divided by 5.
notes.B: Adding 5 does not help here. The product ends in 6, so adding 5 makes it end in 1. Look at how far 6 is from the next 0.
notes.C: Adding 7 would work only if the product ended in 3 or 8. Multiply the ones digits, 7 × 8, again to find the real last digit.
notes.D: One of the numbers given does work. Find the last digit of the product from 7 × 8 and count up to the next number ending in 0.

hints: The L.C.M. is the smallest number that both numbers divide into exactly. It helps to break each number into a multiplication first.
Find the biggest number that divides both 48 and 54. Then write each number as that common number times something.
Example: for the L.C.M. of 12 and 18, the biggest number dividing both is 6. So 12 = 6 × 2 and 18 = 6 × 3. The L.C.M. is 6 × 2 × 3 = 36. Check: 36 ÷ 12 = 3 and 36 ÷ 18 = 2.

steps.text: The biggest number that divides both 48 and 54 is 6. So 48 = 6 × 8 and 54 = 6 × 9.
The leftover parts, 8 and 9, share no factor except 1. So the L.C.M. is the common part once, times 8, times 9.
Check: 432 ÷ 48 = 9 and 432 ÷ 54 = 8, both exact. The L.C.M. of 48 and 54 is 432.

notes.A: Well done! 432 is the smallest number that both 48 and 54 divide exactly.
notes.B: 216 is 54 × 4, so 54 divides it, but 48 does not. The L.C.M. must be divisible by both numbers.
notes.C: 480 is 48 × 10, so 48 divides it, but 54 does not. The L.C.M. must be divisible by both numbers.
notes.D: 540 is 54 × 10, so 54 divides it, but 48 does not. The L.C.M. must be a multiple of both numbers.

hints: Each piece must fit an exact number of times into both ribbons. So you are looking for the greatest number that divides both lengths, which is the H.C.F.
List the factors of 84, the shorter ribbon. Then see which of them also divide 108.
Example: ribbons of 30 metres and 45 metres. The factors of 30 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30. The largest one that also divides 45 is 15, so each piece is 15 metres long.

steps.text: The piece length must divide both 84 and 108 exactly, with nothing left over. The greatest such length is the H.C.F. of 84 and 108.
Try the big ones on 108. 84, 42, 28, 21 and 14 do not divide 108, but 12 does, because 108 ÷ 12 = 9.
Also 84 ÷ 12 = 7. The greatest possible length of each piece is 12 metres.

notes.A: 6 does divide both 84 and 108, but it is not the greatest length that does. Try a larger number that divides both.
notes.B: 14 divides 84, because 14 × 6 = 84, but it does not divide 108. The piece length must divide both ribbons exactly.
notes.C: Great work! 12 goes into 84 seven times and into 108 nine times, and no bigger length fits both.
notes.D: 18 divides 108, because 18 × 6 = 108, but it does not divide 84. The piece length must divide both ribbons exactly.

hints: Factors come in pairs that multiply to give the number. Listing the pairs in order makes sure none is missed.
Start with 1 × 30. Then try 2, 3, 4 and 5 in turn, and write down each pair that multiplies to 30.
Example: the factors of 28. The pairs are 1 × 28, 2 × 14 and 4 × 7. That is 3 pairs, so 28 has 6 factors.

steps.text: Write 30 as a product of two numbers in every possible way: 1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10 and 5 × 6.
4 does not divide 30, and after 5 × 6 the pairs would only repeat. So the list is complete.
Each pair gives 2 factors: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30. There are 4 pairs, so 30 has 8 factors.

notes.A: It looks as if one pair was missed. The pairs are 1 × 30, 2 × 15, 3 × 10 and 5 × 6, so count the factors again.
notes.B: 4 is the number of pairs, not the number of factors. Each pair has two factors in it, so count both numbers of every pair.
notes.C: 10 is one of the factors of 30, but the question asks how many factors there are. List them all and count them.
notes.D: Yes! The factors are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30, which makes 8 of them.

hints: A number is divisible by 9 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. Use that rule on the digits you know and the two missing ones.
Add the digits you can see, 8 and 2. The two stars are the same digit, so together they add twice that digit to the sum.
Example: 5 ★ 3 ★ is divisible by 9. The known digits give 5 + 3 = 8. The next multiple of 9 is 18, so the two stars must add 10, and each star is 5. Check: 5 + 5 + 3 + 5 = 18.

steps.text: A number is divisible by 9 when its digits add up to a multiple of 9. The known digits add up to 8 + 2 = 10.
The next multiples of 9 after 10 are 18 and 27. So the two stars together must add 8 or 17.
The two stars are the same digit, so their total is an even number. That rules out 17, and 8 ÷ 2 = 4.
Check: 8 + 4 + 2 + 4 = 18, and 8,424 ÷ 9 = 936. The digit represented by ★ is 4.

notes.A: 8 is what the two stars add up to together, not the value of one star. Share it equally between the two stars.
notes.B: Well done! With 4 in both places the digits add up to 18, which is a multiple of 9.
notes.C: With 5 in both places the digits add up to 8 + 5 + 2 + 5 = 20, and 20 is not a multiple of 9. Aim for a digit sum of 18.
notes.D: With 3 in both places the digits add up to 8 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 16, and 16 is not a multiple of 9. Aim for a digit sum of 18.

hints: This question has two parts. Find the H.C.F. and the L.C.M. of the two numbers separately, and then add them.
Start with the H.C.F. List the factors of 24 and pick the largest one that also divides 32.
Example: for 12 and 18, the H.C.F. is 6. The multiples of 18 are 18, 36, and 36 is also a multiple of 12, so the L.C.M. is 36. The sum is 36 + 6 = 42.

steps.text: The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24. The largest one that also divides 32 is 8, so the H.C.F. is 8.
For the L.C.M., list the multiples of 32: 32, 64, 96. The first one that 24 also divides is 96, because 24 × 4 = 96.
Add the two: 96 + 8 = 104. The sum of the L.C.M. and H.C.F. is 104.

notes.A: 96 is the L.C.M. on its own. The question asks for the sum, so the H.C.F. still has to be added.
notes.B: Great job! The L.C.M. is 96 and the H.C.F. is 8, and 96 + 8 = 104.
notes.C: It looks as if 4 was used as the H.C.F. A bigger number divides both 24 and 32, so look at the common factors again.
notes.D: It looks as if 12 was used as the H.C.F. 12 divides 24 but not 32, so look for the largest number that divides both.

hints: Think about where a 2 could sit in a prime number below 100: in the ones place or in the tens place. Then remember what kind of numbers end in 2.
Any number ending in 2 is even, so check whether any prime at all can end in 2. After that, look at the numbers from 20 to 29 and pick out the primes.
Example: how many times is the digit 6 used in the primes up to 100? A number ending in 6 is even, so none of those is prime. In the sixties, only 61 and 67 are prime. So the digit 6 is used 2 times.

steps.text: First look for a 2 in the ones place. Numbers ending in 2 are even, so 2 divides them. The only prime among them is 2 itself. That is one 2.
Now look for a 2 in the tens place, from 20 to 29. The even ones are out, and 21 = 3 × 7, 25 = 5 × 5 and 27 = 3 × 9. Only 23 and 29 are prime. That is two more.
The trap is to forget the prime 2 itself, or to count numbers like 12 and 22, which are not prime. The primes with a 2 are 2, 23 and 29, so the digit 2 is used 3 times.

notes.A: Yes! The digit 2 appears in 2, 23 and 29, and in no other prime below 100.
notes.B: One prime may have been missed. Count the 2 in 23, the 2 in 29, and also the prime number 2 itself.
notes.C: 19 is how many numbers from 1 to 100 have a 2 in them. Only the prime numbers count here, so first pick out the primes that contain a 2.
notes.D: Some primes do contain a 2. The number 2 is itself prime, and there are two more primes between 20 and 29.

hints: A number is divisible by 6 when it is divisible by both 2 and 3. Think about what swapping two digits changes and what it leaves the same.
Add the digits of 73251 to test for 3. Swapping digits does not change this sum, so then think about which digit must be in the ones place to make the number even.

Example: which two digits of 4,563 could be swapped to make it divisible by 6? The digits add up to 18, so 3 already divides it. It needs an even last digit. Swapping 6 and 3 gives 4,536, which is even, so it is divisible by 6.

steps.text: To be divisible by 6, a number must be divisible by 3 and by 2. The digits of 73251 add up to 18, so 3 already divides it.
Swapping two digits never changes the digit sum, so the number stays divisible by 3. The key idea is that only the test for 2 matters now.
The number must end in an even digit. Its only even digit is 2, so the 2 must move to the ones place, where the 1 is now.
The swap gives 73152, and 73152 ÷ 6 = 12192. The digits to interchange are 2 & 1.

notes.A: Well done! Moving the 2 to the end gives 73152, which is even and has a digit sum of 18.
notes.B: Swapping 5 and 1 gives 73215, which ends in 5 and is odd. A number divisible by 6 must be even, so think about which digit has to go last.
notes.C: Swapping 2 and 5 gives 73521, which still ends in 1 and is odd. The even digit has to move to the ones place.
notes.D: Swapping 3 and 2 gives 72351, which still ends in 1 and is odd. The even digit has to move to the ones place.

hints: The test for 9 uses the sum of the digits: it must be a multiple of 9. Remember that the same missing digit is used twice.
Add the digits you know, 9 and 8. Then find which multiple of 9 the total can reach when the same digit is added twice.
Example: 7 ★ 5 ★ is divisible by 9. The known digits give 7 + 5 = 12. The next multiple of 9 is 18, so the two stars add 6 and each star is 3. Check: 7 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 18.

steps.text: A number is divisible by 9 when its digits add up to a multiple of 9. The known digits add up to 9 + 8 = 17.
The next multiples of 9 after 17 are 18, 27 and 36. So the two stars together must add 1, 10 or 19.
The two stars are the same digit, so their total is an even number. Only 10 fits, and 10 ÷ 2 = 5.
Check: 9 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 27, and 9,585 ÷ 9 = 1,065. The digit at the ★ place is 5.

notes.A: Well done! With 5 in both places the digits add up to 27, which is a multiple of 9.
notes.B: With 4 in both places the digits add up to 9 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 25, and 25 is not a multiple of 9. Aim for a digit sum of 27.
notes.C: With 3 in both places the digits add up to 9 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 23, and 23 is not a multiple of 9. Aim for a digit sum of 27.
notes.D: Adding 1 once to 17 would give 18, but the star appears twice. With 1 in both places the digits add up to 19, which is not a multiple of 9.

hints: Each way of writing a number as a product of two numbers is a factor pair. So this is really a question about finding all the factor pairs.
Start with 1 × 136, then test 2, 3, 4 and so on. Each time a number divides 136 exactly, write down the pair.
Example: in how many ways can 50 be written as a product of two numbers? The pairs are 1 × 50, 2 × 25 and 5 × 10. That makes 3 ways.

steps.text: Find every pair of numbers that multiply to 136. Start small: 1 × 136 and 2 × 68.
3 does not divide 136. 4 does, giving 4 × 34. Then 5, 6 and 7 do not, and 8 gives 8 × 17.
Going further only repeats the same pairs the other way round, such as 17 × 8. The trap is to count those again, or to leave out 1 × 136.
The pairs are 1 × 136, 2 × 68, 4 × 34 and 8 × 17. So 136 can be written as a product of two numbers in 4 ways.

notes.A: 6 is more than the number of pairs. Check that a pair such as 8 × 17 and 17 × 8 was counted only once, since it is the same way.
notes.B: One pair may have been missed. Remember that 1 × 136 counts, and so does 8 × 17.
notes.C: Yes! The pairs are 1 × 136, 2 × 68, 4 × 34 and 8 × 17, which makes 4 ways.
notes.D: There is one way too many here. List the pairs in order starting from 1 × 136 and check that each one really multiplies to 136.

hints: A number in both notebooks is a multiple of 4 and also a multiple of 5. Such numbers are the common multiples of the two.
Find the smallest number that is a multiple of both 4 and 5. Every common number is a multiple of that one.
Example: multiples of 3 and multiples of 4 up to 50. The smallest common multiple is 12. The multiples of 12 up to 50 are 12, 24, 36 and 48, so there are 4 common numbers.

steps.text: A number in both notebooks must be a multiple of 4 and of 5. The smallest such number is 20.
Every common number is a multiple of 20. Up to 100 these are 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100.
Counting them, or working out 100 ÷ 20, gives 5. There are 5 common numbers in both notebooks.

notes.A: 15 is too many. The shared numbers must be multiples of both 4 and 5, so list the multiples of 20 up to 100 and count them.
notes.B: Great job! The common numbers are 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100, which makes 5.
notes.C: 10 is a multiple of 5 but not of 4, so counting in tens gives too many. The shared numbers go up in steps of 20.
notes.D: 20 is the smallest number in both notebooks, and it is also how many numbers Vijay writes. The question asks how many numbers are in both.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly. Breaking each number into a multiplication helps you see what they share.
Write 39 as a product of two smaller numbers. Then check whether either of those numbers divides 65.
Example: the HCF of 34 and 51. 34 = 2 × 17 and 51 = 3 × 17. Both contain 17 and share nothing else, so the HCF is 17.

steps.text: Break 39 into a multiplication: 39 = 3 × 13.
Do the same for 65: 65 = 5 × 13.
Both numbers contain 13, and 3 and 5 share nothing more. The HCF of 39 and 65 is 13.

notes.A: 26 is the difference, 65 − 39. The HCF must divide both numbers, and 26 does not divide 39.
notes.B: 19 does not divide 39 or 65. Try writing 39 as 3 times something and see if that something divides 65.
notes.C: Well done! 39 = 3 × 13 and 65 = 5 × 13, so 13 is the largest number that divides both.
notes.D: 5 divides 65 but not 39, since 39 does not end in 0 or 5. The HCF must divide both numbers.

hints: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. So look for the number that no smaller number, other than 1, divides.
Test each number with small divisors such as 3 and 5. A number ending in 5 can always be divided by 5.
Example: is 39 or 37 prime? 39 = 3 × 13, so it is not prime. 37 cannot be divided by 2, 3 or 5, so 37 is prime.

steps.text: 35 and 15 end in 5, so 5 divides them: 35 = 5 × 7 and 15 = 3 × 5. They are not prime.
21 = 3 × 7, so 21 is not prime either.
29 is odd, its digits add up to 11 so 3 does not divide it, and it does not end in 0 or 5. 7 does not divide it either, because 7 × 4 = 28. So the prime number is 29.

notes.A: Yes! Only 1 and 29 divide 29, so it is a prime number.
notes.B: 35 ends in 5, so 5 divides it: 35 = 5 × 7. A prime number has no factors other than 1 and itself.
notes.C: 21 is in the 3 times table: 21 = 3 × 7. A prime number has no factors other than 1 and itself.
notes.D: 15 ends in 5, so 5 divides it: 15 = 3 × 5. A prime number has no factors other than 1 and itself.

hints: There is a quick test for 3 that uses the digits. A number is divisible by 3 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
Add the four digits of each number. Then check which total is in the 3 times table.
Example: is 4,362 divisible by 3? 4 + 3 + 6 + 2 = 15, and 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so yes. Is 2,518? 2 + 5 + 1 + 8 = 16, which is not in the 3 times table, so no.

steps.text: A number is divisible by 3 when the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. So add the digits of each number.
5,123 gives 5 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 11. 4,532 gives 14 and 8,206 gives 16. None of these totals is in the 3 times table.
7,251 gives 7 + 2 + 5 + 1 = 15, and 15 ÷ 3 = 5. So the number divisible by 3 is 7,251.

notes.A: Well done! The digits of 7,251 add up to 15, and 15 is in the 3 times table.
notes.B: The digits of 5,123 add up to 5 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 11, and 11 is not in the 3 times table. Try the digit sums of the other numbers.
notes.C: The digits of 4,532 add up to 4 + 5 + 3 + 2 = 14, and 14 is not in the 3 times table. Try the digit sums of the other numbers.
notes.D: The digits of 8,206 add up to 8 + 2 + 0 + 6 = 16, and 16 is not in the 3 times table. Try the digit sums of the other numbers.

hints: There is a quick test for 4. You only need to look at the number made by the last two digits.
Write down the last two digits of each number. Then check which of those two-digit numbers is in the 4 times table.
Example: is 5,728 divisible by 4? Its last two digits make 28, and 28 ÷ 4 = 7, so yes. Is 6,142? Its last two digits make 42, which is not in the 4 times table, so no.

steps.text: A number is divisible by 4 when its last two digits make a number divisible by 4.
The last two digits of the four numbers are 16, 34, 31 and 18. 34, 31 and 18 are not in the 4 times table.
16 ÷ 4 = 4, with nothing left over. So the number divisible by 4 is 2,316.

notes.A: Yes! The last two digits make 16, and 16 is 4 × 4.
notes.B: The last two digits make 34, and 34 ÷ 4 leaves 2 over. Being even is not enough for 4, so test the last two digits.
notes.C: 7,531 is odd, so it cannot be divided by 4. Look for a number whose last two digits are in the 4 times table.
notes.D: The last two digits make 18, and 18 ÷ 4 leaves 2 over. Being even is not enough for 4, so test the last two digits.

hints: The LCM is the smallest number that is a multiple of both numbers. Listing multiples is a good way to find it.
Write out the multiples of 8, starting 8, 16. Stop at the first one that 6 also divides.
Example: the LCM of 4 and 6. The multiples of 6 are 6, 12. The number 12 is also a multiple of 4, so the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.

steps.text: List the multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30.
List the multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32.
The first number that is in both lists is 24. The LCM of 6 and 8 is 24.

notes.A: 14 is 6 + 8. The LCM is not the sum; it is the smallest number that is in both times tables.
notes.B: Great job! 24 is 6 × 4 and 8 × 3, and no smaller number is in both times tables.
notes.C: 2 is the HCF, the largest number that divides both 6 and 8. The LCM is a multiple of both, so it cannot be smaller than 8.
notes.D: 48 is 6 × 8, and it is a common multiple, but it is not the smallest one. Look for an earlier number in both lists.

hints: A prime factorization writes a number as a product of prime numbers only. Every number in the product must be prime.
Start by dividing 60 by the smallest prime, 2. Keep splitting any part that is not prime.
Example: 84 = 2 × 42, then 42 = 2 × 21, then 21 = 3 × 7. So the prime factorization of 84 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 7.

steps.text: Split 60 using the smallest prime: 60 = 2 × 30.
30 is not prime, so split again: 30 = 2 × 15. Then 15 = 3 × 5.
Now every part is prime. The prime factorization of 60 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.

notes.A: This does multiply to 60, but 10 is not prime, because 10 = 2 × 5. Keep splitting until every number is prime.
notes.B: This does multiply to 60, but 15 is not prime, because 15 = 3 × 5. Keep splitting until every number is prime.
notes.C: Well done! 2, 3 and 5 are all prime, and 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60.
notes.D: This does multiply to 60, but neither part is prime: 4 = 2 × 2 and 15 = 3 × 5. Keep splitting until every number is prime.

hints: There is a test for 11 that uses the digits in turn. You add every other digit to make two totals, and then compare the two totals.
Add the 1st and 3rd digits, 8 and 9. Add the 2nd and 4th digits, 2 and 4. Then find the difference between the two totals.
Example: is 3,729 divisible by 11? 3 + 2 = 5 and 7 + 9 = 16. The difference is 16 − 5 = 11, which is a multiple of 11, so 3,729 is divisible by 11. Check: 11 × 339 = 3,729.

steps.text: For 11, add the digits in the 1st and 3rd places: 8 + 9 = 17.
Add the digits in the 2nd and 4th places: 2 + 4 = 6.
The difference is 17 − 6 = 11. When this difference is 0 or a multiple of 11, the number is divisible by 11.
Check: 11 × 754 = 8,294. Yes, 8,294 is divisible by 11.

notes.A: Well done! The two digit totals are 17 and 6, and their difference is 11.
notes.B: It can be worked out. Use the test for 11, or simply divide 8,294 by 11 and see if anything is left over.
notes.C: Try the test again: 8 + 9 = 17 and 2 + 4 = 6. Look at the difference between 17 and 6.
notes.D: Dividing by 2 first is not needed. A number is divisible by 11 when 11 goes into it exactly, so test 8,294 itself.

hints: The bells ring together whenever the minutes passed are a multiple of both gaps. The first time this happens is the smallest common multiple, the LCM.
List the multiples of 18, starting with 18 itself. Stop at the first one that is also a multiple of 12.

Example: two bells ring every 10 and 15 minutes and ring together at 8:00 AM. The multiples of 15 are 15, 30, and 30 is also a multiple of 10. So they ring together again 30 minutes later, at 8:30 AM.

steps.text: The first bell rings after 12, 24, 36 and 48 minutes. The second bell rings after 18, 36 and 54 minutes.
The first number in both lists is 36, so the LCM of 12 and 18 is 36. The bells ring together 36 minutes after 9:00 AM.
36 minutes after 9:00 AM is 9:36 AM. The bells ring together again at 9:36 AM.

notes.A: At 9:18 AM only the second bell rings, because 18 is not a multiple of 12. Both bells must ring at the same minute.
notes.B: 30 is 12 + 18, but neither 12 nor 18 divides 30, so neither bell rings then. Look for the smallest number in both times tables.
notes.C: After 60 minutes the first bell rings, but the second does not, because 18 does not divide 60. Look for the smallest common multiple of 12 and 18.
notes.D: Great job! 36 is the smallest number that both 12 and 18 divide, so the bells meet at 9:36 AM.

hints: Every box holds the same number of fruits, and nothing may be left over. So the number in a box must divide both totals, and you want the largest such number.
List the factors of 36, the smaller number. Then test them on 48, starting from the largest.

Example: 40 pens and 30 pencils go into packets of equal size, one kind per packet. The factors of 30 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30. Testing from the largest, 30 and 15 do not divide 40, but 10 does. So each packet holds 10.

steps.text: The number of fruits in a box must divide both 48 and 36 exactly. The largest such number is the HCF of 48 and 36.
The factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36. Testing from the largest, 36 and 18 do not divide 48, but 12 does.
48 ÷ 12 = 4 boxes of apples and 36 ÷ 12 = 3 boxes of oranges. The maximum number of fruits in each box is 12.

notes.A: 24 divides 48 but not 36, so the oranges could not be packed evenly. The number must divide both totals.
notes.B: Well done! 12 divides both 48 and 36, and no bigger number does.
notes.C: 6 does divide both 48 and 36, but a bigger number also does. The question asks for the maximum.
notes.D: 4 does divide both 48 and 36, but a bigger number also does. The question asks for the maximum.

hints: There is a test for 8 that uses only the end of the number. Look at the number made by the last three digits.
Write down the last three digits of each number. Then divide each of those three-digit numbers by 8 and see which one leaves nothing over.
Example: is 3,128 divisible by 8? Its last three digits make 128, and 128 ÷ 8 = 16, so yes. Is 4,620? Its last three digits make 620, and 620 ÷ 8 leaves 4 over, so no.

steps.text: A number is divisible by 8 when its last three digits make a number divisible by 8.
The last three digits of the four numbers are 214, 234, 648 and 342. Dividing by 8, 214 leaves 6 over, 234 leaves 2 over and 342 leaves 6 over.
648 ÷ 8 = 81 exactly. So the number divisible by 8 is 5,648.

notes.A: The last three digits make 214, and 214 ÷ 8 leaves 6 over. Test the last three digits of the other numbers.
notes.B: The last three digits make 234, and 234 ÷ 8 leaves 2 over. Test the last three digits of the other numbers.
notes.C: Yes! The last three digits make 648, and 648 ÷ 8 = 81 with nothing left over.
notes.D: The last three digits make 342, and 342 ÷ 8 leaves 6 over. Test the last three digits of the other numbers.

hints: A perfect number has a special link with its own factors. Think about what happens when you add up the factors that are smaller than the number.
List the factors of 6. Leave out 6 itself and add the others.
Example: 28 is also a perfect number. Its factors, leaving out 28 itself, are 1, 2, 4, 7 and 14, and 1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28.

steps.text: The factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6.
Leave out 6 itself. The factors that remain are 1, 2 and 3.
Add them up. 6 is called perfect because it equals the sum of its factors, excluding itself: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

notes.A: 6 does have 4 factors, but so do 8 and 10, and they are not perfect. Look at what the factors add up to.
notes.B: The smallest composite number is 4, not 6. A perfect number is about the sum of its factors.
notes.C: Yes! The factors of 6 that are smaller than 6 are 1, 2 and 3, and they add up to 6.
notes.D: Many numbers are even without being perfect, such as 8. Try adding the factors of 6 that are smaller than 6.

hints: All the numbers end in 1, so the last digit will not help. Think about what kind of numbers these are, and test each one for factors.
Check whether each number can be divided by a small number such as 3 or 7. The digit sum test for 3 is quick.
Example: which number does not belong in 13, 23, 33, 43? 33 = 3 × 11, so it is not prime. 13, 23 and 43 are all prime, so 33 does not belong.

steps.text: 31, 41, 61 and 71 cannot be divided by 2, 3, 5 or 7. So they are all prime numbers.
The trap is 51, which looks prime because it is odd and ends in 1. But its digits add up to 6, so 3 divides it.
51 = 3 × 17, so it is not prime while the others are. The number that does not belong to the group is 51.

notes.A: 61 is prime: 2, 3, 5 and 7 do not divide it. Look for the one number in the group that has another factor.
notes.B: Well done! 51 = 3 × 17, so it is the only number in the group that is not prime.
notes.C: 71 is prime: 2, 3, 5 and 7 do not divide it. Look for the one number in the group that has another factor.
notes.D: 31 is prime: 2, 3 and 5 do not divide it. Look for the one number in the group that has another factor.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly. It can never be bigger than the smaller of the two numbers.
List the factors of 60, the smaller number. Then test them on 72, starting from the largest.
Example: the HCF of 40 and 56. The factors of 40 are 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20 and 40. Testing from the largest, 40, 20 and 10 do not divide 56, but 8 does. So the HCF of 40 and 56 is 8.

steps.text: Test them on 72, starting from the largest. 60, 30, 20 and 15 do not divide 72.
The next one, 12, does divide 72, because 72 ÷ 12 = 6. So the HCF of 72 and 60 is 12.

notes.A: 60 divides itself but it does not divide 72. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.B: 360 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 72 and 60 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 60.
notes.C: 24 divides 72 but it does not divide 60. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.D: Well done! 12 goes into 72 six times and into 60 five times, and no bigger number fits both.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers. Splitting each number into a multiplication shows what they share.
65 ends in 5, so write it as 5 times something. Then see whether that something also divides 91.
Example: the HCF of 51 and 85. 51 = 3 × 17 and 85 = 5 × 17. Both contain 17 and share nothing else, so the HCF is 17.

steps.text: Break 65 into a multiplication: 65 = 5 × 13.
Do the same for 91: 91 = 7 × 13.
13 is in both, and 5 and 7 share nothing more. The HCF of 65 and 91 is 13.

notes.A: 65 divides itself but it does not divide 91. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.B: Great job! 65 = 5 × 13 and 91 = 7 × 13, so 13 is the largest number that divides both.
notes.C: 26 is the difference, 91 − 65, but it does not divide 65 or 91. Split each number into a multiplication instead.
notes.D: 455 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 65 and 91 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 65.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly. With small numbers you can list all the factors.
Write down the factors of 4 and the factors of 6. Then look for the numbers that are in both lists.
Example: the HCF of 9 and 6. The factors of 9 are 1, 3 and 9. The factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6. The largest number in both lists is 3, so the HCF is 3.

steps.text: The factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6.
The factors of 4 are 1, 2 and 4.
The numbers in both lists are 1 and 2. The larger of these is 2, so the HCF of 6 and 4 is 2.

notes.A: 3 divides 6 but it does not divide 4. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.B: 4 divides itself but it does not divide 6. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.C: Yes! 2 divides both 6 and 4, and no bigger number does.
notes.D: 12 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 6 and 4 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 4.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers. Splitting each number into a multiplication shows what they share.
26 is even, so write it as 2 times something. Then see whether that something also divides 91.
Example: the HCF of 22 and 77. 22 = 2 × 11 and 77 = 7 × 11. Both contain 11 and share nothing else, so the HCF is 11.

steps.text: Break 26 into a multiplication: 26 = 2 × 13.
Do the same for 91: 91 = 7 × 13.
13 is in both, and 2 and 7 share nothing more. The HCF of 26 and 91 is 13.

notes.A: 14 does not divide 26 or 91. Split 26 into 2 times something and test that something on 91.
notes.B: 182 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 26 and 91 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 26.
notes.C: 26 divides itself but it does not divide 91, which is odd. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.D: Well done! 26 = 2 × 13 and 91 = 7 × 13, so 13 is the largest number that divides both.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly. Start from the factors of the smaller number.
List the factors of 16. Then test them on 20, starting from the largest.
Example: the HCF of 18 and 30. The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. Testing from the largest, 18 and 9 do not divide 30, but 6 does. So the HCF of 18 and 30 is 6.

steps.text: The factors of 16 are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16.
Test them on 20, starting from the largest. 16 and 8 do not divide 20.
The next one, 4, does divide 20, because 20 ÷ 4 = 5. So the HCF of 16 and 20 is 4.

notes.A: 8 divides 16 but it does not divide 20. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.B: 80 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 16 and 20 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 16.
notes.C: 16 divides itself but it does not divide 20. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.D: Great job! 4 goes into 16 four times and into 20 five times, and no bigger number fits both.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly. Start from the factors of the smaller number.
List the factors of 30. Then test them on 45, starting from the largest.
Example: the HCF of 28 and 42. The factors of 28 are 1, 2, 4, 7, 14 and 28. Testing from the largest, 28 does not divide 42, but 14 does. So the HCF of 28 and 42 is 14.

steps.text: The factors of 30 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30.
Test them on 45, starting from the largest. 30 does not divide 45.
The next one, 15, does divide 45, because 45 ÷ 15 = 3. So the HCF of 30 and 45 is 15.

notes.A: 16 does not divide 30 or 45. Both numbers end in 0 or 5, so look at factors such as 5 and its multiples.
notes.B: 90 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 30 and 45 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 30.
notes.C: 30 divides itself but it does not divide 45. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.D: Well done! 15 goes into 30 twice and into 45 three times, and no bigger number fits both.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly. It can never be bigger than the smaller of the two numbers.
List the factors of 24. Then test them on 60, starting from the largest.
Example: the HCF of 18 and 45. The factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. Testing from the largest, 18 does not divide 45, but 9 does. So the HCF of 18 and 45 is 9.

steps.text: The factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24.
Test them on 60, starting from the largest. 24 does not divide 60, because 24 × 2 = 48 and 24 × 3 = 72.
The next one, 12, does divide 60, because 60 ÷ 12 = 5. So the HCF of 24 and 60 is 12.

notes.A: 24 divides itself but it does not divide 60. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.B: 120 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 24 and 60 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 24.
notes.C: Yes! 12 goes into 24 twice and into 60 five times, and no bigger number fits both.
notes.D: 13 does not divide 24 or 60. It is close, so go through the factor list of 24 once more.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers. Splitting each number into a multiplication shows what they share.
55 ends in 5, so write it as 5 times something. Then see whether that something also divides 44.
Example: the HCF of 39 and 52. 39 = 3 × 13 and 52 = 4 × 13. Both contain 13, and 3 and 4 share nothing else, so the HCF is 13.

steps.text: Break 55 into a multiplication: 55 = 5 × 11.
Do the same for 44: 44 = 4 × 11.
11 is in both, and 5 and 4 share no factor except 1. The HCF of 55 and 44 is 11.

notes.A: 220 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 55 and 44 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 44.
notes.B: 22 divides 44 but it does not divide 55, which is odd. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.C: Great job! 55 = 5 × 11 and 44 = 4 × 11, so 11 is the largest number that divides both.
notes.D: 44 divides itself but it does not divide 55. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.

hints: The HCF is the largest number that divides both numbers exactly. With small numbers you can list all the factors.
Write down the factors of 10 and the factors of 12. Then look for the numbers that are in both lists.
Example: the HCF of 14 and 21. The factors of 14 are 1, 2, 7 and 14. Of these, 14 does not divide 21, but 7 does. So the HCF of 14 and 21 is 7.

steps.text: The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
The factors of 10 are 1, 2, 5 and 10.
The numbers in both lists are 1 and 2. The larger of these is 2, so the HCF of 12 and 10 is 2.

notes.A: 60 is the LCM, the smallest number that both 12 and 10 divide into. The HCF divides both numbers, so it cannot be bigger than 10.
notes.B: Yes! 2 divides both 12 and 10, and no bigger number does.
notes.C: 4 divides 12 but it does not divide 10. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.
notes.D: 10 divides itself but it does not divide 12. The HCF must divide both numbers exactly.

hints: The three fractions have different bottom numbers. They must all be changed to the same bottom number before you add or subtract.
Find the smallest number that 4, 3 and 2 all divide into. Change each fraction so that it has that number at the bottom.
Example: 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/6. All three can be written in sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 − 1/6. The tops give 3 + 2 − 1 = 4, so the result is 4/6, which simplifies to 2/3.

steps.text: The smallest number that 4, 3 and 2 all divide into is 12. So change every fraction into twelfths.
Now work on the tops and keep 12 below: 3 + 8 − 6 = 5.

notes.A: Well done! In twelfths the sum is 3/12 + 8/12 − 6/12, which is 5/12.
notes.B: Check each change to twelfths: 1/4 is 3/12, 2/3 is 8/12 and 1/2 is 6/12. Then work out 3 + 8 − 6 for the top.
notes.C: 1/3 is the same as 4/12, which is close. Check the tops once more: 3 + 8 − 6.
notes.D: It looks as if the tops and the bottoms were added and subtracted separately. Fractions need the same bottom number first, so change them all into twelfths.

hints: An improper fraction becomes a mixed fraction by division. The top number is shared out by the bottom number.
Divide 57 by 17. Find how many whole 17s fit into 57 and how much is left over.
Example: 53/12. 12 × 4 = 48, so 12 fits 4 times with 53 − 48 = 5 left over. So 53/12 = 4 5/12.

steps.text: Divide 57 by 17. 17 × 3 = 51 and 17 × 4 = 68, so 17 fits into 57 three whole times.
The remainder is 57 − 51 = 6.
The whole part is 3, the remainder 6 goes on top, and the bottom stays 17. So 57/17 = 3 6/17.

notes.A: 2 7/17 is only 41/17, because 2 × 17 + 7 = 41. Check how many times 17 fits into 57.
notes.B: Yes! 17 fits into 57 three times with 6 left over, so 57/17 = 3 6/17.
notes.C: The whole part and the remainder are right, but the bottom number must stay 17. The pieces are still seventeenths.
notes.D: The whole part 3 is right, but the fraction part must be the remainder over 17. Find 57 − 51 and put it over 17.

hints: Each friend eats one part of a pizza that is cut into equal parts. Think about how many friends one whole pizza can feed.
Work out how many friends one whole pizza feeds, if each friend eats 1/3 of it.
Example: 20 children each eat 1/4 of a cake. One cake feeds 4 children, and 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so they need 5 cakes.

steps.text: Each friend eats 1/3 of a pizza, so one whole pizza feeds 3 friends.
Count the groups of 3 among the 12 friends: 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
They should order 4 pizzas.

notes.A: 3 is the number of friends one pizza feeds, not the number of pizzas. Divide the 12 friends into groups of 3.
notes.B: 5 pizzas would be 15 thirds, which is more than the 12 thirds needed. Divide 12 by 3.
notes.C: Great job! One pizza feeds 3 friends, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4.
notes.D: 6 pizzas would be right if each friend ate half a pizza. Here each friend eats one third, so one pizza feeds 3 friends.

hints: In each fraction the top is just 1 less than the bottom. So each one is a whole with one small piece missing. Think about which missing piece is the smallest.
Write down how much each fraction is short of 1. For example, 17/18 is 1/18 short of a whole. Then compare those missing pieces.
Example: which is larger, 5/6 or 7/8? 5/6 is 1/6 short of 1, and 7/8 is 1/8 short of 1. 1/8 is the smaller piece, so 7/8 is closer to 1 and is the larger fraction.

steps.text: Each fraction is one piece short of a whole. 16/17 is short by 1/17, 17/18 by 1/18, 18/19 by 1/19 and 19/20 by 1/20.
When a whole is cut into more parts, each part is smaller. So 1/20 is the smallest of the missing pieces.
The key idea is that the fraction with the smallest piece missing is the closest to 1, so it is the largest.
The largest fraction is 19/20.

notes.A: 17/18 is 1/18 short of a whole. Look for the fraction with an even smaller piece missing.
notes.B: 18/19 is 1/19 short of a whole, which is very close. One fraction has an even smaller piece missing.
notes.C: 16/17 is 1/17 short of a whole, which is the biggest gap of the four. That makes it the smallest of these fractions, not the largest.
notes.D: Well done! 19/20 is only 1/20 short of a whole, the smallest gap of all.

hints: To change an improper fraction into a mixed fraction, divide the top by the bottom. The quotient is the whole part and the remainder goes over the bottom number.
Divide 115 by 8. It may help to take out 80 first, which is 8 × 10, and then deal with what is left.
Example: 97/6. 6 × 16 = 96, so 6 fits 16 times with 97 − 96 = 1 left over. So 97/6 = 16 1/6.

steps.text: Divide 115 by 8. First, 8 × 10 = 80, which leaves 115 − 80 = 35.
Next, 8 × 4 = 32, which leaves 35 − 32 = 3. So 8 fits 10 + 4 = 14 times, with remainder 3.
The whole part is 14 and the remainder 3 goes over 8. So 115/8 = 14 3/8.

notes.A: The whole part 14 is right. Check the remainder: 8 × 14 = 112, so find 115 − 112.
notes.B: 12 5/8 is only 101/8, because 8 × 12 + 5 = 101. See how many times 8 really fits into 115.
notes.C: The whole part 14 is right. The remainder is 115 − 112, so check that subtraction.

hints: Equivalent fractions show the same amount. Two fractions are equivalent if both simplify to the same fraction.
Take the pairs one at a time. Simplify each fraction to its lowest terms, starting with 15/20 and 9/12, and see whether the two match.
Example: are 6/8 and 9/12 equivalent? 6/8 simplifies to 3/4 and 9/12 also simplifies to 3/4, so yes. Are 3/10 and 5/20? 5/20 simplifies to 1/4, which is not 3/10, so no.

steps.text: 15/20 and 9/12 both simplify to 3/4, so they are equivalent.
16/24 simplifies to 2/3. Also 33/55 and 15/25 both simplify to 3/5. So those two pairs are equivalent too.
7/25 cannot be simplified. To compare, write it with 50 below: 7/25 = 14/50, which is not the same as 15/50.
So the pair that is not equivalent is 7/25, 15/50.

notes.A: 15/20 and 9/12 both simplify to 3/4, so this pair is equivalent. Look for the pair that does not match.
notes.B: 16/24 simplifies to 2/3, since 16 ÷ 8 = 2 and 24 ÷ 8 = 3. This pair is equivalent, so look for the pair that does not match.
notes.C: 33/55 and 15/25 both simplify to 3/5, so this pair is equivalent. Look for the pair that does not match.
notes.D: Yes! 7/25 is the same as 14/50, which is a little less than 15/50, so the two are not equivalent.

hints: The second amount is a fraction of what was left, not of the whole cake. Keep track of how much cake remains after each day.
First find what fraction of the cake is left after Saturday. Then think of that remainder as three equal parts, because James eats two of the three on Sunday.
Example: Meena eats half a pizza, then three quarters of the remainder. The remainder is 1/2, and she leaves one quarter of it. A quarter of 1/2 is 1/8, so 1/8 of the pizza is left.

steps.text: After Saturday, half of the cake is left.
On Sunday James eats two thirds of that half, so one third of the half is left. The trap is to take two thirds of the whole cake instead.
Cut the half into 3 equal parts. Each part is 1/6 of the whole cake, because 6 such parts make the whole cake.
The fraction of the cake left for Monday is 1/6.

notes.A: 1/4 would be left if he ate half of the remainder on Sunday. He ate two thirds of the remaining half, so one third of the half is left.
notes.B: 1/3 is the part of the remainder that is left, not the part of the whole cake. The remainder was only half the cake, so take one third of a half.
notes.C: Well done! One third of the remaining half is 1/6 of the whole cake.
notes.D: The amount can be found, and it is among the fractions given. Find one third of the half that was left after Saturday.

hints: Equivalent fractions show the same amount. In an equivalent pair, the top and the bottom have both been multiplied or divided by the same number.
Take the pairs one at a time. Simplify both fractions in a pair to their lowest terms and see whether they match.
Example: are 4/6 and 10/15 equivalent? Both simplify to 2/3, so yes. Are 3/8 and 6/24? 6/24 simplifies to 1/4, which is not 3/8, so no.

steps.text: 14/21 and 8/12 both simplify to 2/3, so they are equivalent.
15/20 and 9/12 both simplify to 3/4, so they are equivalent.
From 7/15 to 14/45 the top was doubled but the bottom was multiplied by 3. Doubling both gives 7/15 = 14/30, not 14/45.
So the pair that is not equivalent is 7/15, 14/45.

notes.A: 14/21 and 8/12 both simplify to 2/3, so this pair is equivalent. Look for the pair that does not match.
notes.B: Yes! 7/15 is the same as 14/30, not 14/45, so the two are not equivalent.
notes.C: 15/20 and 9/12 both simplify to 3/4, so this pair is equivalent. Look for the pair that does not match.
notes.D: One pair here does not match. Look at 7/15 and 14/45: the top was multiplied by 2 but the bottom by 3.

hints: The right side is a mixed fraction and the left side is an improper fraction with the same bottom number. Change the mixed fraction into an improper fraction.
Each whole is 19 nineteenths. Start by finding how many nineteenths there are in 6 wholes.
Example: 4 5/12 as an improper fraction. 4 wholes are 4 × 12 = 48 twelfths. Adding the 5 extra twelfths gives 48 + 5 = 53, so 4 5/12 = 53/12.

steps.text: One whole is 19 nineteenths. So 6 wholes are 6 × 19 = 114 nineteenths.
Add the 15 extra nineteenths: 114 + 15 = 129.
So 6 15/19 = 129/19, and ★ represents 129.

notes.A: Check 6 × 19 again. It is 114, and then the 15 is added on top of that.
notes.B: 139 is 10 too many. 6 × 19 = 114, and 114 + 15 is what you need.
notes.D: 119 is 10 too few. 6 × 19 = 114, and then add 15, taking care with the carry.

hints: Like fractions are fractions whose bottom numbers are all the same. The top numbers can be different.
Look only at the bottom numbers in each group. Find the group where they all match.
Example: 1/9, 4/9 and 7/9 are like fractions because every bottom number is 9. But 1/3, 1/5 and 1/8 are not, because their bottom numbers are different.

steps.text: Like fractions have the same bottom number, which is called the denominator.
In 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 the tops match but the bottoms are 2, 3 and 4. The groups 2/3, 4/5, 1/6 and 3/7, 5/9, 2/11 have different bottoms as well.
Only one group has the same bottom number, 5, in every fraction. The like fractions are 2/5, 3/5, 4/5.

notes.A: Yes! All three fractions have 5 as the bottom number, so they are like fractions.
notes.B: These have the same top number, 1, but the bottoms are 2, 3 and 4. Like fractions need the same bottom number.
notes.C: The bottom numbers here are 3, 5 and 6, which are all different. Like fractions need the same bottom number.
notes.D: The bottom numbers here are 7, 9 and 11, which are all different. Like fractions need the same bottom number.

hints: All four fractions have the same bottom number, so the pieces are all the same size. Only the number of pieces differs.
Compare the top numbers 3, 5, 2 and 6. More pieces of the same size make a bigger fraction.
Example: in 2/9, 8/9, 4/9 and 5/9 the pieces are all ninths. 8 is the biggest top number, so 8/9 is the largest.

steps.text: Every fraction has 7 below, so each one counts sevenths, and the pieces are the same size.
The tops are 3, 5, 2 and 6. The biggest top number is 6, which means the most pieces.
The largest fraction is 6/7.

notes.A: 3/7 has only 3 sevenths. Look for the fraction with the most sevenths.
notes.B: 5/7 is large, but one of the fractions has even more sevenths.
notes.C: 2/7 has the fewest sevenths, so it is the smallest. The question asks for the largest.
notes.D: Well done! 6 sevenths is more than 2, 3 or 5 sevenths.

hints: All four fractions have the same top number, so each has the same number of pieces. What changes is the size of each piece.
Think about cutting a whole into 2, 4, 5 or 8 equal pieces. Decide which cut gives the smallest pieces.
Example: in 2/3, 2/9, 2/5 and 2/7, each fraction has 2 pieces. Ninths are the smallest pieces, so 2/9 is the smallest fraction.

steps.text: Every fraction has 3 pieces. The bottom number tells how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.
The more pieces a whole is cut into, the smaller each piece is. Eighths are smaller than fifths, quarters and halves.
So 3 eighths is the least amount. The smallest fraction is 3/8.

notes.A: Quarters are bigger pieces than eighths, so 3/4 is more than 3/8. Look for the biggest bottom number.
notes.B: Great job! Eighths are the smallest pieces here, so 3 of them make the smallest fraction.
notes.C: Fifths are bigger pieces than eighths, so 3/5 is more than 3/8. Look for the biggest bottom number.
notes.D: 3/2 has the smallest bottom number, but that means the biggest pieces. 3/2 is more than a whole, so it is the largest of the four.

hints: An improper fraction counts everything in the same size of piece. Here that means turning the whole numbers into fifths too.
Each whole is 5 fifths. Find how many fifths there are in 3 wholes.
Example: 2 3/4. Two wholes are 2 × 4 = 8 quarters. Adding the 3 extra quarters gives 8 + 3 = 11, so 2 3/4 = 11/4.

steps.text: Each whole is 5 fifths, so 3 wholes are 3 × 5 = 15 fifths.
Add the 2 extra fifths: 15 + 2 = 17 fifths.

notes.A: Yes! 3 wholes are 15 fifths, and 2 more fifths make 17/5.
notes.B: 15/5 is just the 3 wholes. The 2 extra fifths still need to be added.
notes.C: 32 comes from writing the 3 and the 2 side by side. Instead, multiply 3 by 5 and then add 2.
notes.D: It looks as if 3 was multiplied by 2 and then 5 was added. Multiply the whole number by the bottom number, 3 × 5, and then add the top number, 2.

hints: To change an improper fraction into a mixed number, divide the top by the bottom. The quotient is the whole part and the remainder becomes the new top.
Divide 23 by 4. Find how many whole 4s fit into 23 and how much is left over.
Example: 19/6. 6 × 3 = 18, so 6 fits 3 times with 19 − 18 = 1 left over. So 19/6 = 3 1/6.

steps.text: Divide 23 by 4. 4 × 5 = 20 and 4 × 6 = 24, so 4 fits into 23 five whole times.
The remainder is 23 − 20 = 3.
The whole part is 5 and the 3 left over are quarters. So 23/4 = 5 3/4.

notes.A: 5 1/4 is 21/4, because 5 × 4 + 1 = 21. Check the remainder: 23 − 20.
notes.B: Well done! 4 fits into 23 five times with 3 left over, so 23/4 = 5 3/4.
notes.C: 6 wholes would need 24 quarters, and there are only 23. See how many times 4 fits into 23 without going over.
notes.D: 4 3/4 is only 19/4, because 4 × 4 + 3 = 19. One more whole fits into 23 quarters.

hints: Both fractions are eighths, so the pieces are the same size. Adding them means counting the pieces altogether.
Add the top numbers 3 and 5 and keep 8 at the bottom. Then look at what that fraction equals.
Example: 2/6 + 3/6. The tops give 2 + 3 = 5, and the bottom stays 6, so the sum is 5/6.

steps.text: Both fractions are eighths. Add the tops and keep the bottom: 3 + 5 = 8, so the sum is 8/8.
8 eighths make one whole. So 3/8 + 5/8 = 1.

notes.A: The top 8 is right, but the bottoms were added too. The pieces are still eighths, so the bottom stays 8.
notes.B: Great job! 3 eighths and 5 eighths make 8 eighths, which is one whole.
notes.C: 2 comes from subtracting, 5 − 3. This is an addition, so add the tops.
notes.D: 15 comes from multiplying 3 by 5. When adding, add the tops: 3 + 5.

hints: Thirds and quarters are pieces of different sizes. Before adding, both fractions must be changed to the same bottom number.
Find the smallest number that both 3 and 4 divide into. Change each fraction so that it has that number at the bottom.
Example: 1/2 + 1/3. Both can be written in sixths: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Then 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

steps.text: Thirds and quarters are different sizes, so change both into twelfths, because 3 × 4 = 12.
Add the tops and keep the bottom: 4 + 3 = 7. So 1/3 + 1/4 = 7/12.

notes.A: The tops and the bottoms were both added. Thirds and quarters are different sizes, so change both into twelfths first.
notes.B: Well done! 1/3 is 4/12 and 1/4 is 3/12, and together they make 7/12.
notes.C: The bottoms were added to get 7. Bottom numbers are never added; find a common bottom number, 12, instead.
notes.D: 12 is the right bottom number, but the tops must change too. 1/3 becomes 4/12 and 1/4 becomes 3/12.

hints: The two fractions have different bottom numbers. Make the bottoms the same before you subtract.
6 is a multiple of 3. Change 1/3 into sixths by multiplying its top and bottom by 2.
Example: 7/8 − 1/4. Change 1/4 into eighths: 1/4 = 2/8. Then 7/8 − 2/8 = 5/8.

steps.text: Change 1/3 into sixths. Multiply its top and bottom by 2 to get 2/6.
Subtract the tops and keep the bottom: 5 − 2 = 3, so the result is 3/6.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 3. So 5/6 − 1/3 = 1/2.

notes.A: The tops and the bottoms were subtracted separately, 5 − 1 and 6 − 3. First change 1/3 into sixths, then subtract only the tops.
notes.B: Great job! 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, and 3/6 is the same as 1/2.
notes.C: 1 was taken from 5 without changing 1/3 into sixths. 1/3 is the same as 2/6, so take away 2.
notes.D: 7/6 comes from adding. This is a subtraction, so the result must be less than 5/6.

hints: Ascending means from smallest to largest. To compare fractions with different bottom numbers, change them all to the same bottom number.
Find the smallest number that 3, 4, 6 and 2 all divide into. Write every fraction with that number below.
Example: arrange 1/2, 3/8 and 3/4 in ascending order. In eighths they are 4/8, 3/8 and 6/8. From smallest to largest that is 3/8, 1/2, 3/4.

steps.text: The smallest number that 3, 4, 6 and 2 all divide into is 12. So change every fraction into twelfths.
Put the tops in order from smallest to largest: 6/12, 8/12, 9/12, 10/12.
In ascending order the fractions are 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 5/6.

notes.A: Well done! In twelfths these are 6/12, 8/12, 9/12 and 10/12, which go up in order.
notes.B: 1/2 is 6/12 and 2/3 is 8/12, so 1/2 is the smaller one and must come first.
notes.C: This is the right order turned around, from largest to smallest. Ascending means the smallest comes first.
notes.D: 3/4 is 9/12 and 2/3 is 8/12, so 2/3 must come before 3/4.

hints: Place value tells how much a digit is worth because of where it sits in the number. It is the digit multiplied by the value of its place.
Count the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. Find which place the 1 sits in, then multiply 1 by the value of that place.
Here is a similar one: in 3,582 the digit 3 is in the thousands place. Its place value is 3 × 1000 = 3000.

steps.text: Count the places in 16378 from the right: 8 is ones, 7 is tens, 3 is hundreds, 6 is thousands and 1 is ten-thousands.
Multiply the digit by the value of its place.
The place value of the digit 1 is 10000.

notes.A: 10001 has an extra 1 at the end. A place value is the digit followed only by zeros, so count the places after the 1 again.
notes.B: 100000 has one zero too many; that would be the lakhs place. In 16378 there are only four digits after the 1.
notes.C: Well done! The 1 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 1 × 10000 = 10000.
notes.D: 1 is the face value, which is just the digit itself. The place value also uses where the digit sits, so multiply by the value of the ten-thousands place.

hints: This is about place value. Each place is worth ten times the place on its right, so think about how many places apart two digits must be for one to be worth a thousand times the other.
In each number, find the two 6s and name the place each one sits in. Write the place value of each 6 and compare them. Test every number, not just the first one that fits.

Here is a similar one with the digit 4. In 40,040 one 4 is in the ten-thousands place and is worth 40,000. The other 4 is in the tens place and is worth 40. Since 40 × 1000 = 40,000, one is a thousand times the other.

steps.text: A thousand times means three places to the left, because 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000. So look for two 6s that are three places apart.
In 576006 the 6s are worth 6000 and 6.
In 567060 the 6s are worth 60000 and 60.
In 657600 the 6s are worth 600000 and 600.
The rule works in every number, so the answer is All of them. The trap is stopping at the first number that fits.

notes.A: 576006 does fit, because its 6s are worth 6000 and 6. Keep going, though, and test the other numbers in the same way before you choose.
notes.B: 567060 does fit, because its 6s are worth 60000 and 60. Keep going, though, and test the other numbers in the same way before you choose.
notes.C: 657600 does fit, because its 6s are worth 600000 and 600. Keep going, though, and test the other numbers in the same way before you choose.
notes.D: Great checking! In every number the two 6s are three places apart, so one is always worth a thousand times the other.

hints: This is a careful counting problem with Roman numerals. The symbol V appears in some numbers and not in others, so the safest way is to go through the numbers in order.
Write the Roman numerals from I to X first and mark every one that has a V in it. Then notice that XI to XX are the same numerals with an X in front.
Here is a similar one: how many times is the symbol I used in writing I to V? I has one, II has two, III has three, IV has one and V has none. That is 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 7 times.

steps.text: From I to X, the numerals with a V are IV, V, VI, VII and VIII. Each has one V, so that is 5 times.
From XI to XX the same pattern repeats with an X in front: XIV, XV, XVI, XVII and XVIII. That is 5 more.
IX, XIX and XX are written with X and have no V at all. It is also easy to miss IV and XIV, where the V hides after an I.
Add the two groups. The symbol V is used 10 times.

notes.A: 9 is one short. Check that you counted both IV and XIV, where the V comes after an I.
notes.B: 11 is one too many. IX and XIX are written with X, not V, so they should not be counted.
notes.C: Well counted! Five numerals from I to X use a V and five more from XI to XX, which makes 10.
notes.D: 12 is two too many. Only the numbers 4 to 8 and 14 to 18 use a V; IX and XIX do not.

hints: To write a number in Roman numerals, split it into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Then write each part with its own symbols, biggest part first.
Split 1946 into 1000 + 900 + 40 + 6. Remember that 900 and 40 are each written by putting a smaller symbol before a bigger one.
Here is a similar one: 1494 = 1000 + 400 + 90 + 4. These parts are M, CD, XC and IV, so 1494 is MCDXCIV.

steps.text: Split the number by place.
1000 is M. 900 is 100 less than 1000, so it is CM.
40 is 10 less than 50, so it is XL. 6 is 5 and 1 more, so it is VI.
Join the parts in order: M, CM, XL and VI. So 1946 is MCMXLVI.

notes.A: Here the C comes before both Ms, so the thousands and the hundreds are in a muddled order. Write 1000 first as M, and then 900 as CM.
notes.B: Exactly right! M is 1000, CM is 900, XL is 40 and VI is 6, which makes 1946.
notes.C: MMC means 1000 + 1000 + 100, so this numeral is 2146. For 900 the C must come before the M.
notes.D: This one starts well, but XXX is 30, so it shows 1936. The tens part needs to be 40, which is XL.

hints: This is about writing a number name in figures. In the Indian system the periods are lakhs, then thousands, then the last three digits for hundreds, tens and ones.
Write each part on its own: how many lakhs, how many thousands, and what the last three digits are. The thousands period needs two digits, so use a zero to fill an empty place.
Here is a similar one: two lakh five thousand three hundred forty. There are 2 lakhs, 05 thousands and 340 at the end, so it is written 2,05,340.

steps.text: One lakh is 1,00,000. One thousand is 1,000. One hundred ten is 110.
Add the three parts.
The thousands period shows 01 because there is only one thousand. So the number in figures is 101110.

notes.A: 1001110 has seven digits, which makes it ten lakh one thousand one hundred ten. One lakh needs only six digits.
notes.B: 1010110 has seven digits, so it is more than ten lakh. One lakh is a 1 followed by five more digits.
notes.C: Correct! 1 lakh, 01 thousand and 110 written together make 101110.
notes.D: In 111110 the thousands period reads 11, so it is one lakh eleven thousand one hundred ten. There is only one thousand here, so that period should be 01.

hints: This is a puzzle about a two-digit number and the number made by swapping its digits. The difference between them depends on how far apart the two digits are.
To make 'MN' − 'NM' as large as possible, make M as big as you can and N as small as you can. Read the rules carefully: neither digit may be zero.
Here is a similar one. Suppose the digits could only be chosen from 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. The biggest gap is between 6 and 2, so the numbers are 62 and 26, and 62 − 26 = 36.

steps.text: 'MN' has tens digit M and units digit N, and 'NM' is the same two digits swapped. For a large difference, 'MN' should be big and 'NM' should be small.
The biggest digit is 9, so M is 9. The smallest digit allowed is 1, because the digits cannot be zero. So N is 1.
The two numbers are 91 and 19.
The trap is choosing 0 for N, which is not allowed. With 9 and 1, the largest possible value is 72.

notes.A: Excellent! The digits 9 and 1 are as far apart as the rules allow, and 91 − 19 = 72.
notes.B: 81 comes from 90 − 9, which uses a zero as one digit. The question says both digits are non zero, so the smallest N can be is 1.
notes.C: 63 comes from digits that are 7 apart, such as 92 and 29. You can make the gap bigger by using 9 and 1.
notes.D: 54 comes from digits that are 6 apart, such as 93 and 39. Try the biggest digit with the smallest digit that is allowed.

hints: This question uses place value twice and then asks for a difference. Difference means you subtract the smaller value from the bigger one.
Find which place the 7 sits in and which place the 5 sits in, in 978652. Write the place value of each digit before you subtract.
Here is a similar one: in 483926, find the difference between the place values of 8 and 2. The 8 is worth 80000 and the 2 is worth 20, so the difference is 80000 − 20 = 79980.

steps.text: In 978652 the 7 is in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 70000.
The 5 is in the tens place, so it is worth 50.
Subtract the smaller value from the bigger one.
The difference between the two place values is 69950.

notes.A: 70050 is 70000 + 50, which is the sum of the two place values. The word difference tells you to subtract.
notes.B: Well done! The 7 is worth 70000 and the 5 is worth 50, and 70000 − 50 = 69950.
notes.C: Check the place of each digit again. The 7 is worth 70000 and the 5 is worth 50, so take 50 away from 70000.
notes.D: Write the two place values, 70000 and 50, one under the other and subtract carefully. Borrowing across the zeros needs extra care.

hints: This is about odd and even numbers. You do not need to know m and n exactly; you only need the rules for what happens when odd and even numbers are multiplied and added.
Remember that any number times an even number is even, and odd times odd is odd. Decide whether each part of an expression is odd or even, then think about adding the parts.
Here is a similar one. Suppose p is even and q is odd, and we look at 7p + q. 7p is even because p is even, and even + odd is odd. Trying p = 2 and q = 3 gives 14 + 3 = 17, which is odd.

steps.text: Any number times an even number is even, and odd times odd is odd. Also even + even is even, and even + odd is odd.
In m + 3n, m is even. 3n is odd times odd, so it is odd. Even + odd is odd.
In 3m + 4n and in 5m + 6n both parts are even, so the totals are even. 5mn has the even number m as a factor, so it is even too.
Check with m = 2 and n = 1.
5 is odd, so the expression that is always odd is m + 3n.

notes.A: 3m is even because m is even, and 4n is even because 4 is even. Even + even is even, so look for an expression with exactly one odd part.
notes.B: Great thinking! m is even and 3n is odd, and an even number plus an odd number is always odd.
notes.C: 5m is even because m is even, and 6n is even because 6 is even. Two even parts add up to an even number.
notes.D: A product is even as soon as one of its factors is even, and m is even. Try m = 2 and n = 1 to see that 5mn is 10.

hints: Before comparing Roman numerals, check that each one is written by the rules. A numeral that breaks the rules is not a proper number, so it cannot be the answer.

Remember two rules: a symbol may be repeated at most three times in a row, and only one smaller symbol may be placed before a bigger one to subtract. Set aside any numeral that breaks a rule, then work out the value of the rest.

Here is a similar one: compare XXIV and XVIII. XXIV is 10 + 10 + 4 = 24 and XVIII is 10 + 5 + 3 = 18. Both follow the rules, so XXIV is larger. A numeral like IIII would not count, because I is repeated four times.

steps.text: XXXXIX repeats X four times in a row, which is not allowed. XXLIV puts two Xs before L, which is not allowed either. So neither is a proper Roman numeral.
XXXIX is three tens and a nine.
XXVIII is two tens, a five and three ones.
39 is more than 28, so the largest proper numeral is XXXIX. The trap is picking the longest numeral without checking the rules.

notes.A: Well spotted! XXXIX is 39, and it is the largest of the numerals that follow the rules.
notes.B: XXXXIX looks big, but X is written four times in a row. A symbol may be repeated only three times, so this is not a proper numeral; 49 is written XLIX.
notes.C: In XXLIV two Xs stand before L, and only one smaller symbol may be put before a bigger one. It is not a proper numeral, so check the values of the others.
notes.D: XXVIII is a proper numeral, but it is only 10 + 10 + 5 + 3 = 28. One of the other proper numerals is bigger.

hints: This is a counting problem with two rules to obey at once. An even number must end in an even digit, and a four-digit number cannot begin with 0.
The even digits here are 0 and 4, so sort the numbers into two groups: those ending in 0 and those ending in 4. Count each group separately, taking care with the first digit.

Here is a similar one: using 5, 2 and 0 once each, how many three-digit even numbers are there? Ending in 0 there are 250 and 520. Ending in 2 there is only 502, because 052 begins with 0. That makes 2 + 1 = 3 numbers.

steps.text: Even numbers here end in 0 or 4. If the last digit is 0, the digits 7, 4 and 3 fill the other three places.
If the last digit is 4, the first digit cannot be 0, so it is 7 or 3. The two digits left can fill the middle places in 2 ways.
