Start with 2 and 3. Their squares are 4 and 9. Add them and decide whether the total is a square number, then test the other pairs the same way.
Here is a similar one. Try 3 and 4. 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 4 = 16, and 9 + 16 = 25. Since 25 is 5 × 5, the squares of 3 and 4 add up to a square number.

steps.text: Test 2 and 3. Their squares are 4 and 9, and 4 + 9 = 13. 13 is not a square number.
Test 5 and 6: 25 + 36 = 61. Test 4 and 6: 16 + 36 = 52. Both totals lie between 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64, so neither is a square number.
Test 6 and 8. Their squares are 36 and 64, which add up to 100.
100 is 10 × 10, which is a square number. So the two numbers are 6 and 8.

notes.A: The squares of 2 and 3 are 4 and 9, which add up to 13. 13 is not a square number, so test the other pairs.
notes.B: The squares of 5 and 6 are 25 and 36, which add up to 61. 61 lies between 49 and 64, so it is not a square number.
notes.C: The squares of 4 and 6 are 16 and 36, which add up to 52. 52 lies between 49 and 64, so it is not a square number.
notes.D: Great job! 36 + 64 = 100, and 100 is 10 × 10, a square number.

hints: A square number is a number multiplied by itself. List the square numbers that have two digits, then pick out the even ones.
Start with 4 × 4, which is the first square with two digits. Carry on with 5 × 5, 6 × 6 and so on until the answer has three digits.
Here is a similar one. How many odd square numbers are less than 100? The squares below 100 are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 and 81. The odd ones are 1, 9, 25, 49 and 81, so there are 5.

steps.text: List the square numbers with two digits: 4 × 4 = 16, 5 × 5 = 25, 6 × 6 = 36, 7 × 7 = 49, 8 × 8 = 64 and 9 × 9 = 81. The next one, 10 × 10 = 100, has three digits.
Pick out the even ones. They are 16, 36 and 64.
So there are 3 even two-digit square numbers.

notes.A: Excellent thinking! The even two-digit squares are 16, 36 and 64, which makes 3.
notes.B: There is more than one. Check 16, 36 and 64, which are all even squares with two digits.
notes.C: You are close. List all the squares from 4 × 4 to 9 × 9 and check each one, so that none is missed.
notes.D: 6 is the number of all the two-digit squares. Only the even ones are wanted, so leave out 25, 49 and 81.

hints: You need the square number that comes just after 710. Find it by multiplying numbers by themselves, then see how far it is from 710.
Start with a square you know: 25 × 25 = 625, which is less than 710. Try the next numbers after 25 until the square goes past 710.
Here is a similar one. What must be added to 300 to make a square number? 17 × 17 = 289 is too small, and the next square is 18 × 18 = 324. 324 − 300 = 24, so add 24.

steps.text: Find the squares near 710. 26 × 26 = 676 is less than 710, and 27 × 27 = 729 is more than 710.
So 729 is the first square number after 710. Find the gap between them.
Test the other choices so that you are sure: 710 + 15 = 725, 710 + 25 = 735 and 710 + 31 = 741. None of these is a square, because the square after 729 is 28 × 28 = 784.
So 19 should be added to 710, which gives the square number 729.

notes.B: 710 + 15 = 725, which lies between 26 × 26 = 676 and 27 × 27 = 729. It is not a square number.
notes.C: 710 + 25 = 735, which is just past 27 × 27 = 729. Find the exact gap from 710 to 729.
notes.D: 710 + 31 = 741, which lies between 27 × 27 = 729 and 28 × 28 = 784. It is not a square number.

hints: The square root of a number is the number that gives it when multiplied by itself. Use squares you know to get close, then use the last digit to decide.
20 × 20 = 400 and 30 × 30 = 900, so the square root is between 20 and 30. Now think about which last digits give a square ending in 6.

Here is a similar one: the square root of 324. 10 × 10 = 100 and 20 × 20 = 400, so it lies between 10 and 20. A square ending in 4 comes from a number ending in 2 or 8. 12 × 12 = 144 is too small, and 18 × 18 = 324, so the square root is 18.

steps.text: 20 × 20 = 400 and 30 × 30 = 900. 576 lies between them, so its square root is between 20 and 30.
576 ends in 6. A number ending in 4 or 6 gives a square ending in 6, so the number to try is 24 or 26.
24 times 24 is 576, so the square root of 576 is 24.

notes.A: 25 × 25 = 625, which is too big, and it ends in 5 instead of 6. Try a number just below 25.
notes.B: 288 is half of 576. A square root is not a half: it is the number that gives 576 when multiplied by itself.
notes.C: Well done! 24 × 24 = 576, so 24 is the square root of 576.
notes.D: 23 × 23 = 529, which is too small. Try the next number up.

hints: The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself. This is a two-digit multiplication, so break it into easier parts.
Write the sum as 23 × 23. Split one 23 into 20 and 3, and multiply 23 by each part.
Here is a similar one. The square of 14 is 14 × 14. Split it: 14 × 10 = 140 and 14 × 4 = 56. Then 140 + 56 = 196, so the square of 14 is 196.

steps.text: The square of 23 means 23 × 23.
Split the second 23 into 20 and 3. 23 × 20 = 460 and 23 × 3 = 69.
Add the two parts together. The square of 23 is 529.

notes.A: 46 is 23 × 2, the same as 23 + 23. Squaring means multiplying 23 by 23.
notes.B: 552 is 23 × 24. For the square, both numbers must be 23.
notes.C: Great job! 23 × 20 = 460 and 23 × 3 = 69, and together they make 529.
notes.D: 528 is 1 too few. Check the last digit: 3 × 3 = 9, so the square of 23 ends in 9.

hints: A date moves forward by 1 day of the week after an ordinary year, because 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day. It moves forward by 2 days when a 29 February falls in between.
Republic Day is 26 January. 2016 is a leap year, and its 29 February comes after Republic Day. So first work out the day for 26 January 2017, then go on year by year.

Here is a similar one. 15 August 2010 was a Sunday. An ordinary year pushes the day on by 1, so 15 August 2011 was a Monday. Between 15 August 2011 and 15 August 2012 there is a 29 February, so the day moves on by 2, to Wednesday.

steps.text: Republic Day is 26 January. A year of 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day, so the day of the week moves on by 1. If a 29 February falls in between, it moves on by 2.
2016 is a leap year and its 29 February comes after 26 January. So from 2016 to 2017 the day moves on by 2: Tuesday becomes Thursday. This is the step that is easy to miss.
From 2017 to 2018 the day moves on by 1 to Friday, and from 2018 to 2019 it moves on by 1 to Saturday.
From 26 January 2019 to 26 January 2020 there is no 29 February in between, because the leap day of 2020 comes later. The day moves on by 1 to Sunday.
So Republic Day falls on a Sunday in 2020.

notes.A: Excellent thinking! The day moves from Tuesday to Thursday, Friday, Saturday and then Sunday, which is in 2020.
notes.B: In 2019 Republic Day was on a Saturday. Count again from 2016, and remember that the leap day of 2016 pushes 2017 on by 2 days.
notes.C: In 2021 Republic Day was on a Tuesday, because the leap day of 2020 falls before 26 January 2021. Sunday comes one year earlier.
notes.D: In 2022 Republic Day was on a Wednesday. Count on from Tuesday in 2016 one year at a time, adding 2 days when a 29 February is passed.

hints: All Fool's Day is 1 April and Teachers' Day is 5 September. Count the days from one to the other, then see how many are left over after full weeks.
Count the days left in April after the 1st, then all of May, June, July and August, then the 5 days of September. Remember which months have 30 days and which have 31.

Here is a similar one. If 1 March is a Monday, what day is 10 April? There are 30 more days in March and 10 in April, which is 40 days. 40 days is 5 weeks and 5 days, and 5 days after Monday is Saturday.

steps.text: Teachers' Day is 5 September. Count the days after 1 April: 29 more in April, 31 in May, 30 in June, 31 in July, 31 in August and 5 in September.
Add them up to get 157 days.
Every 7 days brings back the same day of the week. 22 weeks is 22 × 7 = 154 days, so 157 days is 22 weeks and 3 days.
Three days after Saturday is Tuesday. Teachers' Day fell on a Tuesday.

notes.A: Monday is 2 days after Saturday. Count the days once more: after the full weeks are taken out, 3 days should be left over.
notes.B: Sunday is only 1 day after Saturday. Check the month lengths: May, July and August have 31 days each.
notes.C: Friday would be 6 days after Saturday. Add the days from 1 April to 5 September again and take out the full weeks.
notes.D: You got it! There are 157 days from 1 April to 5 September, which is 22 weeks and 3 days, and 3 days after Saturday is Tuesday.

hints: On a clock face, the minute hand takes 5 minutes to move from one number to the next. Count the steps the hand moves, always going forward the way a clock turns.
Work out how many 5-minute steps make 50 minutes. Then count the steps for each choice, going forward past XII where you need to.
Here is a similar one. How long does the minute hand take to go from VIII to II? Going forward, it passes IX, X, XI, XII, I and II, which is 6 steps. 6 × 5 = 30, so it takes 30 minutes.

steps.text: The minute hand takes 5 minutes to go from one number to the next. So 50 minutes is 10 steps.
From IX forward to III, the hand passes 12 and moves 6 steps, which is 30 minutes. From X to VI is 8 steps and from IV to XII is 8 steps, which is 40 minutes each.
From VI, the hand moves 6 steps up to XII and then 4 more steps on to IV. That is 10 steps.
10 steps of 5 minutes make 50 minutes. So the movement of 50 minutes is VI to IV.

notes.A: From IX forward to III is 6 steps, which is 30 minutes. Look for a move of 10 steps.
notes.B: From X forward to VI is 8 steps, which is 40 minutes. Look for a move of 10 steps.
notes.C: From IV forward to XII is 8 steps, which is 40 minutes. Look for a move of 10 steps.
notes.D: Well done! From VI the hand moves forward 10 steps to reach IV, and 10 steps of 5 minutes make 50 minutes.

hints: A watch that gains runs a little ahead of the real time. Find how much it gains altogether, then decide whether to add that or take it away.
Count the hours from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. The watch gains 2 minutes in each of those hours.
Here is a similar one. A clock gains 3 minutes every hour and is set right at 6:00 a.m. By 11:00 a.m., 5 hours have passed, so it has gained 5 × 3 = 15 minutes. It shows 11:15 a.m.

steps.text: From 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. is 12 hours.
The watch gains 2 minutes in every hour, so in 12 hours it gains 24 minutes.
A watch that gains is ahead of the real time, so the 24 minutes are added. Taking them away is the trap here.
24 minutes after 8:00 p.m. is 8:24 p.m. The watch shows 8:24 p.m.

notes.A: 8:20 p.m. is a gain of 20 minutes, which is only 10 hours of gaining. From 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. is 12 hours.
notes.B: 7:36 p.m. is 24 minutes behind the real time. A watch that gains runs ahead, so the 24 minutes are added.
notes.C: Great job! The watch gains 2 minutes in each of 12 hours, which is 24 minutes, so it shows 8:24 p.m.
notes.D: 8:02 p.m. is the gain for just 1 hour. The watch gains 2 minutes in each of the 12 hours.

hints: A watch that runs slow falls a little behind the real time. Find how much it loses altogether, then decide whether to add that or take it away.
Count the hours from 8:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. The watch loses 30 seconds in each of those hours, so find the total in seconds and change it to minutes.
Here is a similar one. A clock loses 20 seconds every hour and is set right at 6:00 a.m. By 3:00 p.m., 9 hours have passed, so it has lost 9 × 20 = 180 seconds, which is 3 minutes. It shows 2:57 p.m.

steps.text: From 8:00 a.m. to noon is 4 hours, and from noon to 10:00 p.m. is 10 hours. That is 14 hours.
The watch loses 30 seconds in each hour, so in 14 hours it loses 420 seconds.
Change the seconds to minutes. 420 seconds is 7 minutes.
A slow watch is behind the real time, so the 7 minutes are taken away, not added. 7 minutes before 10:00 p.m. is 9:53 p.m., so the watch shows 9:53 p.m.

notes.A: 9:57 p.m. is only 3 minutes behind. Count the hours from 8:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. again: there are 14, and each one loses half a minute.
notes.B: 9:46 p.m. is 14 minutes behind, which would be a whole minute lost every hour. The watch loses only 30 seconds an hour, which is half a minute.
notes.C: Excellent thinking! In 14 hours the watch loses 7 minutes, so it shows 9:53 p.m.
notes.D: 10:07 p.m. is 7 minutes ahead. A slow watch falls behind, so the 7 minutes are taken away.

hints: A decimal shows parts out of 10 or 100, but minutes are parts out of 60. Work out what fraction of an hour the minutes make before you write a decimal.
Keep the 3 whole hours as they are. Write 45 minutes as a fraction of 60 minutes and make that fraction as simple as you can.
Here is a similar one. Write 2 hours 30 minutes as a decimal. 30 minutes out of 60 is 30/60, which is 1/2 of an hour, or 0.5 of an hour. So it is 2.5 hours.

steps.text: An hour has 60 minutes, so 45 minutes is 45/60 of an hour.
Make the fraction simpler by dividing the top and the bottom by 15. 45/60 is the same as 3/4.
3/4 is the same as 75/100, which is 0.75 as a decimal.
Add this to the 3 whole hours. 3 hrs 45 min is 3.75 hr.

notes.A: 0.15 of an hour is only 9 minutes. 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour, so find the decimal for three quarters.
notes.B: 3.45 just copies the minutes after the point. Minutes are parts of 60, not parts of 100, so 45 minutes is 45/60 of an hour.
notes.C: You got it! 45 minutes is 3/4 of an hour, which is 0.75, so the time is 3.75 hr.
notes.D: 0.045 of an hour is less than 3 minutes. Write 45 minutes as 45/60 of an hour and make the fraction simpler.

hints: A date moves forward by 1 day of the week after an ordinary year, because 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day. After a leap year of 366 days it moves forward by 2 days.
List the four years that pass: 2006, 2007, 2008 and 2009. Decide which of them is a leap year by checking which one divides exactly by 4.

Here is a similar one. 1 January 2014 was a Wednesday. 2014 and 2015 are ordinary years, so 1 January 2015 was a Thursday and 1 January 2016 was a Friday. 2016 is a leap year, so the day moves on by 2, and 1 January 2017 was a Sunday.

steps.text: An ordinary year has 365 days, which is 52 weeks and 1 day. So 1 January moves on by 1 day after an ordinary year and by 2 days after a leap year.
2006 and 2007 are ordinary years. So 1 January 2007 was a Monday and 1 January 2008 was a Tuesday.
2008 is a leap year, because it divides exactly by 4. So the day moves on by 2, and 1 January 2009 was a Thursday. This is the step that is easy to miss.
2009 is an ordinary year, so the day moves on by 1. 1st January 2010 fell on a Friday.

notes.A: Saturday is one day too far. Only one of the four years, 2008, is a leap year, so the day moves on by 5 days in all.
notes.B: Thursday counts 1 day for each of the four years. 2008 is a leap year, so it moves the day on by 2.
notes.C: Monday is where 1 January 2007 fell, after just one year. Keep going for all four years.
notes.D: Well done! Three ordinary years and one leap year move the day on by 5 days, from Sunday to Friday.

hints: A month of 30 days is 4 full weeks and 2 extra days. Every day of the week comes 4 times, and the days that fall on the first two dates come a fifth time.
Go back from the 19th in steps of 7 to find a Thursday early in April. Then work out what day the 1st was.

Here is a similar one. Suppose 17 June is a Friday. Going back in 7s, 10 June and 3 June are Fridays too, so 1 June is a Wednesday. June has 30 days, so the days on the 1st and 2nd, Wednesday and Thursday, come 5 times.

steps.text: Go back from Thursday 19 April in steps of 7. The 12th and the 5th of April are Thursdays too.
Count back from Thursday the 5th. The 4th is a Wednesday, the 3rd a Tuesday, the 2nd a Monday and the 1st a Sunday.
April has 30 days, which is 4 weeks and 2 days. The 29th and 30th fall on the same days as the 1st and 2nd.
Only the days of the 1st and 2nd come 5 times, and every other day comes 4 times. The days that appeared 5 times are Sunday & Monday.

notes.A: Monday is right, but Tuesday is the 3rd, and April has no 31st to give it a fifth turn. Check what day the 1st was.
notes.B: Only 2 days can come 5 times in a month of 30 days. Thursday falls on the 5th, 12th, 19th and 26th, which is just 4 times.
notes.C: Sunday is right, but Saturday falls on the 7th, 14th, 21st and 28th, which is only 4 times. The extra days are the 29th and 30th.
notes.D: Great job! 1 April was a Sunday, so Sunday and Monday also fall on the 29th and 30th and come 5 times.

hints: A leap year is a year that divides exactly by 4. Years that end in 00 are special: they are leap years only if they divide exactly by 400.
Sort the four years into two groups: those that end in 00 and those that do not. Test the 00 years with 400 and the others with 4.

Here is a similar one. Is 2016 a leap year? 2016 ÷ 4 = 504 with nothing left over, and it does not end in 00, so 2016 is a leap year. But 1800 ends in 00 and does not divide exactly by 400, so 1800 is not a leap year.

steps.text: A year is a leap year if it divides exactly by 4. Years ending in 00 must divide exactly by 400 instead.
2023 is an odd number, so it does not divide exactly by 4. It is not a leap year.
2100 and 1900 end in 00, and neither divides exactly by 400. So they are not leap years, even though they divide by 4. This is the trap.
2024 divides exactly by 4 and does not end in 00. So the leap year is 2024.

notes.A: 2100 divides by 4, but it ends in 00, so it must divide exactly by 400. It does not, so 2100 is not a leap year.
notes.B: 1900 divides by 4, but it ends in 00, so it must divide exactly by 400. It does not, so 1900 is not a leap year.
notes.C: Excellent thinking! 2024 ÷ 4 = 506 exactly, and it does not end in 00, so 2024 is a leap year.
notes.D: 2023 is an odd number, so it cannot be divided exactly by 4. Look for a year that divides by 4.

hints: Count the days month by month. Remember how many days each month has, and notice that both the first date and the last date are to be counted.
Start with March: count every day from the 1st to the 31st. Then think about how many days April has, and what is still left to count after April.
Here is a similar one. How many days are there from 1 April to 10 May, counting both dates? April has 30 days, and then there are 10 days in May. 30 + 10 = 40, so there are 40 days.

steps.text: Count all of March. From the 1st to the 31st is 31 days.
Count all of April, which has 30 days.
Then count 1 May itself, because both dates are included. That is 1 more day.
Add the three parts. There are 62 days.

notes.A: 61 counts March and April but leaves out 1 May. Both dates are included, so add 1 more day.
notes.B: You got it! 31 days in March, 30 in April and 1 day in May make 62 days.
notes.C: 63 is one too many. March has 31 days and April has 30, and then comes just 1 day in May.
notes.D: 60 treats both months as 30 days and leaves out 1 May. March has 31 days, and 1 May is counted too.

hints: From 1 January of one year to 1 January of the next is one whole year. Find how many days that is, then see how many are left over after full weeks.
Decide whether 2023 is a leap year by checking if it divides exactly by 4. That tells you how many days pass.
Here is a similar one. 1 January 2021 was a Friday. 2021 is not a leap year, so 365 days pass, which is 52 weeks and 1 day. The day moves on by 1, so 1 January 2022 was a Saturday.

steps.text: From 1 January 2023 to 1 January 2024 is the whole of 2023. 2023 is not a leap year, so that is 365 days.
52 weeks is 52 × 7 = 364 days. So 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day.
After 52 full weeks it is Sunday again. One more day makes it Monday, so 1st January 2024 was a Monday.

notes.A: It would be Sunday again only if a year were exactly 52 weeks, which is 364 days. 2023 has 365 days, so there is 1 day extra.
notes.B: Saturday is one day back. The extra day moves the date forward, not backward.
notes.C: Tuesday is a move of 2 days, which happens when 366 days pass. The days being counted here are all in 2023, which has 365 days.
notes.D: Well done! 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day, so the day moves on from Sunday to Monday.

hints: Count the days from one Republic Day to the next, then see how many are left over after full weeks. Check whether a 29 February falls between the two dates.
Republic Day is 26 January. 2008 is a leap year, but its 29 February comes after 26 January. So decide how many days there are from 26 January 2007 to 26 January 2008.
Here is a similar one. 15 August 2013 was a Thursday. No 29 February lies between that day and 15 August 2014, so 365 days pass. That is 52 weeks and 1 day, so the day moves on by 1, to Friday.

steps.text: Republic Day is 26 January. Between 26 January 2007 and 26 January 2008 there is no 29 February, because the leap day of 2008 comes later, in February.
So 365 days pass. 52 weeks is 364 days, so that is 52 weeks and 1 day.
The day moves on by 1, from Friday to Saturday. In 2008, Republic Day was celebrated on a Saturday.

notes.A: Thursday is one day back. The extra day in 365 days moves the date forward, not backward.
notes.B: Great job! 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day, so Republic Day moves on from Friday to Saturday.
notes.C: It would be Friday again only if exactly 52 weeks, or 364 days, had passed. There are 365 days between the two dates.
notes.D: Sunday is a move of 2 days. 2008 is a leap year, but its extra day comes on 29 February, after Republic Day, so only 1 day is added.

hints: A month of 31 days is 4 full weeks and 3 extra days. The days that come 5 times are the days that fall on the 1st, 2nd and 3rd.
Wednesday, Thursday and Friday come 5 times, so decide which of them falls on 1 July. Then count forward to the first Sunday.

Here is a similar one. In a month of 30 days, Monday and Tuesday come 5 times. The two extra days, the 29th and 30th, match the 1st and 2nd, so the 1st is a Monday. The first Sunday is then the 7th, and the other Sundays are the 14th, 21st and 28th.

steps.text: July has 31 days, which is 4 weeks and 3 days. The three extra days, the 29th, 30th and 31st, fall on the same days as the 1st, 2nd and 3rd.
The days that come 5 times are Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. So 1 July is a Wednesday, 2 July a Thursday and 3 July a Friday. Seeing this is the key to the question.
Then 4 July is a Saturday and 5 July is the first Sunday.
Add 7 each time to find the other Sundays: the 12th, the 19th and the 26th. The date that fell on a Sunday is 26th July.

notes.A: The 20th is the day after Sunday the 19th, so it is a Monday. Find the first Sunday and keep adding 7.
notes.B: 1 July is a Wednesday, so the 8th and the 15th are Wednesdays too. Count on from the 1st to find the first Sunday.
notes.C: Excellent thinking! 1 July is a Wednesday, so the Sundays are the 5th, 12th, 19th and 26th.
notes.D: The 31st falls on the same day as the 3rd, which is a Friday. The Sundays are the 5th and every 7 days after it.

hints: Hours and minutes are different units. Change the hours into minutes first, then put all the minutes together.
One hour is 60 minutes. Work out how many minutes there are in 3 hours.
Here is a similar one. How many minutes are in 2 hours 20 minutes? 2 hours is 2 × 60 = 120 minutes. Add the 20 minutes: 120 + 20 = 140 minutes.

steps.text: One hour is 60 minutes, so 3 hours is 180 minutes.
Add the extra 45 minutes. There are 225 minutes in 3 hours 45 minutes.

notes.A: 215 is 10 too few. Add 180 and 45 again, tens first and then ones.
notes.B: 345 just puts the 3 and the 45 side by side. An hour is 60 minutes, so change the 3 hours into minutes first.
notes.C: You got it! 3 hours is 180 minutes, and 180 + 45 = 225.
notes.D: 180 is the number of minutes in 3 hours. The 45 extra minutes still need to be added.

hints: To find how long something lasts, count up from the start time to the end time. Counting up in easy jumps is safer than subtracting.
Start at 2:40 PM and jump to the next full hour, 3:00 PM. Note how many minutes that jump is, then carry on to 5:10 PM.

Here is a similar one. A class starts at 9:50 AM and ends at 12:15 PM. From 9:50 to 10:00 is 10 minutes, from 10:00 to 12:00 is 2 hours, and from 12:00 to 12:15 is 15 minutes. That is 2 hours and 10 + 15 = 25 minutes.

steps.text: Count up from 2:40 PM in easy jumps. From 2:40 to 3:00 is 20 minutes.
From 3:00 to 5:00 is 2 hours.
From 5:00 to 5:10 is 10 minutes.
Put the jumps together: 2 hours, and 20 minutes plus 10 minutes. The movie is 2 hours 30 minutes long.

notes.A: 3 hours after 2:40 PM is 5:40 PM, which is already past the end of the movie. Count up to 3:00 first, then to 5:00, then to 5:10.
notes.B: Well done! 20 minutes, then 2 hours, then 10 minutes make 2 hours 30 minutes.
notes.C: 70 minutes is more than an hour, so this is really 3 hours 10 minutes, which is too long. Count up from 2:40 PM in jumps instead.
notes.D: 2 hours 10 minutes after 2:40 PM is only 4:50 PM. There are 20 more minutes to go to reach 5:10 PM.

hints: In 24-hour time the hours do not start again after noon. They carry on counting past 12, all the way to 23.
For a PM time, add 12 to the hours and leave the minutes as they are. Do that with the 3 in 3:45 PM.
Here is a similar one. Write 7:20 PM in 24-hour time. For a PM time, add 12 to the hours: 7 + 12 = 19. The minutes stay the same, so it is 19:20.

steps.text: In 24-hour time the hours carry on counting after 12 noon. For a PM time, add 12 to the hours.
Add 12 to the 3 hours to get hour 15.
The minutes stay the same. So 3:45 PM is 15:45.

notes.A: 13:45 is 1:45 PM, which adds only 10 to the hours. Add 12 to the 3 instead.
notes.B: 03:45 is 3:45 in the morning. For a PM time, add 12 to the hours.
notes.C: A day has only 24 hours, so there is no hour 35. Add 12 to the 3 hours and keep the minutes as 45.
notes.D: Great job! 3 + 12 = 15, and the minutes stay the same, so 3:45 PM is 15:45.

hints: Odd days are the days left over after you take out all the full weeks. Count the odd days that the ordinary years and the leap years give, then take out full weeks again.
An ordinary year has 1 odd day and a leap year has 2. First find how many leap years there are in 400 years, remembering that a year ending in 00 is a leap year only if it divides exactly by 400.

Here is a similar one. How many odd days are there in 5 years, if one of them is a leap year? The four ordinary years give 4 odd days and the leap year gives 2. 4 + 2 = 6, which is less than a full week, so there are 6 odd days.

steps.text: An ordinary year is 52 weeks and 1 day, so it has 1 odd day. A leap year is 52 weeks and 2 days, so it has 2 odd days.
In 400 years, every 4th year makes 100 years. Three of the four years ending in 00 are not leap years, so there are 97 leap years and 303 ordinary years.
The ordinary years give 303 odd days and the leap years give 97 × 2 = 194 odd days. Together that is 497 days.
497 days is exactly 71 weeks, with nothing left over. So there are 0 odd days in 400 years.

notes.A: 3 does not fit here. Count the leap years carefully, 97 of them in 400 years, then add up the odd days and take out full weeks of 7.
notes.B: Excellent thinking! The 497 extra days make exactly 71 weeks, so there are 0 odd days left over.
notes.C: 5 is the number of odd days in 100 years. In 400 years there is one more leap year than in four separate hundreds, and the total comes to full weeks exactly.
notes.D: 1 is the number of odd days in a single ordinary year. Add up the odd days for all 400 years, then take out the full weeks.

hints: This is a calendar problem. The same date moves forward by a day or two of the week each year, so think about how many days lie between the two dates and whether a 29th of February falls between them.
Check whether 2004 is a leap year and whether its February comes before 1st April 2004. Then find how many days are left over after full weeks from 1st April 2003 to 1st April 2004.

Here is a similar problem. 15th August 2015 was a Saturday. Between 15th August 2015 and 15th August 2016 there is a 29th of February, because 2016 is a leap year, so there are 366 days. 366 days make 52 weeks and 2 days left over. Two days after Saturday is Monday, so 15th August 2016 was a Monday.

steps.text: From 1st April 2003 to 1st April 2004 is one full year. The year 2004 is a leap year and its 29th of February comes before 1st April, so this stretch has 366 days.
A week has 7 days. 366 days make 52 full weeks with 2 days left over.
Full weeks bring us back to the same day, so only the 2 extra days matter. This is the trap: an ordinary year moves the day forward by 1, but the leap day makes it 2.
Two days after Tuesday is Thursday. So in 2004 it was celebrated on Thursday.

notes.A: Monday is one day before Tuesday. The day moves forward, not back, as the years go by, so count on from Tuesday.
notes.B: A date falls on the same day again only when the days in between make full weeks. Here 366 days leave 2 days over, so count 2 days on from Tuesday.
notes.C: Wednesday is what an ordinary year of 365 days would give, moving the day on by 1. Look for the 29th of February 2004 that falls in between.
notes.D: Yes! The leap day in February 2004 makes 366 days, which is 52 weeks and 2 days, and 2 days after Tuesday is Thursday.

hints: This is a calendar problem. Every month has four full weeks plus a few extra days, and only the days of the week that land on those extra days come five times.
April has 30 days. Start by finding which day of the week the 1st of April was, by counting back in sevens from the 9th.

Here is a similar problem. Suppose 12th July is a Friday. Seven days earlier, the 5th is also a Friday, so the 4th is Thursday, the 3rd is Wednesday, the 2nd is Tuesday and the 1st is Monday. July has 31 days, which is 4 weeks and 3 days, so the first three days of the month, Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, come five times.

steps.text: Counting back 7 days from Monday the 9th gives Monday the 2nd. The day before that, the 1st of April, was a Sunday.
April has 30 days. That is 4 full weeks and 2 days more.
In 4 full weeks every day of the week comes 4 times. The 2 extra days are the 29th and 30th, which fall on the same days as the 1st and 2nd.
Sundays fall on 1, 8, 15, 22 and 29, and Mondays fall on 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30. So the days that occurred five times are Sunday and Monday.

notes.A: Well done! April began on a Sunday and has 4 weeks and 2 extra days, so Sunday and Monday each came five times.
notes.B: Monday does come five times, but check Tuesday: the Tuesdays fall on 3, 10, 17 and 24 only. Find the day on the 1st of April.
notes.C: April has only 30 days, which gives 2 extra days, not 3. The Saturdays fall on 7, 14, 21 and 28 only.
notes.D: There is a pair that works here. Find the day on the 1st of April, then see which days land on the 29th and 30th.

hints: This is a counting-days problem that runs across three months. Split it into the days left in the first month, the whole of the middle month, and the days used in the last month.
August has 31 days. Since 15th August is not counted, first find how many days are left in August after the 15th.

Here is a similar problem: the days from 20th March to 5th May, not counting 20th March. March has 31 days, so 31 − 20 = 11 days are left in March. April has 30 days, and May gives 5 days. 11 + 30 + 5 = 46 days.

steps.text: August has 31 days. Leaving out the 15th, we count the 16th to the 31st, which is 16 days.
September has 30 days, and all of them are counted.
In October we count the 1st and the 2nd, which is 2 days. Take care here: the 15th of August is left out, but the 2nd of October is counted.
Add the three parts: 16 + 30 + 2 = 48. So there are 48 days.

notes.A: 49 comes from counting 15th August as well. The question says not to count it, so August gives only 16 days.
notes.B: Great counting! 16 days in August, 30 in September and 2 in October make 48 days.
notes.C: 47 is one day short. August has 31 days, so 16 days are left after the 15th, and the 2nd of October is counted too.
notes.D: 50 is a little too many. Check that September has 30 days, not 31, and that 15th August is not counted.

hints: This is a time conversion with two jumps: hours to minutes, then minutes to seconds. Remember how many of the smaller unit make one of the bigger unit each time.
Start by changing 2 hours into minutes. One hour has 60 minutes.
Here is a similar problem: how many seconds are there in 3 hours? 3 hours is 3 × 60 = 180 minutes. 180 minutes is 180 × 60 = 10800 seconds.

steps.text: One hour has 60 minutes, so 2 hours have 2 × 60 = 120 minutes.
One minute has 60 seconds, so 120 minutes have 120 × 60 = 7200 seconds.
So there are 7200 seconds in 2 hours.

notes.A: You got it! 2 hours is 120 minutes, and 120 × 60 = 7200 seconds.
notes.B: 1200 comes from multiplying 120 minutes by 10. Each minute has 60 seconds, so multiply by 60.
notes.C: 3600 is the number of seconds in 1 hour. The question asks about 2 hours, so double it.
notes.D: 120 is the number of minutes in 2 hours. One more step is needed: change those minutes into seconds.

hints: This is a calendar problem. The same date moves forward one day of the week after an ordinary year, and two days when a 29th of February falls in between. Follow the date year by year.

Start from Monday in 2000 and find the day for 2nd October 2001. The leap day of 2000 came in February, before October, so check whether any 29th of February lies between October 2000 and October 2001.

Here is a similar problem. 5th July 2010 was a Monday, and we want the first later year when 5th July fell on a Friday. In 2011 it was Tuesday. In 2012 it was Thursday, because 29th February 2012 falls in between and moves it 2 days. In 2013 it was Friday. So the year is 2013.

steps.text: From one 2nd October to the next is usually 365 days, which is 52 weeks and 1 day, so the day moves forward by 1.
The leap day of 2000 was in February, before October, so it does not count here. In 2001 the day was Tuesday, in 2002 Wednesday and in 2003 Thursday.
Between October 2003 and October 2004 comes 29th February 2004. That stretch has 366 days, so the day jumps 2 days, from Thursday to Saturday. This is the trap: Friday is skipped.
One more ordinary year moves Saturday on to Sunday. So it was first celebrated on Sunday in 2005.

notes.A: In 2004 the day jumped from Thursday to Saturday because of the leap day, so 2nd October 2004 was a Saturday. Go one more year.
notes.B: By 2003 the day had moved on only 3 days from Monday, to Thursday. Keep counting year by year.
notes.C: Excellent thinking! The leap day of 2004 made the day jump to Saturday, and one more year brought it to Sunday in 2005.
notes.D: 2006 comes from moving one day every year for six years. The leap day of February 2004 makes one step a jump of 2 days, so Sunday arrives a year earlier.

hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles. The clues about angle B tell you which two angles make the equal pair.
Angle B is bigger than each of the other two angles, so it cannot be equal to either of them. Which two angles are left to be the equal pair?

Here is a similar one: triangle PQR is isosceles, angle P is 35°, and angle Q is bigger than both other angles. Angle Q cannot be in the equal pair, so angle R equals angle P, which is 35°. Then angle Q is 180° − 35° − 35° = 110°.

steps.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles.
Angle B is bigger than angle A and bigger than angle C, so it is not equal to either of them. The equal pair must be angle A and angle C.
Check that this fits: angle B would be 180° − 50° − 50° = 80°, which is bigger than 50°.
So angle C is equal to angle A, and angle C is 50°.

notes.A: 65° comes from sharing 180° − 50° = 130° equally between angles B and C. But angle B is bigger than angle C, so those two cannot be equal.
notes.B: 80° is the size of the biggest angle, angle B. The question asks for angle C, which is one of the equal pair.
notes.C: 130° is what angles B and C make together, 180° − 50°. Angle C is only one of those two angles.
notes.D: Yes! Angle B is the odd one out, so angles A and C are the equal pair and angle C is 50°, the same as angle A.

hints: This is an area of a triangle problem. A triangle covers half the space of a rectangle that has the same base and height.
First multiply the base by the height, 12 × 4. Then remember that the triangle is only half of that rectangle.
Here is a similar problem: a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm. Base times height is 10 × 6 = 60. Half of 60 is 30, so the area is 30 square cm.

steps.text: The area of a triangle is half of its base times its height.
Base times height is 12 × 4 = 48.
Half of 48 is 24. So the area is 24 square cm.

notes.A: 16 comes from adding the base and the height, 12 + 4. For area we multiply them and then take half.
notes.B: 96 comes from doubling 12 × 4 when it should be halved. A triangle is half of the rectangle.
notes.C: Great job! 12 × 4 = 48, and half of 48 is 24.
notes.D: 48 is 12 × 4, the area of the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of that.

hints: This is an area of a triangle problem. A triangle covers half the space of a rectangle that has the same base and height.
First multiply the base by the height, 16 × 20. Then remember that the triangle is only half of that rectangle.
Here is a similar problem: a triangle with base 14 cm and height 10 cm. Base times height is 14 × 10 = 140. Half of 140 is 70, so the area is 70 square cm.

steps.text: The area of a triangle is half of its base times its height.
Base times height is 16 × 20 = 320.
Half of 320 is 160. So the area is 160 square cm.

notes.A: 640 comes from doubling 16 × 20 when it should be halved. A triangle is half of the rectangle.
notes.B: 36 comes from adding the base and the height, 16 + 20. For area we multiply them and then take half.
notes.C: 320 is 16 × 20, the area of the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of that.
notes.D: Well done! 16 × 20 = 320, and half of 320 is 160.

hints: This is a perimeter problem about a shape made by joining two triangles. The perimeter is only the outside boundary, so think about which sides end up inside the new figure.
First find the length of one side of a triangle. An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, and its perimeter is 24 cm.

Here is a similar problem. Two equal squares, each with a perimeter of 20 cm, are joined along one full side. Each side is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. The two joined sides are hidden inside, so 8 − 2 = 6 sides are left on the outside. The perimeter is 6 × 5 = 30 cm.

steps.text: Each triangle has 3 equal sides and a perimeter of 24 cm, so each side is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 cm.
The triangles are joined along one full side. Those two sides now lie inside the new figure, so they are not part of its boundary.
The two triangles have 6 sides in all. Taking away the 2 joined sides leaves 4 sides on the outside.
The perimeter of the new figure is 4 × 8 = 32 cm. The trap is to add 24 and 24 without removing the hidden sides.

notes.A: 24 cm is the perimeter of just one triangle. The new figure has 4 outside sides of 8 cm each.
notes.B: 48 cm comes from adding 24 and 24. The two sides that are joined together are inside the figure, so they must be left out.
notes.C: Excellent thinking! Four sides of 8 cm are left on the outside, and 4 × 8 = 32 cm.
notes.D: 40 cm comes from taking away only one hidden side of 8 cm. Each triangle loses a side where they join, so take away 2 sides.

hints: This is an angle problem about an isosceles triangle, which has two equal angles, and the three angles of any triangle add up to 180°. The given angle could be one of the equal pair or the odd one out, so try both cases.
First suppose 57° is one of the two equal angles and find the third angle. Then suppose 57° is the odd angle and share what is left equally between the other two.

Here is a similar problem. One angle of an isosceles triangle is 40°. If 40° is one of the equal pair, the angles are 40°, 40° and 180 − 40 − 40 = 100°. If 40° is the odd one, the other two share 180 − 40 = 140° equally, so each is 70°. So another angle can be 40°, 100° or 70°.

steps.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles, and the three angles add up to 180°. The angle of 57° could be one of the equal pair or the odd one out.
Case one: 57° is one of the equal pair. Then the angles are 57°, 57° and 180 − 57 − 57 = 66°.
Case two: 57° is the odd angle. The other two share 180 − 57 = 123° equally, so each is half of 123°.
Half of 123 is 61.5. Of the choices given, only this one fits, so the other angle can be 61.5°.

notes.A: With 57° and 50°, the third angle would be 180 − 57 − 50 = 73°, and no two angles would be equal. Try both places where 57° can sit.
notes.B: 123° is what the other two angles add up to together, 180 − 57. Share that 123° equally between the two of them.
notes.C: Well done! When 57° is the odd angle, the other two share 123° equally and each is 61.5°.
notes.D: 33° is 90 − 57, which fits a right-angled triangle. With 57° and 33° the third angle is 90°, so no two angles would be equal.

hints: This is about the angles of a triangle. In an equilateral triangle all three angles are equal, and the angles of any triangle add up to the same total.
The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. Think about how to share 180° equally among 3 angles.
Here is a similar problem. A square has four equal angles, and they add up to 360°. Each angle is 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

steps.text: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°.
In an equilateral triangle all three angles are equal, so we share 180° equally among 3 angles.
180 ÷ 3 = 60. So each angle measures 60°.

notes.A: Three angles of 120° would add up to 360°, which is too much. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
notes.B: Great job! 180° shared equally among 3 angles gives 60° each.
notes.C: Three angles of 45° add up to only 135°. Share 180° equally among the 3 angles.
notes.D: 90° is each angle of a square. Three angles of 90° would add up to 270°, which is too much for a triangle.

hints: This is a perimeter problem. Perimeter is the total distance around a shape, and an equilateral triangle has three equal sides.
All three sides are 7 cm long. Add the three sides together, or multiply the side by 3.
Here is a similar problem: an equilateral triangle with side 9 cm. Its three sides are all 9 cm, so the perimeter is 3 × 9 = 27 cm.

steps.text: An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, so each side is 7 cm.
The perimeter is the sum of all the sides, 7 + 7 + 7, which is 3 × 7 = 21. So the perimeter is 21 cm.

notes.A: You got it! Three sides of 7 cm make 3 × 7 = 21 cm.
notes.B: 14 cm counts only two sides, 7 + 7. A triangle has three sides.
notes.C: 28 cm is 4 × 7, which would be a shape with four sides, like a square. A triangle has three sides.
notes.D: 49 comes from 7 × 7, multiplying the side by itself. For perimeter, add the three sides.

hints: This is a missing-angle problem. The three angles of any triangle always add up to the same total.
The three angles add up to 180°. Start by adding the two angles you know, 35° and 65°.
Here is a similar problem. Two angles of a triangle are 50° and 70°. Together they make 50 + 70 = 120°. The third angle is 180 − 120 = 60°.

steps.text: The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
The two known angles add up to 35 + 65 = 100°.
The third angle is what is left: 180 − 100 = 80. So the third angle is 80°.

notes.B: With 110° the three angles would add up to 210°, which is too much. Add the two known angles first, then take the sum from 180°.
notes.C: With 90° the three angles would add up to 190°, a little more than 180°. Take the sum of the two known angles from 180°.
notes.D: 100° is the sum of the two known angles, 35 + 65. Take that away from 180° to find the third angle.

hints: This asks you to name a triangle by its angles. A triangle is acute-angled if all its angles are less than 90°, right-angled if one angle is exactly 90°, and obtuse-angled if one angle is more than 90°. You need all three angles to decide.
The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°. First find the third angle by adding 28° and 45° and taking the sum away from 180°.

Here is a similar problem. Two angles of a triangle are 60° and 50°. Together they make 110°, so the third angle is 180 − 110 = 70°. All three angles are less than 90°, so that triangle is acute-angled.

steps.text: The two known angles add up to 28 + 45 = 73°.
The three angles add up to 180°, so the third angle is 180 − 73 = 107°.
107° is more than 90°, so it is an obtuse angle.
A triangle with one obtuse angle is an obtuse-angled triangle.

notes.A: The two given angles are acute, but the third angle must be checked too. It is 107°, which is more than 90°.
notes.B: Well done! The third angle is 107°, which is more than 90°, so the triangle is obtuse-angled.
notes.C: An isosceles triangle needs two equal angles. The angles here are 28°, 45° and 107°, which are all different.
notes.D: Two angles are enough, because the third can be found by taking their sum away from 180°. Find it and see how big it is.

hints: This is about which three lengths can make a triangle. The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side, or they cannot meet.
For each set, add the two shorter lengths and compare the sum with the longest length. Start with 2 cm, 5 cm and 9 cm.

Here is a similar problem. Can 3 cm, 4 cm and 9 cm make a triangle? 3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 9, so they cannot. Can 4 cm, 7 cm and 10 cm make a triangle? 4 + 7 = 11, which is more than 10, so they can.

steps.text: Three lengths make a triangle only when the two shorter sides together are longer than the longest side.
For 2 cm, 5 cm and 9 cm: 2 + 5 = 7, which is less than 9, so the short sides cannot meet.
For 1 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm: 1 + 5 = 6, which is only equal to the longest side, so the short sides would lie flat along it.
For 6 cm, 8 cm and 12 cm: 6 + 8 = 14, which is more than 12. So the lengths that can make a triangle are 6 cm, 8 cm and 12 cm.

notes.A: Here 2 + 5 = 7, which is shorter than 9, so the two short sides cannot reach each other. Look for a set where the two shorter sides add up to more than the longest.
notes.B: You got it! 6 + 8 = 14 is more than 12, so these three sides can meet to make a triangle.
notes.C: Here 1 + 5 = 6, exactly the same as the longest side, so the short sides would lie flat along it. The sum must be more than the longest side.
notes.D: Not every set here can make a triangle. Test each one by adding the two shorter sides and comparing with the longest.

hints: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides, and so it also has two equal angles. Look for a set of angles with a matching pair.
Go through each set and see whether any angle appears twice. Start with 30°, 60° and 90°.

Here is a similar problem. Which is isosceles: a triangle with angles 50°, 60°, 70° or one with angles 40°, 40°, 100°? The first has three different angles. The second has two angles of 40°, and 40 + 40 + 100 = 180, so the second one is isosceles.

steps.text: An isosceles triangle has two equal angles.
In 30°, 60°, 90°, in 40°, 120°, 20° and in 50°, 90°, 40°, all three angles are different.
In the remaining set two angles are both 75°, and the three angles add up to 180°.
So the angles of an isosceles triangle are 30°, 75°, 75°.

notes.A: 30°, 60° and 90° are all different, so this triangle is scalene. Look for a set with two equal angles.
notes.B: 40°, 120° and 20° are all different, so this triangle is scalene. Look for a set with two equal angles.
notes.C: 50°, 90° and 40° are all different, so this triangle is scalene. Look for a set with two equal angles.
notes.D: Great job! Two of the angles are both 75°, and that matching pair makes the triangle isosceles.

hints: This is a missing-angle problem in a right-angled triangle. One angle is 90°, and the three angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
Since one angle is 90°, the two acute angles share the other 90° between them. Take the acute angle you know away from 90°.
Here is a similar problem. One acute angle of a right-angled triangle is 35°. The two acute angles add up to 90°, so the other is 90 − 35 = 55°. Check: 90 + 35 + 55 = 180.

steps.text: A right-angled triangle has one angle of 90°. The three angles add up to 180°, so the two acute angles together make 180 − 90 = 90°.
One acute angle is 27°, so the other is 90 − 27 = 63.
So the other acute angle is 63°.

notes.A: 73° is 10° too big: 27 + 73 = 100, but the two acute angles must add up to 90°. Try the subtraction 90 − 27 again.
notes.B: Well done! The two acute angles add up to 90°, and 90 − 27 = 63°.
notes.C: The two acute angles are equal only when each is 45°. Here they must add up to 90°, so find 90 − 27.
notes.D: 90° is the right angle itself. The question asks for the other acute angle, which is less than 90°.

hints: This triangle is both right-angled and isosceles. So one angle is 90° and the other two angles are equal.
The three angles add up to 180°. First take away the right angle to find what the two equal angles share.
Here is a similar problem. An isosceles triangle has one angle of 110° and two equal angles. The two equal angles share 180 − 110 = 70°, so each one is 70 ÷ 2 = 35°.

steps.text: One angle is 90°. The three angles add up to 180°, so the other two together make 180 − 90 = 90°.
The other two angles are equal, so each is half of 90°.
So each of the equal angles measures 45°.

notes.A: 90° is the right angle. Two angles of 90° would use up all 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle.
notes.B: Excellent thinking! The two equal angles share 90°, so each is 45°.
notes.C: 60° is each angle of an equilateral triangle. Here one angle is 90°, so the other two share only 90°.
notes.D: Two angles of 40° with 90° add up to 170°, which is 10° short. Share the remaining 90° equally.

hints: Two things must both be true here. Obtuse-angled means one angle is more than 90°, and scalene means all three angles are different.
First set aside any set that has no angle bigger than 90°. Then, in the sets that are left, see whether all three angles are different.

Here is a similar problem. Which is an acute-angled isosceles triangle: 70°, 70°, 40° or 100°, 40°, 40°? Both have two equal angles, so both are isosceles. Only in the first are all the angles less than 90°, so 70°, 70°, 40° is the acute-angled isosceles triangle.

steps.text: An obtuse-angled triangle has one angle more than 90°. A scalene triangle has three different angles.
The sets 30°, 60°, 90° and 50°, 90°, 40° each have a largest angle of exactly 90°, so they are right-angled, not obtuse-angled.
The set 150°, 15°, 15° has an obtuse angle, but two of its angles are equal, so it is isosceles, not scalene.
In the last set, 120° is more than 90° and all three angles are different. So the obtuse-angled scalene triangle is 40°, 120°, 20°.

notes.A: The largest angle here is exactly 90°, which makes the triangle right-angled. An obtuse-angled triangle needs an angle bigger than 90°.
notes.B: The largest angle here is exactly 90°, which makes the triangle right-angled. An obtuse-angled triangle needs an angle bigger than 90°.
notes.C: Well done! 120° is more than 90°, and 40°, 120° and 20° are all different, so it is obtuse-angled and scalene.
notes.D: This set does have an obtuse angle of 150°, but two angles are both 15°, which makes it isosceles. Scalene needs three different angles.

hints: This is about an exterior angle of a triangle. An exterior angle and the interior angle next to it lie on a straight line, so together they make 180°.
First find the third interior angle. The three interior angles add up to 180°, so take 55° and 70° away from 180°.

Here is a similar problem. Two interior angles of a triangle are 40° and 60°. The third interior angle is 180 − 40 − 60 = 80°. The exterior angle next to it is 180 − 80 = 100°. Notice that this is the same as 40 + 60.

steps.text: The three interior angles add up to 180°, so the third interior angle is 180 − 55 − 70 = 55°.
The exterior angle and the third interior angle lie on a straight line, so together they make 180°.
180 − 55 = 125, which is the same as 55 + 70. So the exterior angle is 125°.

notes.A: 180° is the total of the exterior angle and the interior angle beside it. Take the third interior angle away from 180°.
notes.B: 55° is the third interior angle. The question asks for the exterior angle beside it, which is 180 − 55.
notes.C: Great job! The third interior angle is 55°, and the exterior angle beside it is 180 − 55 = 125°.
notes.D: 110° is 180 − 70, the exterior angle beside the 70° angle. The one asked for is beside the third angle, which is 55°.

hints: This uses a fact about triangles: an exterior angle is equal to the sum of the two interior angles opposite it, the ones that are not next to it.
The two opposite interior angles add up to 130°. One of them is 50°, so think about what must be added to 50° to make 130°.
Here is a similar problem. An exterior angle of a triangle is 110°, and one of the opposite interior angles is 45°. The two opposite interior angles add up to 110°, so the other is 110 − 45 = 65°.

steps.text: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles. So those two angles add up to 130°.
One of them is 50°, so the other is 130 − 50 = 80.
Check: the interior angle beside the exterior angle is 180 − 130 = 50°, and 50 + 50 + 80 = 180. So the other angle is 80°.

notes.A: 50° is the interior angle beside the exterior angle, 180 − 130. The question asks for the other opposite angle, which is 130 − 50.
notes.B: With 50° and 60° the two opposite angles add up to 110°, not 130°. Find 130 − 50.
notes.C: 130° is the exterior angle itself. It is shared between the two opposite interior angles, so take 50° away from it.
notes.D: You got it! The two opposite interior angles add up to 130°, and 130 − 50 = 80°.

hints: This is a missing-angle problem. An isosceles triangle has two equal base angles and one vertex angle, and the three angles add up to 180°.
Both base angles are 70°. First add the two base angles together.
Here is a similar problem. Each base angle of an isosceles triangle is 65°. The two base angles make 65 + 65 = 130°. The vertex angle is 180 − 130 = 50°.

steps.text: The two base angles are 70° each, so together they make 70 + 70 = 140°.
The three angles add up to 180°, so the vertex angle is 180 − 140 = 40.
So the vertex angle is 40°.

notes.A: That would make all three angles 70°, which add up to 210°. Take the two base angles away from 180°.
notes.B: 110° comes from taking away only one base angle, 180 − 70. There are two base angles of 70° each.
notes.C: With 80° the three angles would add up to 220°. The two base angles make 140°, so find 180 − 140.
notes.D: Well done! The base angles make 140° together, and 180 − 140 = 40°.

hints: This is a missing-angle problem. An isosceles triangle has one vertex angle and two equal base angles, and the three angles add up to 180°.
First take the vertex angle of 50° away from 180° to find what the two base angles share.
Here is a similar problem. The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is 40°. The two base angles share 180 − 40 = 140°. They are equal, so each one is 140 ÷ 2 = 70°.

steps.text: The three angles add up to 180°, so the two base angles together make 180 − 50 = 130°.
The base angles are equal, so each is half of 130°.
So each base angle is 65°.

notes.A: 130° is what the two base angles make together, 180 − 50. Share it equally between the two.
notes.B: Three angles of 50° add up to only 150°. Take 50° from 180° and share what is left between the two base angles.
notes.C: Two angles of 55° with 50° add up to 160°, which is 20° short. Take 50 from 180 and halve what is left.
notes.D: Great job! The base angles share 130° equally, so each is 65°.

hints: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves of a shape match exactly. For a triangle, think about which sides would have to land on each other.
Remember what scalene means: all three sides have different lengths. Imagine folding the triangle through each corner and ask whether the two halves would match.

Here is a similar problem. How many axes of symmetry does a triangle with exactly two equal sides have? Folding through the corner where the two equal sides meet lays one equal side on the other, so that fold line is an axis of symmetry. A fold through either of the other corners would put a longer side on a shorter one. So it has 1 axis of symmetry.

steps.text: An axis of symmetry is a fold line that makes the two halves match exactly.
In a triangle, a fold through a corner makes matching halves only when the two sides that meet at that corner are equal.
A scalene triangle has three different sides, so no two sides are equal and no fold gives matching halves. So a scalene triangle has 0 axes of symmetry.

notes.A: Well done! With three different sides, no fold can make the two halves match.
notes.B: One axis of symmetry belongs to an isosceles triangle, which has two equal sides. A scalene triangle has no equal sides.
notes.C: Three axes of symmetry belong to an equilateral triangle, where all the sides are equal. In a scalene triangle all the sides are different.
notes.D: Think about whether a scalene triangle has any equal sides that could fold onto each other. Without a pair of equal sides there is no fold line.

hints: This is a perimeter problem. The perimeter of a shape is the total distance around it.
Add the three sides. Start with 8 + 11, then add 15 to that.
Here is a similar problem. A triangle has sides 6 cm, 9 cm and 13 cm. 6 + 9 = 15, and 15 + 13 = 28. Its perimeter is 28 cm.

steps.text: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides.
First add two of the sides: 8 + 11 = 19.
Then add the third side: 19 + 15 = 34. So the perimeter is 34 cm.

notes.A: 1320 comes from multiplying the three sides, 8 × 11 × 15. For perimeter we add the sides.
notes.B: You got it! 8 + 11 + 15 = 34 cm.
notes.C: 24 cm is 10 too few. Add again carefully: 8 + 11 = 19, and then add 15.
notes.D: 44 cm is 10 too many. Add again carefully: 8 + 11 = 19, and then add 15.

hints: This is a perimeter problem worked backwards. The perimeter is the total of all three sides, and you know two of them.
First add the two sides you know, 12 cm and 9 cm. The third side is whatever is still needed to reach 36 cm.
Here is a similar problem. The perimeter of a triangle is 40 cm and two sides are 14 cm and 10 cm. The two known sides add up to 14 + 10 = 24 cm. The third side is 40 − 24 = 16 cm.

steps.text: The perimeter is the sum of the three sides, so the three sides add up to 36 cm.
The two known sides add up to 12 + 9 = 21 cm.
The third side is what is left: 36 − 21 = 15. So the third side is 15 cm.

notes.A: 17 cm is a little too much: 12 + 9 + 17 = 38. Add the two known sides first, then take that from 36.
notes.B: 21 cm is the sum of the two known sides, 12 + 9. Take it away from the perimeter of 36 cm.
notes.C: 3 cm is the difference between the two known sides, 12 − 9. The three sides must add up to 36 cm.
notes.D: Well done! 12 + 9 = 21, and 36 − 21 = 15 cm.

hints: This is an area problem for a right-angled triangle. The two legs meet at the right angle, so one is the base and the other is the height. The triangle is half of the rectangle made with them.
Multiply the two legs, 6 × 8, to get the area of the rectangle. Then remember that the triangle is half of it.
Here is a similar problem. A right-angled triangle has legs of 10 cm and 6 cm. The rectangle made with them has area 10 × 6 = 60 cm². The triangle is half of that, so its area is 30 cm².

steps.text: The legs meet at the right angle, so one leg is the base and the other is the height.
Base times height is 6 × 8 = 48.
The triangle is half of that rectangle: 48 ÷ 2 = 24. So the area is 24 cm².

notes.A: Great job! 6 × 8 = 48, and half of 48 is 24 cm².
notes.B: 14 comes from adding the legs, 6 + 8. For area, multiply them and then take half.
notes.C: 10 cm is the length of the third side of this triangle, not its area. Multiply the two legs and take half.
notes.D: 48 cm² is 6 × 8, the area of the whole rectangle. The triangle is half of that.

hints: This is about the meaning of a word. The word median is related to the word middle.
Picture a line drawn from one corner of a triangle across to the opposite side. Think about which special point on that side would cut the side into two equal parts.
Here is an example. In triangle PQR, side QR is 10 cm long. The point M on QR is 5 cm from Q and 5 cm from R. The line from P to M is a median of the triangle, because M cuts QR into two equal parts.

steps.text: A median starts at a vertex of the triangle and goes across to the opposite side.
It meets that side exactly in the middle, cutting it into two equal parts. The point in the middle of a side is called its midpoint.
So a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

notes.A: A line to just any point of the opposite side is not always a median. A median goes to one special point, the one that cuts the side into two equal parts.
notes.B: A side has no highest point that stays the same when the triangle is turned around. Look for the point that cuts the side into two equal parts.
notes.C: Well done! A median goes to the midpoint, the point that cuts the opposite side into two equal parts.
notes.D: The end points of the opposite side are the other two corners, so that line would just be a side of the triangle. A median goes to the middle of the side.

hints: A median joins a vertex of a triangle to the middle of the opposite side. Think about how many different vertices a median can start from.
Count the vertices of a triangle. One median can be drawn from each vertex.
Here is a similar problem. How many diagonals does a rectangle have? A diagonal joins two opposite corners. A rectangle has 4 corners, which make 2 pairs of opposite corners, so it has 2 diagonals.

steps.text: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
A triangle has 3 vertices, and each vertex has exactly one opposite side, so each vertex gives one median.
So a triangle has 3 medians.

notes.A: 6 counts each median twice. Each of the 3 vertices gives just one median.
notes.B: Two medians come from two of the vertices. There is one more vertex, and it has a median too.
notes.C: One median comes from one vertex. The other two vertices have medians as well.
notes.D: You got it! One median from each of the 3 vertices makes 3 medians.

hints: This is a perimeter problem worked backwards. An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, and the perimeter is the total of all three.
The three equal sides add up to 45 cm. Think about how to share 45 cm equally among 3 sides.
Here is a similar problem. The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 36 cm. Its three sides are equal, so each side is 36 ÷ 3 = 12 cm.

steps.text: An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, and together they make the perimeter of 45 cm.
Share 45 cm equally among the 3 sides: 45 ÷ 3 = 15.
So each side is 15 cm long.

notes.A: 135 cm comes from multiplying 45 by 3. The perimeter is already the total of the three sides, so divide it by 3.
notes.B: Well done! 45 cm shared equally among 3 sides gives 15 cm each.
notes.C: 9 cm comes from dividing 45 by 5. A triangle has 3 sides, so divide by 3.
notes.D: 22.5 cm comes from dividing 45 by 2. An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, so divide by 3.

hints: This is a weight conversion. The whole-number part of the decimal is the kilograms, and the part after the point is a fraction of a kilogram that must be changed into grams.
Remember that 1 kg = 1000 g. Split 11.11 kg into its whole kilograms and 0.11 kg, then change 0.11 kg into grams by multiplying by 1000.
Here is a similar problem: write 5.25 kg in kilograms and grams. 5.25 kg is 5 kg and 0.25 kg. 0.25 × 1000 = 250, so 0.25 kg is 250 g. So 5.25 kg is 5 kg 250 g.

steps.text: Split 11.11 kg into 11 kg and 0.11 kg.
So 11.11 kg is equal to 11 kg 110 gm.

notes.A: 11 g is only 0.011 kg, so this weight is 11.011 kg. The part after the point is 0.11 kg, and 0.11 × 1000 gives the grams.
notes.B: 1111 g is only 1.111 kg, because 1000 g make 1 kg. 11.11 kg is more than 11 whole kilograms.
notes.C: Well done! 0.11 kg is 0.11 × 1000 = 110 g, so 11.11 kg is 11 kg 110 g.
notes.D: A milligram is far smaller than a gram, so 11 mg is a tiny amount. Change 0.11 kg into grams by multiplying by 1000.

hints: This is a rate problem with a unit change. Find how many sheets make each centimetre of thickness, and put the whole thickness of the stack into centimetres.
First change 1 metre 22.5 cm into centimetres. Then find how many sheets are in 1 cm of the stack, using the fact that 500 sheets are 5 cm thick.

Here is a similar problem. A pack of 200 cards is 4 cm thick, and a pile of the same cards is 1 metre 10 cm high. The pile is 100 + 10 = 110 cm high. Each centimetre holds 200 ÷ 4 = 50 cards. So the pile has 110 × 50 = 5500 cards.

steps.text: 1 metre is 100 cm, so the stack is 100 + 22.5 = 122.5 cm thick.
500 sheets are 5 cm thick, so 1 cm holds 500 ÷ 5 = 100 sheets.
The stack is 122.5 cm thick, so it has 122.5 × 100 = 12250 sheets.
So there were 12250 sheets in all.

notes.A: 10250 sheets would make a stack only 102.5 cm thick. Check the thickness: 1 metre 22.5 cm is 100 + 22.5 = 122.5 cm.
notes.B: Great job! The stack is 122.5 cm thick with 100 sheets in every centimetre, which makes 12250 sheets.
notes.C: 17750 sheets would make a stack 177.5 cm thick, which is too much. The stack is 122.5 cm, with 100 sheets in every centimetre.
notes.D: 10750 sheets would make a stack only 107.5 cm thick. The stack is 122.5 cm thick, with 100 sheets in every centimetre.

hints: This is a length sum with mixed units. Before adding, every length has to be in the same unit, and the choices are all in centimetres.
Change 2 m into centimetres and 2 dm into centimetres. Remember that 1 m = 100 cm and 1 dm = 10 cm.
Here is a similar problem: 3 m + 4 dm + 12 cm. 3 m is 300 cm and 4 dm is 40 cm. 300 + 40 + 12 = 352 cm.

steps.text: 1 m is 100 cm, so 2 m is 2 × 100 = 200 cm.
1 dm is 10 cm, so 2 dm is 2 × 10 = 20 cm.
Now add the three lengths: 200 + 20 + 15 = 235. So the total is 235 cm.

notes.A: 2215 comes from writing 2, 2 and 15 side by side. Each length must be changed into centimetres first, and then they are added.
notes.B: 225 cm is 10 cm short. Check the 2 dm: one decimetre is 10 cm, so 2 dm is 20 cm.
notes.C: You got it! 200 cm + 20 cm + 15 cm = 235 cm.
notes.D: 212 cm is too small. 2 m gives 200 cm, 2 dm gives 20 cm, and there are 15 cm more to add.

hints: This is a weight conversion. The kilograms stay as the whole-number part, and the grams must be written as a fraction of a kilogram after the decimal point.
1 kg = 1000 g, so to change grams into kilograms we divide by 1000. Work out 70 ÷ 1000 first, taking care with the zeros.
Here is a similar problem: write 4 kg 30 g in kilograms. 30 g is 30 ÷ 1000 = 0.03 kg. Adding the 4 kg gives 4 + 0.03 = 4.03 kg.

steps.text: Take care with the place: 0.70 kg would be 700 g, so 70 g must be written as 0.07 kg.
Add this to the 7 kg: 7 + 0.07 = 7.07. So 7 kg 70 gm is 7.07 kg.

notes.A: 7.70 kg is 7 kg 700 g, because 0.70 kg is 700 g. 70 g is 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.07 kg.
notes.B: 70.7 kg is more than 70 kg, far heavier than 7 kg 70 g. Keep 7 as the whole number and write the grams after the point.
notes.C: Well done! 70 g is 0.07 kg, so 7 kg 70 g is 7.07 kg.
notes.D: 7.007 kg is 7 kg 7 g, because 0.007 kg is 7 g. 70 g is 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.07 kg.

hints: This is a weight conversion. The whole-number part of the decimal is the kilograms, and the part after the point is a fraction of a kilogram that must be changed into grams.
Remember that 1 kg = 1000 g. Split 8.05 kg into its whole kilograms and 0.05 kg, then multiply 0.05 by 1000 to get grams.
Here is a similar problem: write 3.08 kg in kilograms and grams. 3.08 kg is 3 kg and 0.08 kg. 0.08 × 1000 = 80, so 0.08 kg is 80 g. So 3.08 kg is 3 kg 80 g.

steps.text: Split 8.05 kg into 8 kg and 0.05 kg.
So 8.05 kg is the decimal way of writing 8 kg 50 gm.

notes.A: 500 g is 0.5 kg, so 8 kg 500 g would be written 8.5 kg. Here the part after the point is 0.05 kg.
notes.B: Great job! 0.05 kg is 0.05 × 1000 = 50 g, so 8.05 kg is 8 kg 50 g.
notes.C: 5 g is 0.005 kg, so 8 kg 5 g would be written 8.005 kg. Change 0.05 kg into grams by multiplying by 1000.
notes.D: 805 g is less than 1 kg; it is 0.805 kg. 8.05 kg is more than 8 whole kilograms.

hints: This is a multiplication problem with a unit change at the end. You need the number of notebooks, then the total thickness, and then the same unit as the choices.
A dozen is 12. First find how many notebooks there are in twelve dozens.

Here is a similar problem. Five dozens of books are piled up and each book is 4 mm thick. There are 5 × 12 = 60 books. The pile is 60 × 4 = 240 mm high. Since 10 mm make 1 cm, the pile is 240 ÷ 10 = 24 cm high.

steps.text: A dozen is 12, so twelve dozens is 12 × 12 = 144 notebooks.
Each notebook is 5 mm thick, so the pile is 144 × 5 = 720 mm high.
10 mm make 1 cm, so 720 mm is 720 ÷ 10 = 72 cm.
So the height of the pile is 72 cm.

notes.A: Well done! 144 notebooks of 5 mm each make 720 mm, which is 72 cm.
notes.B: 620 mm is close, but 144 × 5 = 720 mm. Try the multiplication again, then change the answer into centimetres.
notes.C: 7 m 20 cm is 720 cm, which is ten times too tall. The pile is 720 mm high, and 10 mm make 1 cm.
notes.D: One of the choices does match. The pile is 720 mm high, so change that into centimetres and look again.

hints: This is a weight conversion. The kilograms are the whole-number part, and the grams become the part after the decimal point once they are changed into kilograms.
There are 1000 g in 1 kg, so divide the grams by 1000. Find 70 ÷ 1000 first and watch where the digit 7 lands.
Here is a similar problem: write 9 kg 40 g as a decimal. 40 g is 40 ÷ 1000 = 0.04 kg. Adding the 9 kg gives 9 + 0.04 = 9.04 kg.

steps.text: There are 1000 g in 1 kg, so 70 g is 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.07 kg.
Add the whole kilograms: 7 + 0.07 = 7.07.
So 7 kg 70 gram written as a decimal is 7.07 Kg.

notes.A: 7.007 kg is 7 kg 7 g, because 0.007 kg is 7 g. 70 g is 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.07 kg.
notes.B: 700.7 kg is hundreds of kilograms, far heavier than 7 kg 70 g. Keep 7 as the whole number and write the grams after the point.
notes.C: You got it! 70 g is 0.07 kg, so 7 kg 70 g is 7.07 kg.
notes.D: 7.70 kg is 7 kg 700 g, because 0.70 kg is 700 g. 70 g is 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.07 kg.

hints: This is a sharing problem with two different units. Before dividing, the ribbon and the pieces must be measured in the same unit.
Change 6.9 metres into centimetres first. Remember that 1 m = 100 cm.
Here is a similar problem. A rope is 4.8 metres long and is cut into pieces of 4 cm each. 4.8 m is 4.8 × 100 = 480 cm. 480 ÷ 4 = 120, so 120 pieces can be cut.

steps.text: Each piece is 3 cm long, so the number of pieces is 690 ÷ 3 = 230.
So 230 pieces can be cut from the ribbon.

notes.A: 23 comes from 69 ÷ 3. But 6.9 m is 690 cm, not 69 cm, so divide 690 by 3.
notes.B: 2.3 comes from dividing 6.9 by 3 without changing the units. Change 6.9 m into 690 cm first.
notes.C: Well done! 6.9 m is 690 cm, and 690 ÷ 3 = 230 pieces.
notes.D: 2300 is ten times too many. 6.9 m is 690 cm, and 690 ÷ 3 gives the number of pieces.

hints: This is a sharing problem with two different units. Before dividing, the oil and the bottle must be measured in the same unit.
Change 2.5 litres into millilitres first. Remember that 1 litre = 1000 ml.
Here is a similar problem. A cup holds 250 ml. How many cups are needed for 1.5 litres of juice? 1.5 litres is 1.5 × 1000 = 1500 ml. 1500 ÷ 250 = 6, so 6 cups are needed.

steps.text: 1 litre is 1000 ml, so 2.5 litres is 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 ml.
Each bottle holds 125 ml, so the number of bottles is 2500 ÷ 125. Since 125 × 20 = 2500, this is 20.
So 20 bottles are needed.

notes.A: 200 bottles would hold 200 × 125 = 25000 ml, which is 25 litres. 2.5 litres is only 2500 ml.
notes.B: 25 bottles would hold 25 × 125 = 3125 ml, which is more than 2500 ml. Divide 2500 by 125.
notes.C: Great job! 2.5 litres is 2500 ml, and 2500 ÷ 125 = 20 bottles.
notes.D: 100 bottles would hold 100 × 125 = 12500 ml, which is 12.5 litres. Only 2500 ml of oil is needed.

hints: This is about the ladder of metric units of length: kilometre, hectometre, decametre, metre, decimetre, centimetre, millimetre. Each unit is 10 times as long as the one after it.
Find decametre and decimetre on the ladder and count the steps between them. Going to a smaller unit means multiplying by 10 for every step.

Here is a similar problem: how do we convert metre to millimetre? On the ladder, the steps are metre to decimetre, decimetre to centimetre, and centimetre to millimetre, which is 3 steps down. Each step multiplies by 10, and 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000. So we multiply by 1000.

steps.text: One decametre is 10 metres.
One metre is 10 decimetres.
So one decametre is 10 × 10 = 100 decimetres.
A decimetre is the smaller unit, so there are more of them. To convert decametre to decimetre, multiply by 100.

notes.A: Well done! Decametre to metre is 10 times, and metre to decimetre is 10 times again, so multiply by 100.
notes.B: The number 100 fits, but dividing is for changing to a bigger unit. A decimetre is smaller than a decametre, so there are more of them.
notes.C: Dividing is for changing to a bigger unit, and decimetre is the smaller one. Decametre and decimetre are also only 2 steps apart on the ladder.
notes.D: Multiplying by 10 takes you just one step, from decametre to metre. Decimetre is one step further down.

hints: This is a weight conversion. The whole-number part of the decimal is the kilograms, and the part after the point is a fraction of a kilogram that must be changed into grams.
Remember that 1 kg = 1000 g. Split off the part after the decimal point, 0.02 kg, and multiply it by 1000 to get grams.
Here is a similar problem: write 6.04 kg in kilograms and grams. 6.04 kg is 6 kg and 0.04 kg. 0.04 × 1000 = 40, so 0.04 kg is 40 g. So 6.04 kg is 6 kg 40 g.

steps.text: Split 37.02 kg into 37 kg and 0.02 kg.

notes.A: You got it! 0.02 kg is 0.02 × 1000 = 20 g, so 37.02 kg is 37 kg 20 g.
notes.B: 2 g is 0.002 kg, so 37 kg 2 g would be written 37.002 kg. Change 0.02 kg into grams by multiplying by 1000.
notes.C: The fraction 2/100 does match 0.02, but the unit here is grams, and 37.02 kg is far more than about 37 g. Keep 37 kg and change 0.02 kg into grams.
notes.D: 3702 g is only 3.702 kg, because 1000 g make 1 kg. 37.02 kg is 37 whole kilograms and a little more.

hints: This is a length sum with mixed units. Before adding, every length has to be in the same unit, and the question asks for metres.
Change 4 km into metres and 400 cm into metres. Remember that 1 km = 1000 m and 100 cm = 1 m.
Here is a similar problem: 3 km + 20 m + 500 cm in metres. 3 km is 3000 m, and 500 cm is 500 ÷ 100 = 5 m. 3000 + 20 + 5 = 3025 metres.

steps.text: 100 cm make 1 m, so 400 cm is 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m.
Now add the three lengths: 4000 + 40 + 4 = 4044. So the total is 4044 metres.

notes.A: 40404 comes from writing the numbers side by side. Each length must be changed into metres first, and then they are added.
notes.B: 4.404 is far too small, since 4 km alone is 4000 m. Change each part into metres and add.
notes.C: 4440 comes from counting 400 cm as 400 m. 100 cm make 1 m, so 400 cm is only 4 m.
notes.D: Well done! 4000 m + 40 m + 4 m = 4044 m.

hints: This is a cutting-into-equal-pieces problem, so it needs division. The ribbon is in metres and the pieces are in centimetres, so they must be put into the same unit first.
Start by changing the ribbon's length into centimetres. There are 100 cm in 1 m.
Here is a similar problem. A wire is 7.5 metres long and is cut into pieces of 5 cm each. 7.5 m is 7.5 × 100 = 750 cm. 750 ÷ 5 = 150, so 150 pieces can be cut.

steps.text: There are 100 cm in 1 m, so the ribbon is 6.9 × 100 = 690 cm long.
Each piece is 3 cm long, so divide: 690 ÷ 3 = 230.
So 230 pieces can be cut from the ribbon.

notes.A: 3.9 comes from subtracting, 6.9 − 3. We are cutting equal pieces, so change the ribbon into centimetres and divide.
notes.B: Great job! The ribbon is 690 cm long, and 690 ÷ 3 = 230 pieces.
notes.C: 23 comes from 69 ÷ 3. But 6.9 m is 690 cm, not 69 cm, so divide 690 by 3.
notes.D: 2.3 comes from dividing 6.9 by 3 without changing the units. Change 6.9 m into 690 cm first.

hints: This is about the ladder of metric units of length: kilometre, hectometre, decametre, metre, decimetre, centimetre, millimetre. Each unit is 10 times as long as the one after it.
Go through metres. First change 5 hm into metres, remembering that 1 hm = 100 m. Then change the metres into decimetres.
Here is a similar problem: 3 dam is how many cm? 1 dam is 10 m, so 3 dam is 30 m. 1 m is 100 cm, so 30 m is 30 × 100 = 3000 cm.

steps.text: 1 hm is 100 m, so 5 hm is 5 × 100 = 500 m.
So 5 hm = 5000 dm.

notes.A: 500 is the number of metres in 5 hm. One more step is needed, because each metre is 10 dm.
notes.B: 50000 is ten times too many. Hectometre to decimetre is 3 steps down the ladder, so multiply by 1000.
notes.C: Well done! 5 hm is 500 m, and 500 m is 5000 dm.
notes.D: 50 is the number of decametres in 5 hm. Keep going down the ladder to metres and then to decimetres.

hints: This is a weight conversion from a smaller unit to a bigger unit. When the unit gets bigger, the number gets smaller.
Remember that 1 kg = 1000 g. To change grams into kilograms, divide by 1000.
Here is a similar problem: 300 g is how many kg? Divide by 1000: 300 ÷ 1000 = 0.3. So 300 g is 0.3 kg.

steps.text: 1 kg is 1000 g, so to change grams into kilograms we divide by 1000.
So 800 gm = 0.8 kg.

notes.A: 80 kg would be 80000 g. Going from grams to kilograms makes the number smaller, so divide 800 by 1000.
notes.B: 0.08 kg is only 80 g. Dividing 800 by 1000 moves the digits three places to the right.
notes.C: 8 kg would be 8000 g. It comes from dividing by 100, but there are 1000 g in 1 kg.
notes.D: You got it! 800 ÷ 1000 = 0.8, so 800 g is 0.8 kg.

hints: This is a length conversion from a smaller unit to a bigger unit. When the unit gets bigger, the number gets smaller.
Remember that 1 km = 1000 m. To change metres into kilometres, divide by 1000.
Here is a similar problem: 50 m is how many km? Divide by 1000: 50 ÷ 1000 = 0.05. So 50 m is 0.05 km.

steps.text: 1 km is 1000 m, so to change metres into kilometres we divide by 1000.
Dividing by 1000 moves each digit three places to the right, so 80 ÷ 1000 = 0.08.

notes.A: Well done! 80 ÷ 1000 = 0.08, so 80 m is 0.08 km.
notes.B: 0.008 km is only 8 m. Divide 80 by 1000 and place the digit 8 carefully.
notes.C: 8 km would be 8000 m. Going from metres to kilometres makes the number much smaller, so divide 80 by 1000.
notes.D: 0.8 km is 800 m. It comes from dividing by 100, but there are 1000 m in 1 km.

hints: This is a weight conversion from a smaller unit to a bigger unit. When the unit gets bigger, the number gets smaller.
Remember that 1 g = 1000 mg. To change milligrams into grams, divide by 1000.
Here is a similar problem: 7 mg is how many g? Divide by 1000: 7 ÷ 1000 = 0.007. So 7 mg is 0.007 g.

steps.text: 1 g is 1000 mg, so to change milligrams into grams we divide by 1000.
Dividing by 1000 moves the digit three places to the right, so 5 ÷ 1000 = 0.005.

notes.A: Great job! 5 ÷ 1000 = 0.005, so 5 mg is 0.005 g.
notes.B: 0.5 g is 500 mg. It comes from dividing by 10, but there are 1000 mg in 1 g.
notes.C: 0.05 g is 50 mg. It comes from dividing by 100, but there are 1000 mg in 1 g.
